The demonstration is an HR agent filing a leave request that stops short of the write: the approval gate is enforced by a **single-use token from a CSPRNG**, not by an instruction in the prompt — you can talk the agent into writing, but not into producing a token that was never issued. A scenario runs through the service's real composition root; failures are injected at the tool seam, so a degradation scenario takes the same code path as a real timeout.

repos.name: AgentHelm
repos.oneLiner: A web cockpit for coding agents: one GUI instead of four terminals, with a permission gate and an audit of every decision.
repos.summary: Runs coding-agent sessions (Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Gemini CLI and any agent that speaks {{term:acp|Agent Client Protocol}}) from the browser rather than from a terminal. The core is the Bridge process — an ASP.NET Core Minimal API with 32 endpoints — which starts the agent as a subprocess, talks to it over JSON-RPC on stdio and intercepts every tool-use request before anything runs. The most interesting decision sits in the 69 lines of `PermissionPolicy.cs`: the policy engine is a pure function that **can only auto-allow**, never auto-deny, prefers `allow_once` over `allow_always` so the agent does not persist a broader consent on its side, and deliberately does not auto-allow `fetch`, because a network call can carry out what was read a moment earlier. Every decision, including an automatic one, lands in the transcript as an {{term:audit|audit}} entry. The rest of the workshop has grown up around the chat: a git diff browser resolved on the server side, an xterm.js terminal with a real PTY on Unix, session resumption through `session/load`, handoff between agents and a panel of quality results pulled from the sibling CopilotScope. Helm is the control plane, Scope the observation plane, and that split is stated outright in the repository. Everything the README marks as M0-M3 is finished; correlation with Scope remains a heuristic over overlapping time windows.
repos.tests: 43 `[Fact]` attributes and zero `[Theory]`, all in a single `CoreTests.cs` file 1,012 lines long with 19 classes; the tests were not run in this pass, the attributes were counted in the code.
repos.ci: Four workflows: build and test of the whole solution in Release, a release on a `v*` tag (tests, publish of three projects, zip and GitHub Release), a build of two images on {{term:ghcr}} and publication of the `docs` directory to GitHub Pages. They all work, but `ci.yml` and `pages.yml` listen for a push to `main` while the repository works on `master` — in practice nothing runs on the main branch other than the `pull_request` path.

docs.label: Release checklist (not one item ticked off)

components.name: AcpClient
components.description: An own implementation of an Agent Client Protocol client: JSON-RPC over stdio, `initialize`, `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/prompt`, handling of `fs/read_text_file` and `fs/write_text_file` with a path guard. The transport sits behind `IAcpTransport`, so the protocol is tested against scripted in-memory streams, without starting any agent at all.

components.name: PolicyEngine
components.description: A stateless decision function over a permission request: it returns either an auto-consent with a chosen option, or 'ask the human'. Three policies (`ask`, `auto_read`, `yolo`), read-only means only `read`, `search` and `think`, and the absence of an allowing option on the agent's side also degrades to asking.

components.name: GitService
components.description: The backend of the change browser: it parses `git status --porcelain` including the rename token, counts +/- from the diff, accept is `git add`, reject is `git checkout HEAD --` or deletion of an uncatalogued file. The server establishes a file's status, not the request from the browser, so the UI cannot force the deletion of a tracked file.

components.name: AgentHelm.EchoAgent
components.description: A reference agent speaking full ACP in 181 lines: it streams a response, and on the word 'tool' in the prompt it sends a permission request. It lets you walk the whole flow, gate included, without installing and logging in to a real agent, and it works as a harness for any other ACP client.

components.name: TerminalService
components.description: A shell session next to the chat, 161 lines. On Unix a real PTY obtained through `script -qfe -c bash /dev/null` from util-linux, with no interop and no native package; a 64 kB buffer, subscribers over channels, output streamed to xterm.js. It cannot be extracted without changing a signature: the public subscription method returns `ChannelReader<SessionEventDto>`, and that type is declared in this repository's session manager.

components.name: AgentHelm.Bridge
components.description: The API process and at the same time the security boundary: bind on 127.0.0.1 by default, an optional `x-helm-token` header, three SSE streams (transcript, terminal, provider login output). It holds sessions, permissions, git, the terminal and the write-behind jsonb snapshot to Postgres once a second.

components.name: AgentHelm.Web
components.description: Blazor Server without a single `PackageReference`. The Home page is 703 lines of code-behind plus 447 lines of razor: session list, transcript, permission banner, the Changes and Terminal tabs, history and handoff. All the logic is deliberately in code-behind, communication runs solely through `BridgeClient`.

components.name: ScopeClient
components.description: It pulls sessions with a quality result from the CopilotScope collector and matches them to Helm sessions by overlapping time windows. It has a one-minute backoff when Scope does not answer, and tolerant DTO parsing, but the matching itself remains a heuristic and the UI admits it.

overlaps.reason: A sibling project and an outright integration: Helm queries Scope's REST API for quality results and presets the agents' {{term:otel}} variables so the telemetry reaches the Scope collector. The division of roles is declared: Scope observes, Helm steers.

repos.product: The consumer would be a team that wants to use coding agents under control: a permission gate with an audit, a transcript of every decision and one GUI instead of four CLIs make material for an internal tool or for an argument to compliance. There is no sales channel today and nothing in the repository builds one: an {{term:mit}} licence, distribution by zip and GHCR images, no multi-tenant mode, no authentication beyond a single shared token, no billing at all. This is therefore technical credibility, not a product, and in that role it works: a complete client of a public protocol, a security model stated outright and the limits named by name in the README.
highlights: Bridge has **exactly one NuGet dependency** (Npgsql 8.0.5). The ACP client, the git handling and the terminal are own code over system processes.

repos.summary: Three files served statically: `index.html` fetches `concepts.json` and renders concept tiles, `architecture.html` is a separate essay, and the rest is the licence and `.nojekyll`. repos.name: AquaScope
repos.oneLiner: A simulated water network plus a full monitoring platform around it: OTLP, alert correlation and replay-produced numbers pinned in tests as bounds.
repos.summary: Nine .NET 10 projects impersonate a water distribution network: two pumping stations, twelve sensors across three zones, a meter ingestor and a fault injector with three on-demand scenarios. All telemetry goes through one {{term:otel|OpenTelemetry}} Collector, which fans it out in parallel to Prometheus with Grafana and to an in-house backend, where a hand-written OTLP decoder turns batches into an asset model. Over that model a pipeline of five analyzers behind a single `IIncidentAnalyzer` interface runs every five seconds: threshold, freshness, trend on EWMA and linear drift, correlation over the topology, and AI triage. The most interesting decision is `CorrelationAnalyzer`: 410 lines that glue alerts into one incident by walking the downstream graph within a 180 s window and at most four hops, and rank the candidate cause from four **explicitly written-down weights** (upstream 0.40, onset 0.30, type 0.20, distance 0.10), so every ranking can be challenged by hand instead of taking a model's word for it. The three headline numbers are not typed into the README but produced by a replay of the scenarios; `FindingsMeasurementTests` prints them, and `FaultScenarioAcceptanceTests` pins them with lower bounds. The repository grew around `docs/SPEC.md`, written before the code, whose revision history has four rows: the initial version and three revisions carrying corrections found during implementation (v1.2 declares three, v1.3 four).
repos.tests: 143 cases in a single project, `tests/AquaScope.Tests` (121 [Fact] plus 4 [Theory] with 22 [InlineData]), 3,591 lines across 16 files; the count agrees with row 16 of `docs/COMPLIANCE.md`, but it is counted from the attributes in the code, not from a green `dotnet test` run.
repos.ci: Four workflows: build and test on .NET 10 with a trx artefact and a separate job for the two mechanical guards, CodeQL for csharp and actions with a Monday cron, gitleaks over the **whole history** plus the same scan as a pre-commit hook. The fifth piece is `flyio.yml` (323 lines), triggered by a `v*` tag, which detects changes against the previous tag and deploys in the order postgres, core, simulators.

components.name: AquaScope.ServiceDefaults
components.description: The hosting {{term:servicedefaults|shared kernel}}: OTel, health and alive, service discovery, the standard resilience handler. 142 lines against a ceiling of 800 and **zero references to the Contracts project**, so it copies into another service without dragging the domain along.

components.name: The analyser pipeline
components.description: Five implementations of one interface, run by `AnalysisLoop` every five seconds. Each returns an `AnalyzerReport` with metrics and a rationale, so missing data is reported as no-data instead of quietly vanishing from the result.

components.name: AssetHealthEngine
components.description: A 0–100 score per asset from four dimensions, with the weights renormalised over only the dimensions that have data and confidence reported separately. The construction is carried straight over from the session-quality engine in copilot-scope; what changes is the dimensions plugged in, not the mechanics.

components.name: CorrelationAnalyzer
components.description: 410 lines that assemble alerts into an incident over the `NetworkTopology` graph and rank the cause from four written-down weights. Every component of a candidate's placement in the ranking is recorded, so the result can be challenged without reading the code.

components.name: TrendAnalyzer
components.description: 428 lines of EWMA and linear drift, meant to fire before the threshold. The alert carries its own arithmetic: the slope and the predicted moment of breach. The thresholds are justified by logged runs, not picked by eye.

components.name: AiTriageAnalyzer
components.description: Builds the prompt only from facts established {{term:determinizm|deterministically}} and queues an RCA draft behind a human acceptance gate (`/triage/{incidentId}/approve`). Without an API key it reports no-data and nothing else breaks, but nobody drains the queue either.

highlights: The headline numbers come from a replay of the scenarios, not from being typed into the README, but **they are enforced only as bounds**: `FindingsMeasurementTests` (one `[Theory]`, four `[InlineData]`) prints them through `ITestOutputHelper` and has exactly one assertion, `Assert.True(raw >= 0)`. `docs/RCA-001.md` is the postmortem of one specific run, in which every timestamp is pinned by the `Scenario2RcaEvidenceTests` test. It found a suppression rule structurally incapable of firing, and the fix **worsened** the noise-reduction figure from 8:1 to 4:1 — and it is reported that way.

`docs/SPEC.md` (671 lines) was written before the code, and its revision history has four rows: v1.0 is the initial specification, followed by three revisions carrying corrections forced by the implementation — v1.1 corrects two injection parameters for scenario 1, v1.2 declares 'Three corrections', v1.3 'Four corrections'. A single number of 'cases' cannot be derived from this without an arbitrary choice of whether to count rows, revisions or individual corrections. Every pinned machine in `flyio/` names, in a comment, the synchronous call that forces it, plus the costed alternative: about 2 USD a month to let Core sleep, against losing all telemetry.
risks: **A name collision built into the repository:** the directory is `hydro-scope`, while all the code, every container, the Fly apps and the documents say `AquaScope`. The README explains it, but every external link and every search hits a different name.
Grafana starts with `GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED=true`, the Admin role and the login form disabled. Deliberate for a demo on a laptop; copied anywhere else it is an open admin.
`AiTriageOptions.Model` hard-codes `"claude-sonnet-5"`. A model identifier in a constant is a pin that will age quietly, the more so since nothing uses it today anyway.

Fifteen commits and the last one on 2026-08-15: the repository was produced in one sitting and never touched since. The pins (Aspire 13.4.6, EF Core 10.0.11, Grafana 13.0.6, collector 0.158.0) will age faster than anyone looks in here.

repos.name: ArchGate
repos.oneLiner: Architecture gate for .NET: {{term:roslyn}} analyzers that fail the build when code breaks the declared architecture — counted from the PR diff.
repos.summary: Seven {{term:roslyn}} analyzers on `netstandard2.0` enforce part of the architectural constitution: the shared kernel boundary, persistence portability, controller/DbContext layering, orphan entities, inheritance instead of an interface, vendor SDK types leaking outside the adapter, a missing `AddServiceDefaults`. The gate counts **only the lines changed in a pull request** — without that, every new rule lights up thousands of warnings in existing code and the team switches the tool off in the first week; the problem is documented and reproduced on a two-commit repro. {{term:provenance|Provenance}} is read from real git — `git diff -U0` plus `git blame` plus commit trailers — never from code style, and it serves only to raise the severity threshold; it appears in the PR comment neither as a badge nor as a score. The whole thing ships as two `dotnet` tools — `ArchGate.Cli` and `ArchGate.CiComment`, the only two projects with `PackAsTool` — plus a third package, `ArchGate.Analyzers`, which is not a tool: it is a Roslyn analyzer package with `IncludeBuildOutput=false` whose DLL goes to `analyzers/dotnet/cs`. On top of that, a container image and a composite action.
repos.tests: 150 [Fact] attributes across 21 files (`grep -rho '[Fact]' tests --include='*.cs' | wc -l`; zero `[Theory]`, zero `[InlineData]`); the ROADMAP says 146/146 and is two commits stale — the last change to `ROADMAP-archgate.md` is `716c32a`, and `git rev-list --count 716c32a..HEAD` gives 2 (one working commit and one merge). The tests were not run in this pass — no SDK in the environment.
repos.ci: `archgate-pr-check.yml` runs the gate on the repository's own PRs; `release.yml` on a `v*` tag declares five jobs — `build`, `publish-nuget`, `publish-container`, `release-notes`, `moving-tag` — including verification of the packed analyzer in a temporary consumer project (a step inside `build`). No tag exists, so the release has never run for real.

components.name: ArchGate.Engine (Scanner)
components.description: Harness: parses every `.cs` file into a single compilation, runs the rule registry, maps diagnostics onto a violation record and works out the gate verdict. A neutral wrapper — run any set of analyzers over a directory and get deterministic JSON.

components.name: Model konfiguracji konwencji

components.name: ArchGate.Rules (7 analysers)
components.description: The analyzers themselves are a general package for any C# repository, but the individual rules encode principles P1–P15 from the constitution — outside it, some of them have to be reconfigured.

components.name: ArchGate.CiComment
components.description: Renders the result to Markdown, works out the difference against the previous scan and updates **one** sticky PR comment, found by a hidden marker. Provenance deliberately never gets in there.

components.name: Composite GitHub Action
components.description: Deliberately composite rather than container-based — container actions only run on Linux runners. It checks that a base commit is present before turning on diff mode.

overlaps.reason: It does not invent its own rule language — it enforces principles P1–P15 from that repository and quotes them in the category of every diagnostic. The loop is closed.

The evidence discipline was carried over from there: the {{term:mutation|mutation run}} and the principle that a test suite which has never failed has not been tested.

repos.product: The buyer is named outright: an engineering lead or a platform team in a .NET organisation that can see the debt from AI-written code growing and has nothing to measure it with. Open-core model, with an empty `enterprise/` directory waiting for team features. The problem sits in front of all of that, though: **the sales channel is blocked by the name**. Until that changes, this is a credibility artefact — a finished, documented, mutation-tested engine — and nothing more.
highlights: The repository knocked down its own marketing claim: the competitive document confirms a published namesake in the same package registry, corrects the numbers from two other people's reviews and **lists every place that went out of date as a result**. That is a rarer skill than writing an analyzer.

The release pipeline verifies the packed analyzer in a temporary consumer project and fails if the package does not emit a specific diagnostic. That catches the classic failure 'the DLL landed in the wrong folder, the package installs cleanly and does nothing'.

The analyzers deliberately sit on Roslyn 4.8.0 rather than 4.11.0, because an analyzer built against the newer one emits an error at the consumer. Established by consuming the packed `.nupkg`, not by reading the documentation.
Ten mutation variants of the rules, with tests that the real rule catches a case and the mutant lets it through — evidence that the tests respond to the mechanism and not to their own fixtures.
gaps: **Zero published artefacts.** There is no tag of any kind, so the three packages, the image and the action do not exist, and every install command in the README returns a 404. The README admits it, which is honest and does not change the fact.
Nine of the fifteen principles are not implemented, and four never will be — the tool covers 6/15 of the contract it appeals to.

The engine sees a single compilation parsed straight from files, with no MSBuildWorkspace and no package references — that makes some of the rules purely syntactic, which limits their accuracy and will require a rewrite once the constraint is lifted.
The repository is private, even though all of its distribution value depends on being public.

Fix the copyright line in LICENSE; it carries someone else's name, copied from another repository.

risks: **A name collision with a published, maintained product in the same NuGet registry.** Publishing under the current name would read as a clone or a typosquat — and that is the one thing blocking the whole distribution path.
LICENSE assigns the rights to someone else's name, out of step with the rest of the configuration. In an MIT repository that is a legal defect, not a typo.
Many of the rules are matches on folder name and call shape, with no bound symbol — a risk of false positives, which the vision itself names as the known failure mode of this category of tool.

repos.name: architecture-standards
repos.oneLiner: The estate's architectural constitution: fifteen principles and seventeen guides, also shipped as {{term:plugins|agent plugins}}.
repos.summary: One body of text in two forms. Close to forty-six thousand words of prose in `docs/` (45,893 outside code blocks, 48,664 words in total) is documentation to read **and** the source from which five plugins and twenty-one skills are generated in the {{term:plugins|Agent Plugins 1.0.0}} format. The reason it exists is stated outright: an agent working on another repository is meant to **read** the rules, not reconstruct them from whatever code it happens to see — because that is the most expensive failure in the whole estate. The skills are routers: a short 'use when…' description, a failure-mode table and a checklist, with the full standard sitting alongside and loading only once the skill fires. The generator and the validator are deliberately separate: the first proves the tree agrees with the sources, the second — independently — that a client will accept it. This is the only repository in the portfolio that changes how the rest of the portfolio gets built.
repos.tests: No unit tests. The only automatic verification is the manifest validator (234 lines), which reports '5 plugins, 21 skills, 2 manifests', and the {{term:drift|drift validator}} — and that one fails on HEAD.
repos.ci: Two workflows. `validate-marketplace.yml` runs the generator in `--check` mode and then the validator; the first step exits 1 on HEAD, so **CI is red**. `deploy-pages.yml` publishes the single-page site.

components.name: Konstytucja (P1–P15)
components.description: 667 lines: a diagram of the whole shape of the system, fifteen principles and an eighteen-point compliance checklist. Every principle carries a quoted example from a **working** system — the document is descriptive, not aspirational.

components.name: Seventeen operational guides

components.name: Generator pakowania

components.name: The manifest validator

The potential commercial consumer is a platform team or a consultant who wants **their own** constitution packaged the same way — at which point what sells is the method (prose plus catalogue plus generator), not the content. The mechanism for distributing it across a whole organisation already exists.
highlights: One body of text, two forms: 45,893 words of prose outside code blocks (48,664 words in total across `docs/**/*.md`) are documentation and the source of five plugins at once — without a single line copied by hand.

The skills are routers, not the standard pasted into the prompt: the full text loads only once the skill fires. That is the difference between a hundred tokens and a thousand on every session.

repos.name: architecture-standards-init-example
repos.oneLiner: What the architectural constitution produces when pointed at an empty repository — compliant on the first commit, not after a later cleanup pass.
repos.summary: A worked run of the greenfield initializer: one Aspire composition root, one shared kernel, one service that owns its database, one Next.js surface in front of it, three Fly.io apps and eight workflows. It **ships no domain model, deliberately** — it exists to be read as an example of the architecture, not used as a product. This is the most important companion piece to `architecture-standards`: the constitution describes what a system should look like, and this repository shows that shape without a single line of domain to distract from it. Several things here are done better than in most real systems: the frontend reads its configuration per request from `/api/config` and never from `NEXT_PUBLIC_*`, because that bakes at build time and costs one image per environment; the shared kernel is 477 lines against an 800-line ceiling enforced by a test **and** a CI step; and the setup script **generates** the one mandatory secret, because a human asked to invent one produces `changeme`.
repos.tests: Nine test attributes in `tests/…Api.Tests` (the README says ten tests): the zero-credential health report, list clamping, the error shape and three kernel guards. Alongside them, four Playwright tests through the whole stack, run on every pull request — and those are the strong point here, because they boot exactly the Docker-less path the repository advertises.
repos.ci: Eight workflows — the most of any repository added in this pass: `ci.yml` with the E2E suite, `codeql.yml`, `secret-scan.yml`, `pages.yml`, `build-overview-pdf.yml`, and three Fly.io workflows (deploy, scale, and a teardown gated by a typed confirmation).

docs.label: The setup script — it generates the secret rather than asking for one

components.name: The Aspire composition root
components.description: Declares Postgres, the API and the frontend with `WithReference`, `WaitFor` and `WithHttpHealthCheck`. Explicitly **not** the production topology — and the repository says so outright, which is the most commonly confused point about Aspire.

components.name: The shared kernel
components.description: Telemetry, health, discovery, resilience, JWT, CORS, OpenAPI, the database provider — 477 lines. An architecture test asserts the kernel holds no entity type and exports nothing you can inherit from.

components.name: The product surface
components.description: The browser's only origin. Its server side reads configuration per request from `/api/config` and reaches the API through a catch-all proxy that walks a candidate ladder — one code path works on a laptop, under Aspire and on Fly.

components.name: The setup scripts
components.description: Check prerequisites, restore both dependency graphs, and **generate** the one mandatory secret into `dotnet user-secrets`. `--check` reports what is missing and changes nothing. The PowerShell variant does the same job without `openssl`, which is not a command on Windows.

components.name: The E2E suite
components.description: Four Playwright tests through the whole stack, booting the Docker-less path on every pull request. That is not a convenience — it is principle P8 turned into something checkable.

overlaps.reason: This is that initializer's output and the one complete worked example of the constitution with no domain to distract. A change to the standard that cannot be reproduced here is a standard nobody has executed.

The same skeleton reached from the other side: a 2018 solution modernized there, greenfield here. The kernel with its line ceiling, the in-memory database fallback and post-Kestrel migrations are identical in both.
The kernel carries the JWT wiring but the issuer is external — the same split as everywhere in this portfolio: a service validates tokens and cannot mint them.

repos.product: Credibility, not a transaction, and the highest value-to-size ratio in cluster B. For a consulting buyer it answers the question 'what does your first commit look like': not a slide, but a repository that boots with no credential and carries eight gates from day one. What sells here is the initialization method, not the code.
highlights: Configuration read per request from `/api/config` instead of `NEXT_PUBLIC_*`. That is the mistake most Next.js deployments make, and it costs one image per environment — here it is solved in the skeleton before anyone has a chance to make it.

The setup script generates the secret instead of asking a human to invent one. The justification recorded in the repository is one sentence and it is correct: a human asked to invent a secret produces `changeme`.

The kernel ceiling is enforced by two independent mechanisms — an architecture test and a CI step. The duplication is deliberate: the test protects in the editor, the CI step protects against a test somebody deleted.
The dependency count per project is printed in the README. A rise in a diff becomes a question somebody can ask at review — a cheap mechanism with a disproportionate effect.
gaps: Five open Dependabot pull requests against zero open issues — every open item in this repository is a dependency update.

Shipping no domain model is a decision, but it has a price: the repository cannot show how the constitution copes with a domain that does not fit in one service. The hardest architectural question stays untouched here.
Nine test attributes on the API side is thin for a repository that advertises its gates — the burden of proof rests on four E2E tests.
next: Merge the five Dependabot pull requests. With zero issues open, it is the only outstanding work in this repository.
Add a second service to the example, or record as an explicit decision that one service is the limit of what the initializer demonstrates.
Wire this example into `architecture-standards`' validation: a change to the constitution that cannot be reproduced here should fail that repository's build.
risks: The example is compliant with the constitution as of the day it was generated. Without a gate binding it to the standard it will drift silently — and that would be the worst possible kind of drift, because this repository is cited as the reference shape.
repos.headline: Eight workflows, zero credentials needed to run it, zero domain — exactly as designed

repos.name: AureliusPromptus.AcceptanceTests
repos.oneLiner: 449 Playwright tests in .NET for the AureliusPromptus Portal, plus an audit that showed 196 of them checked nothing.
repos.summary: Two Playwright acceptance-test projects aimed at one Portal application, by default at `http://localhost:3003`. The main project is xUnit v3 on .NET 9 and Playwright 1.52: `BrowserFixture` holds one browser process per collection, `PlaywrightTestBase` gives each test a fresh context and page with video recording and a screenshot on failure, and `AuthTestBase` creates a unique account through the UI and deletes it in teardown. Alongside it sits a second, smaller project on MSTest 4 and .NET 10 with 53 tests, duplicating the same infrastructure against the same application. The most interesting thing in the repository is not the test code, though, but `E2E_Tests_analysis.md`: an audit that catalogued the sham-test patterns and counted them one by one, including 196 empty method bodies, 186 guard-then-bail sites and one mechanical Playwright API mistake (`HasText` with a comma-separated list) disabling 13 calls. Phase 1 of the remediation plan was actually carried out on 2026-08-14: no test was deleted, 196 were explicitly marked `Skip` with an individual reason, and 253 carry an unconditional assertion. This is a rare thing in the portfolio: a repository that documented its own dishonesty and gave a number instead of an adjective.
repos.tests: 449 xUnit test methods across 52 files: 253 `[Fact]` attributes without `Skip` plus 196 `[Fact(Skip = ...)]`, that is 449 occurrences of `[Fact` counted by grep over the tree, skipping `bin/` and `obj/`; zero `[Theory]` and zero `[InlineData]`. The MSTest project has 53 `[TestMethod]` across 14 files. The earlier '63 and 17 files' are the counts of all `.cs` files in both projects (63 + 17 = 80), not of files containing tests. No run has been verified here, because all of them need a live Portal instance, which this repo does not contain.
repos.ci: One workflow, `e2e-manual.yml`, `workflow_dispatch` only, with a required `base_url` and a choice of project, browser and filter. It installs both SDKs (9.0.x and 10.0.x), builds in Release, pulls the browser through `playwright.ps1 --with-deps`, runs `dotnet test` with the trx logger and uploads artefacts for 14 days; there is no `push`, `pull_request` or `schedule` trigger at all.

components.description: A script to dot-source, setting six `AP_AT_*` variables (`AP_AT_BASE_URL`, `AP_AT_BROWSER`, `AP_AT_HEADLESS`, `AP_AT_RECORD_VIDEO`, `AP_AT_SCREENSHOT_ON_FAIL`, `AP_AT_ARTIFACTS_DIR`) plus `AP_PORTAL_BASE_URL` in the current PowerShell session. `AP_AT_CLEANUP_ACCOUNTS` is read in `PlaywrightTestBase`, but this script does not set it — only the default value applies. The default port 3003 is written here as the `-BaseUrl` parameter, and the same fallback also sits in both base classes and in the README.

overlaps.reason: The generalised rules from the audit (assertion discipline, locator conventions, CI as part of the definition of done) were moved into `docs/guides/E2E-ACCEPTANCE-TESTING.md` in that repo.
The audit is a counted case of a suite generated in a single AI run, described as production-ready and checking nothing. It is evidence on exactly the subject of that piece.

repos.product: No buyer. This is the internal quality layer of one private product, and nobody outside will buy or clone tests of somebody else's Portal. The only exportable value lies in `E2E_Tests_analysis.md`: a specific, counted piece of {{term:evidence|evidence}} that a green suite run can mean nothing. That is material for an article or a chapter, not for a product, and it is worth treating as input to a text rather than as a repository to develop.
highlights: The audit does not say "many tests are weak", it gives numbers: **196 empty method bodies across 36 files**, 186 guard-then-bail sites, 45 swallowed assertions and one mechanical API mistake (`HasText` with a comma-separated list) disabling 13 calls.

Phase 1 was carried out, not merely planned: the method count did not change, but **each of the 196 dead tests got an explicit `Skip` with an individual reason** instead of being deleted. The debt is visible in the run result, not in the git history.

Test-account cleanup is solved in the base class rather than in every test: `BeforeContextCloseAsync` fires after the screenshot and before the context closes, so a failure still leaves an artefact and the account disappears anyway. The `AP_AT_CLEANUP_ACCOUNTS` switch leaves a way out for debugging.

PR #12, open for three months, was diagnosed and merged instead of the work being redone, with a byte-level comparison of `QuotaEnforcementTests` between the branches as evidence that it had not touched the test bodies.

The repository openly documents its own genealogy, including the fact that the delivery documents of the original suite boast of "500+ hours of test design" and are dated to an impossible December 2024.
gaps: **The suite has never run automatically and there is no documented green run of the whole thing.** The workflow is `workflow_dispatch` only, so the entire audit stops at static analysis, and its conclusions about coverage are unverified by execution. The tests are not {{term:hermetyczny|hermetic}}: they need a live Portal instance, and nobody here stands one up.

Whole areas have zero real assertions: `QuotaEnforcementTests` 0/10, `OrganizationInvitationReceivingTests` 0/11, `OrganizationInvitationManagementTests` 0/7, `MessageManagementTests` 0/7, `PremiumFeaturesAccessTests` 0/6. The product's monetisation boundary is entirely uncovered.

Three systemic blockers from Phase 1 are still open: `RegisterAndLoginAsync` does not create the workspace the dashboard layout insists on, the system-messages bell has no selector at all, and there is no Premium-account helper. Some of the newly added assertions will fall over on the first live run.

The numbers in the README and in the audit (447 / 252 / 195) disagree with a grep over the code (449 / 253 / 196), and the documents in `docs/` have their own, older {{term:drift|drift}}. The audit admits this and does not fix it.
Phase 2 not done: two projects on two test frameworks and two versions of .NET aim at the same application, and the name `Web.NextJs.E2ETests` points at a frontend that no longer exists.
next: Run `e2e-manual.yml` once against any live Portal instance and publish the actual result, red though it may be. Without that the audit is only a well-counted hypothesis.
Fix the three infrastructure blockers in this order: workspace creation in `RegisterAndLoginAsync`, the system-messages bell selector, the Premium-account helper.
Move the seed-account passwords (`konrad@aurelius.com` / `konrad@aurelius.today`) out into environment variables and add a `LICENSE`.
Reconcile the numbers in the README and the audit with the grep, or generate them from a script during the build, so the drift cannot come back.
Carry out Phase 2: rename the project to `AureliusPromptus.Web.E2ETests`, move the unique scenarios over from the MSTest project and delete it.
risks: Seed-account passwords are hard-coded in the repository: one account in `UserProfileTests/LoginTests.cs:15`, another in two files of the Portal project, both with the same password. The addresses and the password are deliberately **not given here** — this entry is public and the repository it describes is not. If those accounts exist in a publicly reachable environment this is a credential leak: the password has to be changed, not merely removed from the code.
The seed-account domains do not match each other, nor the product's domain after the rebrand, so the suite may have nothing to log in with before it ever reaches the first assertion.

The tests create real data in the environment under test. Nothing removes organisations or prompts, and accounts from `LogoutTests` leak, because after logging out there is no session left to delete with.
No `LICENSE` file, with two versions of .NET and two test frameworks in one solution: nobody else has the right to use this, and maintaining it costs two build paths anyway.

repos.name: authservice
repos.oneLiner: A standalone authentication microservice for ASP.NET Core — and the only finished extraction in the whole portfolio.
repos.summary: Accounts, sign-in, address verification, password reset, TOTP with backup codes, JWT issuance with rotated refresh tokens held as hashes. Google and GitHub sign-in, multi-tenant organisations with roles and invitations, an admin API, an append-only audit log, versioned terms consent and GDPR-compliant data export. It began as a **module lifted out of a private monorepo**, and `EXTRACTION.md` lists exactly what was kept and what was thrown out on purpose. The repository deliberately does not host a canonical instance of its own: it publishes an image to {{term:ghcr}}, and every consumer runs its own instance with its own database and its own signing key. **One codebase, N independent instances, no shared root of trust** — and that is precisely the pattern the rest of the consolidation is meant to repeat.
repos.tests: About 67 executed cases in a single project (61 [Fact] + 2 [Theory] with 6 rows), 1,439 lines. The integration tests boot the whole application on in-memory SQLite — the entire HTTP path with no Docker and no network.
repos.ci: Five workflows: build+test, formatting check, a check that migrations match the model, image build with a smoke test; CodeQL with the security-and-quality suite and a weekly cron; gitleaks over the **full history**; multi-arch image publication on a `v*` tag; GitHub Pages.

components.name: JwtSigningKeys
components.description: Resolves the key material once, at startup, and validates it. The list of **signing keys and the list of validating keys are deliberately different**, which allows a key to be rotated without invalidating tokens already issued. It knows no domain type.

components.description: Schema initialisation after the HTTP server is already listening, with retries. The completion signal drives the readiness endpoint, which returns 503 until the schema is ready. The 'liveness immediately, readiness after the schema' pattern is neutral — and it has been copied into four other repositories.

components.name: AuditService
components.description: An append-only log. Writes are best-effort from the caller's point of view — a failed audit write does not turn a successful operation into a failed one — apart from the method that attaches a row to the unit of work, so that an action and its trace commit together.

components.name: Integration tests on in-memory SQLite
components.description: The factory brings up the real application with the database provider swapped. The entire HTTP path tested with no Docker and no network — a pattern to copy into any ASP.NET Core service.

components.name: TokenService
components.description: Refresh tokens held as hashes, tied into a family; presenting an already-rotated token again invalidates the **whole family** and writes an audit event.

components.name: ProviderEmailVerifier
components.description: Closes the account-takeover path through OAuth: it requires the provider itself to have confirmed the address before it is used to link an account. An unknown provider is treated as unverified by default.

overlaps.reason: Cited there forty times; its extraction pattern is described as a proposed standard with an explicit note that it has one data point — this one.
Consumes the image at v0.3.1 with no source dependency at all — evidence that the pattern works.
Every API validates tokens against this service's JWKS; the service itself is not built there.
Has its own `auto-veritas-authservice` application based on the same image.

repos.product: There is no buyer in the paying sense, and the ADR flatly refuses to compete with Keycloak or Ory on feature count. The real audience is a .NET team that needs a sign-in service of its own and wants to **read it in one afternoon** rather than stand up Keycloak. The portfolio value here is the highest of the lot, though: it is the most engineering-complete security artefact in the whole set, with documentation that records the rejected alternatives.
highlights: Under HS256 the JWKS endpoint returns an **empty set, not a 404** — the consumer gets 'I have no key for you' rather than 'I do not support JWKS'. That is one line that saves someone an hour of diagnosis.
Refresh token reuse detection: the whole family is invalidated plus an audit entry. This is the thing most hand-written identity services do not have.
The image smoke test checks that a container **without a connection string fails and names the missing setting**. It verifies the error message, not only the happy path.
Gitleaks runs over the full history, not over the diff — the only version of that check that means anything in a repository extracted from a monorepo.
A register of six dated deviations and a separate list of closed ones: the project writes down its own weaknesses rather than keeping quiet about them.
gaps: **No committed EF Core migrations.** Both migration projects contain nothing but a project file, and the CI job meant to police this is therefore without effect. The default mode creates the schema and never updates it — so a deployment with a new column will fail at run time.

No tag at all, so the image `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice:v0.1.0`, given in the README as ready to pin, has probably **never been published** — even though six other repositories already pin it in their configuration.
SQL Server support is declared and untested; the deviations register itself calls this a promise with nothing behind it.
No OTLP telemetry — observability is a console logger plus the service's own audit log.
`Program.cs` is 530 lines and concentrates the whole application composition; the register flags it for refactoring.
next: **Generate and commit migrations** for both providers and switch the recommended mode to migrations. That turns the CI job from an apparent check into a real one.
Push a tag and confirm that the image actually reached GHCR and that the package is public. Six repositories already pin it — today they pin a promise.
Settle the SQL Server deviation: either integration tests, or drop the provider and halve the migration surface.
Break `Program.cs` up into composition extensions.
Fix the copyright line in LICENSE — it carries someone else's name, exactly as in two other repositories.
risks: `docker-compose.yml` contains a plaintext signing secret and an administrator account password. They are described as demonstration-only, but these are ready-to-copy credentials **in the repository of an identity service** — that is, exactly where they cost the most.
The documentation promises an image at a specific version whose existence cannot be confirmed from the repository.
The name `authservice` is entirely generic — a collision in the registry and in search is close to certain.
The `iss` claim is a bare string rather than a URL, which departs from OIDC convention. Deliberate and documented, but it will complicate integration with a client that enforces it.

repos.name: Auto Veritas
repos.oneLiner: A comparison tool for car and finance offers on the Spanish market, where every value carries its own verification date.
repos.summary: A service behind a login that sets car and loan offers side by side and holds three timestamps against every number: when the agent checked it at the source, how long the seller declares it valid, and when the source itself was published. Freshness is computed by the server, against thresholds that depend on the data type — prices 7/30 days, instalments 14/45, specifications 183/365 — and published under `/api/v1/meta/freshness-policy`, so the UI renders exactly the values the backend enforces instead of holding a second set of constants that will drift apart (decision D-4). Expired data is degraded and marked, never hidden; an estimated value gets an **estimate** chip and balloon financing a **BALLOON** chip, rather than hiding behind a low instalment. Every `PUT` that changes a price or an instalment writes a snapshot of the previous state, keyed by the offer's `Guid` rather than by the slug — precisely because `PUT` allows the slug to change. Writing goes through the API only and requires the `Admin` or `SuperAdmin` role from {{term:servicedefaults|authservice}}; the frontend has no write surface at all, and that is a product decision, not a shortage of time. The whole thing stands as a four-element topology (Postgres, authservice from an image, OffersService, a BFF in Next.js) built directly against the checklist from `architecture-standards`.
repos.tests: 52 backend cases (40 `[Fact]` plus 3 `[Theory]` with 12 rows of `[InlineData]`) on `WebApplicationFactory` with SQLite, 5 `it()` tests in vitest for web-kit and 7 smoke tests in Playwright — 64 cases in total, all counted directly in the code.
repos.ci: Five workflows. `ci.yml` has four jobs: backend (Release build, test, `dotnet format --verify-no-changes`), **mechanical-guards** (an 800-line limit on the kernel, a grep forbidding domain types in the kernel, a grep forbidding `waitForTimeout` in e2e), frontend, and e2e-smoke, which brings up the whole compose stack, waits for `/health/ready` and publishes a report. On top of that, CodeQL on a matrix of two languages with a weekly cron, gitleaks on push and PR, and a 249-line `flyio.yml` with a {{term:tagdeploy|tag-driven deployment}} and a manual teardown behind a confirmation phrase.

components.description: Seven smoke tests matching one to one the flows in `CHARTER.md`, written **before** the tests along with explicit non-goals. The charter forbids fixed `sleep` calls, and the ban is grepped in a separate CI job, so it cannot be broken quietly.

overlaps.reason: The only source of identity, pinned as the image `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice:v0.3.1` in compose, Aspire and `fly.toml`. The permission model rests directly on that service's platform roles `Admin` and `SuperAdmin` — this is the sixth consumer of the same image.

The repository structure, the full set of `docs/architecture`, the mechanical CI guards and the security review are written against the P1-P15 checklist, and the standard is wired in as a plugin in `.claude/settings.json`. This is the cleanest existing implementation of that standard from scratch.

The same pattern of a domain-neutral `ServiceDefaults` kernel alongside business services. There a hundred lines and a convention, here 361 lines and a limit enforced by a CI job — two data points for the same hypothesis about a shared substrate.

The `LICENSE` file carries `Copyright (c) 2026 dev_insight`, that is a template carried over from that repository without swapping the name. A trace of shared scaffolding ancestry, not an intended dependency.

repos.product: There is no external buyer and there will not be one: this is a tool for one household choosing a car in Spain, with a few invited readers and one agent writing through the API. The value is purely referential — it is evidence that `architecture-standards` can be applied from an empty directory, with a full set of decisions, a register of deviations and a justification of infrastructure costs, rather than only described in a document. If anything here had a buyer, it would be the trust mechanism itself: a verification date on every value, and degradation instead of hiding. The car catalogue is the carrier here, not the product.
highlights: The freshness thresholds are computed by the server and published under `/api/v1/meta/freshness-policy`, so the UI renders exactly what the backend enforces. One source of truth instead of two sets of constants that stop agreeing after three months (D-4).

The architectural guards are CI jobs, not prose: an 800-line limit on the kernel (361 today), a grep forbidding domain types in the kernel and a grep forbidding `waitForTimeout` in e2e. A rule that cannot be broken quietly is worth more than a paragraph in the README.
The change history is keyed by `Guid` rather than by the slug, precisely because `PUT` allows the slug to change — and decision D-13 lists four rejected alternatives with a reason for each.

Decision D-14 turns {{term:dependabot|Dependabot version updates}} off on evidence, not on convenience: of eight PRs, three were harmful and two would have broken `main` (Node 26 removes Corepack, which the web Dockerfile uses; Swashbuckle 10.x does not compile, on CS0234).

The security review goes through the full OWASP skeleton with an endpoint x role matrix, two findings and a priority ledger, including one knowingly accepted as NOT PLANNED. Naming a risk you are not removing is harder than removing it.

No OTLP collector in the Fly topology. The kernel exports telemetry only when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set, so today it exports nowhere — the whole instrumentation is written and unused.

`LICENSE` declares `Copyright (c) 2026 dev_insight`, even though CODEOWNERS points at `@konradcinkusz`. A leftover from a template from another repository, the same one as in two other projects.

Refresh token rotation is serialised in-process only: with more than one web machine, a race will trigger replay detection in authservice and log the user out (D-10). Acceptable at `min_machines_running = 0..1`, blocks horizontal scaling.

repos.name: BlackHoleSim
repos.oneLiner: A Schwarzschild black hole raytracer in C#: one RK4 integrator feeds the CLI, a queued API and a Blazor WASM gallery.
repos.summary: The core integrates photon geodesics in the Schwarzschild metric in the equatorial plane — zero Hamiltonian, an RK4 step over the affine parameter, each ray classified as shadow, accretion disc or background. The same `Raytracer` serves three outputs: a console renderer writing PPM, a minimal API that takes a job onto a `Channel` queue and computes it in a hosted `RenderWorker`, and a Blazor WebAssembly UI with a progress bar and a gallery. Job state and the finished PNG live in Postgres through EF Core. The most interesting decision is not physical but a startup one: migrations run in a separate hosted service **after** the listener comes up, `/health` stays red until the schema is ready, and `RenderWorker` waits on `DatabaseReadyGate` rather than bringing the host down with its first query. Renders are private to an account, but the API holds no key material: tokens are issued by a separate instance of the {{term:ghcr|authservice image from GHCR}}, and the API only verifies them with public keys from JWKS. The operational layer is written out in full — four `fly.toml` files, {{term:tagdeploy|deploy from a tag}} with change detection, scale and destroy workflows, a four-container compose, an {{term:aspire|Aspire}} AppHost — and there is not a single tag in the repository, so it has never been run.
repos.tests: 28 executable cases across five classes: 23 `[Fact]` attributes plus one `[Theory]` with 5 `[InlineData]` rows. Of these, the authorisation boundary is 14 cases in `AuthorizationTests` (9 `[Fact]` and a `[Theory]` with 5 rows) — the earlier figure of 10 came from no count at all. The rest are RK4 convergence, Hamiltonian conservation, state tests and raytracer smoke tests. The numbers come from the attributes in the code (`grep` for `[Fact]`, `[Theory]`, `[InlineData]`, skipping `bin/` and `obj/`) — `dotnet test` was not run in this pass.
repos.ci: Four workflows. Exactly one runs on push: `pages.yml` publishes `docs/` to GitHub Pages on push to `master`, but with a path filter — only `docs/**` and the workflow file itself. None runs on a pull request. `flyio.yml` (519 lines) starts only from a `v*` tag or from `workflow_dispatch`: build, tests, change detection against the previous tag, images built straight into `registry.fly.io` and deployed in the order postgres, auth, api, web; Pages publication is not in that file. On top of that, two `workflow_dispatch` workflows — scale and destroy. Tests and gitleaks therefore live in `scripts/ci-local.sh` and in pre-commit, which the repository itself calls a gap in COMPLIANCE.md.

components.name: BlackHoleSim.ServiceDefaults
components.description: 144 lines of pure infrastructure: `AddServiceDefaults` wires up {{term:otel|OpenTelemetry}} for ASP.NET Core, HttpClient and the runtime, service discovery and `AddStandardResilienceHandler`, and the OTLP exporter only registers itself once `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set. No entities and no DTOs — moving it is a namespace change.

components.name: Konfiguracja i workflowy Fly.io
components.description: Four `fly.toml` files in which the comments carry reasons rather than only values: why only the API has `min_machines_running = 1`, why JWKS goes over the public hostname, why Postgres has no `[http_service]`. The pattern itself — deploy from a tag, diff against the previous tag, a missing app treated as changed — is portable once the names are swapped.

components.name: Skrypty onboardingu i lokalnego CI
components.description: `setup.sh` generates `.env`, the database password and the signing key, installs pre-commit and builds the solution; `ci-local.sh` runs tests, format, gitleaks, a dependency audit, image builds and a compose smoke test. This is in effect the missing PR workflow, only on the developer's side.

components.name: BlackHoleSim.Core
components.description: `IMetric` and `Schwarzschild` with the inverse metric and its radial derivatives, `RK4.Step`, a `Raytracer` parallelised by rows through `Parallel.For`, and PPM and PNG output. The surface is tied to one metric: `State` has the fields t, r, phi, pt, pr, pphi.

components.name: BlackHoleSim.Api
components.description: A minimal API with a `ChannelRenderJobQueue` queue and a worker that recovers jobs left in the Running state after a restart, plus `DatabaseMigrationService`, `DatabaseReadyGate`, per-account rate limiting and JWT verification through JWKS. The queue + worker + schema gate pattern is portable, but the code is not parameterised.

components.name: BlackHoleSim.Web
components.description: Blazor WASM: Render, Gallery, Login, Register, About, plus the `RenderApiClient`, `TokenStore`, `BearerTokenHandler`, `JwtAuthenticationStateProvider` and `AuthSession` layer, with the token refresh after a 401 serialised under a lock so that concurrent requests do not fire three refreshes.

components.name: BlackHoleSim.Tests
components.description: Alongside the numerical tests (RK4 order of convergence, Hamiltonian conservation along a geodesic) sits `AuthorizationTests`, which boots the real API through `WebApplicationFactory` on SQLite with a substituted token and checks that someone else's job returns 404, not 403.

components.name: One-pager i prezentacja beamer
components.description: `docs/index.html` is 601 lines with its own topology SVG and the metric's formulae, published to Pages; `docs/main.tex` is a 450-line presentation on the renderer's implementation. The only portable part is the `beamerthemedeepdiveinto.sty` theme.

overlaps.reason: It runs its own instance of the `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice:v0.3.0` image and verifies its tokens through JWKS, with no source dependency at all. That is the same consumption pattern as in `primates`.
`docs/architecture/COMPLIANCE.md` measures this repository directly against those checklists, and `.claude/settings.json` enables the `architecture-core` plugin from that marketplace.
The same {{term:servicedefaults|shared ServiceDefaults project}} in practically the same shape — two copies of a hundred-odd lines that ought to be one package.
The same calling-card format: a static one-pager in `docs/index.html` published through GitHub Pages.

repos.product: No buyer, and there is no point looking for one — nobody buys Schwarzschild renders. This is a proof project: it shows that numerical physics, background work, JWKS-based authentication and a four-application deployment can be assembled into one coherent whole in which every infrastructure decision has its reasoning written down. The value lies in the channel and in credibility: the one-pager, the beamer presentation, and a CHANGELOG whose Fixed section has fifteen points, ten of which describe a defect together with its mechanism. As a P3 in E-lab it is exactly what it is meant to be, provided the deployment pipeline is ever actually run.
highlights: One RK4 integrator serves three output paths — the CLI, the API and the browser — so the image from the console and the one from the gallery come from identical code, not from two implementations of the same physics.
The API holds no key material: it fetches public keys from the identity service's JWKS, so it can verify a token but cannot issue one. Compromising the API gives no ability to sign.
Someone else's job returns **404, not 403** — a deliberate decision against identifier enumeration, covered by nine facts in `AuthorizationTests`.

The CHANGELOG has one Fixed section with fifteen top-level points, ten of which are entries with the defect in bold and the mechanism described — among them an EF migration without a `.Designer.cs` file (`Database.Migrate` found nothing) and two `.dockerignore` files that Docker never read, because the build context is the root directory.
`AppHost` throws an exception naming the missing file when `secrets/jwt-signing.pem` is absent, instead of quietly falling back to HS256. A configuration failure is loud by design.
gaps: **Zero git tags, with a deploy triggered only by a `v*` tag.** The most involved element in the repository — 519 lines of `flyio.yml` — has not a single documented run, and the existence of the `blackholesim-*` apps cannot be confirmed. The `*.fly.dev` addresses are configuration, not a link.

`docs/architecture/COMPLIANCE.md` item 8 still claims the system has no authentication and marks the JWKS requirement as not applicable. That stopped being true when accounts were added, and nobody recalculated the document.

No workflow on a pull request and no tests on push: `dotnet test` and gitleaks run only on a `v*` tag or locally. The only workflow reacting to a push is `pages.yml`, which publishes `docs/` and checks nothing. A contributor who has not run `pre-commit install` is checked by nothing at all.
Telemetry is instrumented, but there is no collector standing on Fly and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is unset, so nothing is exported in the deployed environment.
PNG renders sit as a blob in the `RenderJobs` table on a 3 GB volume that cannot be shrunk, and there is no retention and no per-account limit.
risks: Name mismatch: the repository and the directory are `black-hole-sim`, but the clone instruction in the README and `\RepoURL` in `docs/main.tex` point at `BlackHoleSim`. The badge above the instruction leads to a different address than the instruction itself.

A hard pin to `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice:v0.3.0`: going back below v0.3.0 breaks login, because older builds sign with HS256 and publish an empty key set. The dependency is deliberate, but it is not resilient to a regression at the provider.

A dozen or so package versions scattered across seven `csproj` files with no `Directory.Packages.props`. {{term:dependabot|Dependabot}} is configured, but without CI on a PR its updates pass through no check at all.
I found no hard-coded credential, but what was checked was the configuration, not the git history — and gitleaks has never run over the full history in CI.
next: Push a `v0.1.0` tag and see whether `flyio.yml` really does stand all four apps up from nothing. Only that verifies the repository's main claim, and only then can the `*.fly.dev` addresses go on the card as links.

Correct item 8 in COMPLIANCE.md to the state after accounts were added, and recalculate the summary in section 1. A document describing a state that no longer exists undermines the whole of the rest of the audit.
Add a pull request workflow with `dotnet test` and gitleaks — it closes item 7 in COMPLIANCE.md and makes Dependabot's updates mean something.
Make the repository address consistent in the README and in `docs/main.tex` as `black-hole-sim`.
Add retention or a per-account render limit before the 3 GB volume becomes a problem with no way back.
repos.headline: A complete deployment pipeline, zero tags — it has never been run

repos.name: BrainTrain 2025
repos.oneLiner: A set of 38 counting and logic exercises, typeset in Beamer with XeLaTeX, released as a PDF in GitHub Releases.
repos.summary: A single-file LaTeX project: `main.tex` assembles a Beamer presentation from five files in `areas/`, which hold 38 exercises in five categories. Each exercise is a pair of slides generated by two macros from `mybraintrainer.sty`: the first slide carries the question, the category badge, the difficulty stars and the time limit, the second carries nothing but the answer plus an optional one-line hint. One layout decision here is interesting: the page format is set by hand to 1080pt × 1920pt with the `landscape` option, so a 16:9 board rather than Beamer's default frame, which makes a slide read like a card for printing rather than a conference foil. A separate commit `01c9d37` cut the step-by-step solutions and left the result alone, which is a deliberate teaching choice rather than a shortcut. The whole publishing layer is one {{term:tagdeploy|tag}}: pushing `v*` builds the PDF in an action and publishes it to Releases, and `.gitignore` deliberately keeps `*.pdf` out of the repository. The trouble is that there is not a single tag in the repo, and nobody in this tree has ever checked whether the typesetting passes at all.
repos.tests: No tests and no verification of the typesetting whatsoever. The review environment has neither `latexmk` nor `xelatex`, so I have not confirmed that `main.tex` compiles without errors.
repos.ci: One workflow, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, triggered only by a push of a `v*` tag: the `build` job typesets `main.tex` through `xu-cheng/latex-action@v4` with XeLaTeX, renames the result to `BrainTrain.pdf` and uploads the artefact, and the `release` job publishes it through `softprops/action-gh-release@v2`. There is no build on push to `main` and none on pull request, so an ordinary commit is not checked at all.

docs.label: README — structure and the level table
Beamer class with the category colours

components.name: mybraintrainer.sty
components.description: The macro layer in 101 lines: the `excounter` counter, `\DifficultyStars` on an `ifcase` over 1–3, the time and category badges drawn in TikZ, and the pair `\ExerciseSlide[badge]{stars}{time}{question}` and `\AnswerSlide[badge]{answer}{hint}`, which numbers the exercises itself and opens a `subsection` for each one. The parameterisation knows no arithmetic and no Polish beyond the words in the frame titles.

components.name: mybraintrainer.cls
components.description: A class inheriting from `beamer`: five category colours given directly as HTML (6BAED6, FD8D3C, 9C27B0, 388E3C, D81B60), matching colours for the section buttons, a footer with a link to the repository, and a replacement of Beamer's navigation symbols with a button back to the table of contents. Apart from one hard-coded URL this is a neutral skeleton for any set of cards.

components.name: Workflow build & release
components.description: The 'tag → PDF in Releases' pattern in two jobs, without committing the artefact to the repository. To move it elsewhere you swap `root_file` and the output file name; both actions are pinned to the major only.

components.name: main.tex
components.description: Ties the whole thing together: sets the geometry through `PassOptionsToPackage` before `documentclass`, typesets the title slide, an introductory slide with four blocks and a clickable table of contents made of five coloured buttons, then pulls in the five files from `areas/`. The number 38 is written into the slide text by hand.

components.name: areas/
components.description: The content proper, in five files: basic arithmetic, order of operations, logic puzzles, sequences and patterns, mixed challenges. Each exercise is exactly one call to `\ExerciseSlide` and one to `\AnswerSlide`, with a subcategory badge. The encoding of Polish characters is not consistent here: files 1 and 2 use no accent command at all and stand on raw UTF-8, files 3-5 use them 32, 12 and 20 times respectively, but each of those also has a few raw characters — 64 accent commands against 37 raw UTF-8 characters in total.

overlaps.reason: The same shape: a LaTeX source with its own preamble and macros, a PDF build in CI, the content as the only product. Only an order of magnitude smaller and with no verification of the typesetting at all.
Also a LaTeX book with its own macros and a `latexmk` pipeline, so the typesetting, encoding and CI conventions are shared and worth settling in one place.
The same learning mechanic — a question/answer pair repeated a few dozen times — only in a different medium, and with no progress path in either case.

repos.product: No buyer, and there is no point pretending otherwise. 38 exercises with no application, no timing beyond a stopwatch in your hand, no progress path and no licensed brand is material for one evening, not a product; to sell anything here you would need several hundred exercises and a variant generator instead of content typed in by hand. The real value is personal (something to print for yourself or for a child) and technical-portfolio: this is the smallest example in the set, readable in a quarter of an hour, of a LaTeX pipeline with an automatic release. The {{term:mit|MIT-0}} licence removes even the attribution requirement, so the author has deliberately given up the only return such a set could yield.
highlights: The 38 exercises, counted by `\ExerciseSlide` calls in `areas/`, match to the last one the number declared on the introductory slide and the number of `\AnswerSlide` calls.
The entire mechanics of the set fits in **101 lines** of `mybraintrainer.sty` and comes down to two macros with an automatic exercise counter.
The answer slides show the result only — commit `01c9d37` deliberately removed the step-by-step solutions so that the route cannot be peeked at.
The coloured table of contents is clickable both ways: five `hyperlink` buttons to `hypertarget`, and the way back replaces Beamer's navigation symbols instead of adding a bar of its own.
The whole distribution channel is one `v*` {{term:tagdeploy|tag}}; `.gitignore` excludes `*.pdf` with a comment saying the artefact goes out through Releases only.
gaps: **The repository name does not agree with itself.** The README and the class footer link to `konradcinkusz/BrainTrain`, while the remote is `konradcinkusz/brain-train`, so both badges (CI and release version) show something untrue or do not render at all.
**Zero tags in the repo**, so the release pipeline has never started from this tree, and the README describes publishing the PDF as a process that works.
CI builds nothing on push to `main` and nothing on pull request, so a broken `.tex` will go in unnoticed and only surface at the first tag.

The preamble is inconsistent with the build: no `fontspec` and no `polyglossia` despite XeLaTeX, but `inputenc utf8` and `fontenc T1`, which are redundant under XeLaTeX. Polish hyphenation is not switched on at all.

**The encoding of Polish characters drifts within `areas/` itself, not only between `main.tex` and the exercises.** Across the five exercise files there are 64 accent commands (`\k{a}`, `\'{o}`, `\l{}`, `\'c`, `\'s`) and 37 raw UTF-8 characters, but the split runs file by file: `1-arytmetyka-podstawy.tex` and `2-kolejnosc-dzialan.tex` have not a single accent command (but 1 and 25 raw characters), while `3-zagadki-logiczne.tex`, `4-ciagi-i-wzorce.tex` and `5-mieszane-wyzwania.tex` have 32, 12 and 20 accent commands and still 5, 2 and 4 raw characters. No file holds to one convention consistently. On top of that, a typo in `areas/3-zagadki-logiczne.tex:31` ('naprawde' instead of 'naprawdę') and an unused `\ChunkedTOC` macro defined in `mybraintrainer.sty:91`.
next: Settle the name: rename the repository to `BrainTrain` or fix the three URLs in the README and the `.cls` footer to `brain-train`. Today the badges lie the moment the page is opened.
Add a job to `ci.yml` that builds `main.tex` on `push` and `pull_request`, so broken typesetting is visible before a tag rather than during a release.
Run the build (locally or from a branch in CI) and only then push `v1.0.0`. Today there is no evidence that the PDF is produced at all.
Sort the preamble out for XeLaTeX: `fontspec` plus `polyglossia` with Polish, out with `inputenc` and `fontenc T1`, and settle the character encoding on raw UTF-8 across every file.

Decide what becomes of the set: either write further sections, or write a generator of arithmetic exercises that produces files into `areas/`. Typing them in by hand will not reach a number that makes sense.
risks: A name collision in three places at once: `BrainTrain` in the README, in the class footer and in the artefact name, against `brain-train` as the actual slug. This breaks the badges and makes the repository harder to find.

The name itself is generic and already taken by existing commercial brain-training applications, and the README refers outright to the *Trening Mózgu* series; with any distribution that is a trademark risk.

The repository is effectively abandoned. The content came in over three non-merge commits, not two: `bf4992b` (7 files, +409), `e6e6cc5` (5 files, +544) and `01c9d37` (6 files, +99/-411), preceded by `a7ea22d` 'Initial commit' (2 files, +23) and closed by a single merge of PR #1 — 5 commits in all, figures from `git log --numstat --no-merges`. Last movement 2026-07-19, zero tags.
Both actions in the workflow (`xu-cheng/latex-action@v4`, `softprops/action-gh-release@v2`) are pinned to the major, so the first run will happen on a version nobody here has seen.
repos.headline: Zero tags, zero builds on main — the PDF release has never run

repos.name: Building AI Coding Assistants in the Age of Foundation Models
repos.oneLiner: A LaTeX article on coding-assistant architecture: three layers, RAG for code and {{term:mcp|MCP}}, with an implementation path in C#.
repos.summary: A single-file academic article (class `article`, ten chapter files pulled in from `main.tex`) on how commercial coding assistants are built and how to build your own. The text breaks the system into three layers: completion through the LSP on a 100-200 ms budget, chat with context assembly, and an agent layer with a tool loop and self-verification through compilation and tests. Chapters 4 and 5 are the core: the indexing pipeline (AST-aware chunking through Tree-sitter, code embeddings, cross-encoder reranking) and {{term:mcp|Model Context Protocol}} as the integration {{term:substrat|substrate}}, with its host, client and server roles. The most interesting substantive decision is in section 4.4: rather than stopping at vector search, the author carries the LspRag pattern over to {{term:roslyn|Roslyn}} and OmniSharp, adding an exact walk of the symbol graph from the language server where textual similarity fails. The article states one falsifiable thesis about retrieval quality dominating model quality, and chapter 8 gives the design of the experiment that would settle it. The experiment has not been run, and every number in the text comes from the 22 cited sources, not from the author's own measurements. The repository has one commit from 2026-04-26 and 17 files: this is a finished draft of a text, not a project under development.
repos.tests: No tests: the repository holds no executable code and no test project. Nor has it been verified that the document typesets, because the environment had neither `latexmk`, nor `xelatex`, nor `plantuml`.
repos.ci: One 53-line `ci.yml` workflow: it installs plantuml and graphviz, renders `figures/*.plantuml` to PNG, typesets the document with XeLaTeX, renames it to `AI_Coding_Assistant.pdf` and publishes it as a GitHub Release. It fires only on a push of a `v*` tag ({{term:tagdeploy|release on tag}}), so an ordinary commit or pull request is not checked at all.
