components.name: main.tex: the preamble and the document driver
components.description: Class `article` 12pt a4paper, `geometry` at 2.5 cm, `hyperref` with coloured links, and a custom `csharpstyle` whose keyword list is extended with `record`, `required`, `McpServer` and `Tool`. The whole text comes in through ten `\input`s, so the preamble is independent of the prose.

components.name: Pipeline build i release
components.description: A sequence of plantuml, `latex-action` and `gh-release` across two jobs, passing the PDF between them as an artefact. It knows not one name from this article beyond the output file name, so it moves to any repository holding a LaTeX document.

components.name: Chapter 4: retrieval for code
components.description: A four-stage indexing pipeline with a two-level chunk hierarchy (the class as parent, the method as child) and incremental reindexing on a file watcher. Section 4.4 adds a walk of the LSP symbol graph on top of vector search, and cites LspRag's line-coverage increase of 213% for Java and 174% for Go.

components.name: Chapter 6: the C# implementation path
components.description: Five listings over 198 lines: hosting an MCP server through `AddMcpServer` and `WithStdioServerTransport`, tools carrying the `McpServerToolType` and `McpServerTool` attributes, a vector index, a chat layer on Semantic Kernel, and `.vscode/mcp.json`. They refer to types that exist nowhere (`ICodebaseIndex`, `TreeSitterChunker`, `Reranker`), and have never been compiled.

components.name: Descriptive chapters 1-3, 5, 7-9
components.description: A taxonomy of tools, the three-layer architecture, MCP, model choice, limitations and conclusions. Chapter 8 is the important one here, because it holds the text's only study design, with three retrieval conditions against a fixed model.

components.name: Bibliografia
components.description: A `thebibliography` environment with 22 entries, in which peer-reviewed work (Lewis 2020, ReAct, SWE-bench, Lost in the Middle, LspRag / arXiv 2510.22210) sits next to blog posts and marketing copy. The `kinde2026` key is cited nowhere, and will print regardless.

components.name: Figura 1: diagram warstw
components.description: A 78-line component diagram: IDE and CLI, the LSP/MCP layer, orchestration in Semantic Kernel, the retrieval subsystem with its vector store and symbol resolver, and the model API. The PNG is in `.gitignore` and is produced only in CI, so a change to the figure reviews as a text diff.

overlaps.reason: The same .NET domain plus MCP, and the same LaTeX format. The article condenses into a dozen-odd pages what maf-book develops over 246. Both works carry the same debt too: an experiment designed and never run.

Both texts describe the orchestration layer above foundation models, retrieval and context management, only from two sides: llm-book from Python and LangGraph, the article from C# and Semantic Kernel.

The same subject from the other side: the article describes how a coding assistant is built, CopilotScope measures telemetry from five such assistants. The three-layer model from chapter 3 is a ready-made vocabulary for that collector.
Topical overlap by name: the agent loop and tool calls from chapter 3. The contents of that repository have not been verified.

repos.product: No buyer. This is channel material and evidence of competence: it shows the author understands coding-assistant architecture, MCP and RAG from the .NET side, which is the side almost nobody writes about. Real value appears only once the chapter 8 experiment has been run, because nobody has published good data on retrieval dominating model quality measured against a specific repository, and the study design is already here. Until then the article is a good survey whose thesis remains a declaration.
highlights: The thesis is stated openly and falsifiably, with a design ready to go: a fixed model, three retrieval conditions (none, baseline, enriched), and measurement of correctness and hallucination rate on tasks from a real repository. A declaration of this kind in a survey text is rare.

Section 4.4 carries the LspRag pattern (arXiv 2510.22210) over to {{term:roslyn|Roslyn}} and OmniSharp: vector search supplies candidates, and `definition` and `references` calls to the language server walk the symbol graph where textual similarity does not reach. The source work reports +213% line coverage for Java and +174% for Go.
A complete and coherent draft in one commit: 6,964 words across ten chapters, an abstract, a table of contents, 22 bibliography entries, a model comparison table and a layer diagram.
The diagram is kept solely as a 78-line PlantUML source, with the PNG in `.gitignore` and generated in CI. A change to the figure reviews as a diff, not as a swapped binary.
CI closes the whole publishing loop in one file: render the diagrams, XeLaTeX, artefact, GitHub Release with the renamed PDF.
gaps: **The central thesis is not verified.** Chapter 8 gives the experiment design and reports no result at all; the article contains not one measurement of the author's own. That is what separates this text from work with an original contribution.

The repository holds no tag, and CI fires only on a push of a `v*` tag. The PDF badge in the README links to `releases/latest/download/AI_Coding_Assistant.pdf`, which most likely does not exist, and the CI badge shows the status of a workflow that has never run.
No ordinary commit or PR is checked. A LaTeX syntax error would surface only at the attempt to release, that is, at the worst possible moment.

The `kinde2026` entry is in the bibliography and is cited in no chapter; `thebibliography` will print it regardless. The bibliography also mixes peer-reviewed work with marketing posts, and it is the latter the market figures in chapter 1 come from.

`main.tex` loads `inputenc` with the `utf8` option, although CI typesets with XeLaTeX, where the package is redundant. The files are pure ASCII, so the build survives it, but it is a leftover from pdflatex.
risks: An identity mismatch: `main.tex` and LICENSE sign the article as K.C. Voss, while the single commit is signed Konrad Cinkusz. In a portfolio under your own name this has to be reconciled or explained outright.

The C# listings have never been compiled and call types that do not exist (`ICodebaseIndex`, `TreeSitterChunker`, `Reranker`), and nowhere does the text note that they are sketches. A reader may take them for working code.

Names in the MCP SDK and Semantic Kernel age fast, and the article itself admits the SDK is in preview, yet it pins no version. The maf-book notes indicate that the `McpClientFactory.CreateAsync` used in the listing has already given way to `McpClient.CreateAsync`.
One commit and zero activity since 2026-04-26. From the outside it looks abandoned, even though the text is finished.
next: Settle the authorship: either sign the article under your own name, or keep the pseudonym deliberately. Today the document and the git history say different things.
Add a CI job on `push` and `pull_request` that typesets the document without publishing a release. At present nothing guards against text that does not compile.
Push a `v1.0.0` tag so that both badges in the README stop pointing at an artefact that is not there.

Compile the five listings from chapter 6 in a small solution against the real ModelContextProtocol and Semantic Kernel packages, correct the type names, and note in the text which versions this was checked against.
Run the chapter 8 experiment against one real C# repository and put the results in. That is the only change that turns a survey into work with an original contribution.
repos.headline: A falsifiable thesis with not one measurement, and the PDF badge leads to an empty release

repos.name: CardsGame
repos.oneLiner: A five-card draw poker engine where a model, a heuristic and a person sit at the table through the same tool boundary.
repos.summary: A game of draw poker in which `CardsGame.Engine` has no I/O and no dependencies and is the only authority on whether a draw is legal and how strong a hand is — everything else asks it. The LLM agent gets exactly two tools, `GetHandState` and `ProposeDiscard`, and `PokerTools` is an instance class with the seat number closed over in the constructor, so there is no argument by which the model could play for someone else; the other players' cards are not in the returned object. The most interesting decision, though, is in `AgentPlayer`: after a turn it **asks the engine whether the draw actually happened**, rather than parsing the move out of the model's prose, and a rejection is an ordinary outcome carrying a reason back — three attempts and the seat stands pat. Who sits in a seat (Foundry, Azure OpenAI, a heuristic, a person) is an entry in the `PokerPlayers:<key>` section rather than code, and an unknown key falls back to the heuristic with a warning instead of throwing. Beyond the game there is `POST /simulations`: one line-up over up to 1000 hands, win rate with ties split, rejection rate, forfeits and p95 turn latency, repeatable through a seed. {{term:aspire|Aspire}} composes the lot — server, Blazor Server, console client — and it starts with no account, no key and no Docker. The one thing never done is playing even a single hand against a live model.
repos.tests: Three test projects (Engine, Agents, Server): 102 `[Fact]`, 32 `[Theory]`, 134 `[InlineData]` and 2 `[MemberData]` expanded over the nine hand rules, so roughly 254 cases — consistent with the '250+' the README declares. The number comes from counting attributes in the sources, not from a `dotnet test` run.
repos.ci: Three workflows. `ci.yml` has a separate `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` job, a build+test matrix on ubuntu/windows/macos with `fail-fast: false`, a CLI smoke test feeding stdin, a publish check for four RIDs and `permissions: contents: read`. `codeql.yml` has a weekly cron, but the `analyze` job is conditional, because the repository is private and has no code scanning; `release.yml` waits for a `v*` tag that has never existed.

components.name: CardsGame.AppHost i ServiceDefaults
components.description: 116 lines of shared infrastructure: {{term:otel|OTel}} self-instrumentation, health checks, service discovery and HTTP resilience, without a single domain entity. AppHost waits for the server's `/health` before letting the UI and the console client in.

components.name: CardsGame.Engine
components.description: 1,193 lines with no dependencies and no I/O: `Card` as a `readonly record struct`, nine `IHandRule` rules with separate tiebreakers, `Deck` with a real draw pile and `DrawPokerGame` as a state machine. Hand precedence follows from `HandCategory` rather than from a separate `Priority` field, which in the previous version managed to drift away from poker.

components.name: PokerTools
components.description: Two methods with `[Description]` attributes and nothing else. The class is an instance class holding the seat number from its constructor, so the model's tool surface is {{term:hermetyczny|sealed off}} from the other players at the level of the type, not of validation.

components.name: AgentPlayer i PokerAgentFactory
components.description: A turn loop with a budget of three attempts and verification on the engine's side instead of parsing the model's reply. The factory has two paths, because `AIProjectClient.AsAIAgent` builds an `AIAgent` bypassing the intermediate `IChatClient`.

components.name: PokerPlayerFactory
components.description: The only place that decides what fills a given chair — Foundry, Azure OpenAI, a heuristic or a person — on the basis of configuration. A missing key degrades to the heuristic with a warning, so a fresh clone plays without any account at all.

components.name: SimulationRunner
components.description: A comparison harness: hands run sequentially, because parallelism would falsify the latency of the model seats, ties are split so that win rate sums to one, p95 by the nearest-rank method. A human seat is rejected, because there is nobody to answer.

components.name: HumanDrawGate
components.description: A `TaskCompletionSource` with `RunContinuationsAsynchronously`, so that the rest of the hand does not finish inline on the HTTP request thread. It carries the engine's `RejectionReason` back to the seat's view, so a person gets the same message as a model.

components.name: ScriptedAgent
components.description: An `AIAgent` stub playing back a planned sequence of tool calls. It gives determinism in the retry and forfeit tests without a network or an Azure subscription, including the case of an agent that never works.

overlaps.reason: The same pattern carried over to another game: `HumanMoveGate` against `HumanDrawGate`, `ChessMetrics` against `GameMetrics`, a tool boundary tied to one side. Comments in the code refer to ChessMas by name.
Also a perfect-information game driven by models, with move validation on the engine's side instead of trust in the model's output.
`SimulationRunner` is in effect an agent benchmark: win rate, rejection rate, forfeits and latency under a repeatable seed. That one measures the same things on tasks, this one on hands.
The repository runs on `Microsoft.Agents.AI` 1.15.0 and `.Foundry`, that is on exactly the API the book describes — and on the version the book has not yet caught up with.
The src/tests layout, the bare xunit and the separation of server DTOs from UI DTOs are copied from there; the changelog and the comments say so outright.

repos.product: No buyer, and there is no point pretending otherwise. This is an {{term:evidence|evidence}} project: it shows how to shut a language model inside a boundary that cannot be talked around, and how to measure the quality of play rather than whether HTTP returned 200. The simulation runner comes closest to being useful, but until a live model has been run through it, there is not a single number in it to publish. The portfolio value is real, the product value zero.
gaps: **The model seats have never played against a live Foundry or Azure OpenAI deployment.** The README says so honestly, but it means the repository's main claim has not a single measurement with a real model behind it — only the construction tests and `ScriptedAgent` cover it.
The sample simulation result in the README is four copies of the heuristic playing each other. It is a demonstration of the mechanics served in the place where the reader expects a result.
The repository is private, so the `analyze` job in `codeql.yml` is conditional and the analysis never runs. The CodeQL badge in the README therefore describes a workflow that does nothing.
Zero git tags against a fully written `release.yml` — no CLI artefact has ever been produced, and the README still says 'Not yet released'.

No containerisation, no authentication and no persistence; `HandRegistry` keeps 200 hands in memory. All three are listed in the 'Deliberately not done' section, so this is deliberate debt, not debt that was missed.
next: Stand up one Foundry deployment and run a few hundred hands of a model-against-three-heuristics line-up. **Keep the raw event streams, not just the summary rows** — repeating the run only to recover the traces costs the same again.
Put that result in the README in place of the four heuristics, and mark plainly what still has not been measured.
Settle the name: the directory is `cards-game`, while the badge, the `git clone` and the URL in the README point at `konradcinkusz/CardsGame`. Two names for one project in one README.
Tag `v0.1.0`, so that `release.yml` stops being a declaration, and while you are there check how much the binaries really weigh without trimming.
Open the repository or turn on code scanning — otherwise remove the CodeQL badge, because it promises a check that is not there.
highlights: The changelog records **seven real correctness bugs** from the previous version, among them a parser registering three of the nine rules (a royal flush reported as `Flush`) and `Rank.Ace` with a value of 0, which made an ace-high straight undetectable. That is rare: a repository that publishes its own domain mistakes instead of quietly rewriting them.

`PokerTools` is an instance class and closes over the seat number in its constructor, and the other players' cards never reach the returned object. The boundary is a property of the type, not a condition in a validator.
After a turn `AgentPlayer` asks the engine whether the draw actually happened, rather than parsing the move out of the model's prose; three rejections with a reason returned and the seat stands pat.

CI builds and tests on ubuntu, windows and macos, checks formatting in a separate job, runs a CLI smoke test feeding stdin and a publish check for four RIDs. `TreatWarningsAsErrors` is on globally in `Directory.Build.props`.
Roughly 254 test cases with no network and no credentials — every seat at the table is a heuristic or a `ScriptedAgent`, including an agent proposing an illegal draw and an agent that never works.
risks: Name collision: the directory is `cards-game`, while the README, the CI badge and the `git clone` command point at `https://github.com/konradcinkusz/CardsGame.git`.
`FluentAssertions` was removed on purpose, because from version 8 it carries Xceed's proprietary licence. An automatic Dependabot bump could put it back into an MIT project with no signal at all.

The pinning runs ahead (Aspire 13.4.6, `Microsoft.Agents.AI` 1.15.0, SDK 10.0.100 with `rollForward latestMinor`) — without a periodic check against NuGet it will go stale faster than the project gets picked up again.
repos.headline: The boundary holds and is tested; no live model has played a single hand

repos.name: Chess Agent System with LLM
repos.oneLiner: Two LLM agents play chess against each other — once in Python with Streamlit, once in .NET 8 on a hand-written chess engine.
repos.summary: The repository carries two parallel implementations of one idea. The first, from August 2025, is Streamlit over `python-chess` with an agent factory, a random agent and a headless `simulate_game`. The second, from April 2026, is a full rewrite: ASP.NET Core Web API, Blazor WebAssembly behind nginx, SignalR for streaming moves and PostgreSQL through EF Core, run as three containers in `docker-compose`. The most interesting engineering decision is dropping the chess library on the .NET side: `ChessBoard.cs` is 692 lines and handles FEN, SAN, legal move generation with castling and en passant, checkmate, stalemate, the 50-move rule, repetition and rendering the board to SVG on its own. The second thing worth noting is the {{term:audit|audit}} layer: every prompt attempt lands in the `PromptLogs` table together with the model's full response and a success flag, and three admin pages let you browse it filtered by game. The engine, the API, the database schema and the panel are finished; what is unfinished is gluing them into something you can run — the README describes only the abandoned Python branch.
repos.tests: Ten test functions in four files under `tests/`: `test_agents.py` 3, `test_game.py` 3, `test_utils.py` 3, `test_simulation.py` 1. The directory has six files — the other two are `conftest.py` and `__init__.py`, in which `test_board`, despite the name, is a fixture (`@pytest.fixture`) rather than a test. All of it in Python; on the .NET side there are no test projects at all. A run could not be confirmed (no pytest and no `chess` module in the environment), but two functions in `test_agents.py` call `pytest.patch`, which does not exist in the pytest API, so those certainly fall over.
repos.ci: No CI — the repository has no `.github` directory and no workflow. So nobody knows whether the .NET stack compiles.

docs.label: README — describes only the Streamlit variant

components.name: Prompt audit and the admin panel
components.description: The `PromptLog` entity records, for **every attempt**, the model, the persona, the full prompt text, the response and a success flag; the controller exposes statistics, a list of games and a paged view of prompts filtered by player. Moving it elsewhere takes more than cutting the `GameId` foreign key, though: the constructor is `AdminController(IDbContextFactory<AppDbContext> dbFactory)`, and `AppDbContext` exposes only `DbSet<Game>`, `DbSet<MoveRecord>` and `DbSet<PromptLog>`, each of which all five actions use. Four of the five signatures return domain types — `Task<ActionResult<AdminStats>> GetStats()`, `Task<ActionResult<List<AdminGameSummary>>> GetGames(string?, int, int)`, `Task<ActionResult<AdminGameDetail>> GetGame(Guid)` and `Task<ActionResult<List<AdminPromptLogItem>>> GetPrompts(Guid?, string?, int, int)`; the only domain-neutral one is `GetPlayers()`, which returns `List<string>`. What is portable is the prompt/response/success pattern itself, not this code.

components.name: ChessBoard — silnik szachowy w C#
components.description: 692 lines without a single external dependency: FEN both ways, SAN, legal move generation with castling and en passant, seven game states including insufficient material and repetition, plus `MaterialCounts`, `KingSafety`, `SimpleEval` and `ToSvg`. Self-contained, but described end to end by the `Piece`, `ChessMove` and `GameStatus` types.

components.name: LlmChessAgent and the validation loop
components.description: The prompt assembles the FEN, the material balance, the recent moves and the full list of legal moves in SAN, sends it at temperature 0.3 with a 15-token output limit, then checks the response against that list and retries up to `MaxRetries` times. Once the attempts run out it plays the first legal move — and returns `Success = true`.

components.name: GameService i ChessGameSession
components.description: Active games live in a `ConcurrentDictionary` in process memory, written to Postgres in parallel. `ChessGameSession` serialises moves with a single `SemaphoreSlim` so that autoplay does not get in its own way.

components.name: GameHub — the move stream over SignalR
components.description: Broadcasts five events to the game's group, including `OnRetryAttempt`, so the UI sees the model's failed attempts too. Autoplay is a loop in `Task.Run` with a `CancellationTokenSource` per connection, cancelled both by `StopAutoPlay` and by `OnDisconnectedAsync`.

components.name: Warstwa danych EF Core
components.description: Three entities with cascade delete, a unique index on `(GameId, Ply)` and default values on the Postgres side (`gen_random_uuid`, `now`). The migration runs itself at application start, so the first `docker-compose up` creates the schema with no manual step.

components.name: ChessBlazor — SPA i trzy strony admina
components.description: `Index.razor` assembles the agent configuration, the board, the position analysis and the move history; `GameHubService` wraps `HubConnection` with automatic reconnect. The admin pages alone are over 1,000 lines of Razor.

components.name: The Python/Streamlit branch
components.description: The original over `python-chess`: an LLM agent and a random one, per-persona prompts, a logger with a timestamp and `simulate_game` for a game without a UI. Frozen since the first commit and replaced by the rewrite, yet it still sits at the root and it is the one the README describes.

overlaps.reason: The same domain and the same idea — a multi-agent system playing chess. Two repositories on the same subject in one portfolio need either separating or merging.
A shared thread: building a prompt for action selection and validating the model's response against a list of permitted moves.
Both set LLM agents against each other and log the run for later analysis.
A game as a proving ground for agents, with hand-written rules and its own model of the game state.
The `PromptLogs` table is the seed of what is done properly there — recording the prompt, the response and the outcome as material for judging session quality.

repos.product: **No buyer.** That language models play chess badly is well documented, so the product itself has no audience and there is no point pretending otherwise. The value is in credibility and in craft: a chess engine written from scratch in C# plus a complete ASP.NET Core + SignalR + Blazor WASM + EF Core + Postgres stack in `docker-compose` is a sensible code sample to bring to an interview. The prompt audit thread is valuable separately, because it shows thinking about agent observability rather than about the model call alone.
highlights: A chess engine in **692 lines of C# with no external library**: FEN, SAN, castling, en passant, checkmate, stalemate, insufficient material, the 50-move rule, repetition and rendering the board to SVG.

A three-container stack in which the API **has no port exposed to the host** — nginx proxies `/api/`, `/health` and the WebSocket on `/gamehub` with `proxy_read_timeout 86400s`, and Postgres has a `pg_isready` healthcheck.

Every prompt attempt, failed ones included, goes into `PromptLogs` with its full text and a success flag; retries are additionally broadcast to the UI as `OnRetryAttempt`, so you can see how many times the model gave an illegal move.
The model's response is validated against the generated list of legal moves rather than parsed and hoped over — the 15-token output limit forces bare SAN notation instead of an argument.
Two EF Core migrations with a unique index on `(GameId, Ply)`, applied automatically by `MigrateAsync()` at container start.
gaps: **The README describes only the Streamlit variant** and says not a word about the `chess-dotnet` directory, which is the larger and newer part of the repository. The clone instruction points at `chess-agent-system-with-llm.git`, a different repository name.

A routing conflict in Blazor: `Home.razor` and `Index.razor` both carry `@page "/"`. This was not verified by running it (no .NET SDK in this environment), but to the Blazor router these are ambiguous routes.

The admin panel and the whole of `AdminController` have **no authentication** — grepping for `Authorize` and `AddAuthentication` in `chess-dotnet` returns nothing, and `/api/admin/prompts` exposes the full text of prompts and responses. CORS is `SetIsOriginAllowed(_ => true)` together with `AllowCredentials`.

Once its attempts run out, `LlmChessAgent` plays the first legal move and returns `Success = true`, so in the database and in the UI the fallback move looks identical to a decision by the model. That corrupts the only data the audit layer was built for in the first place.

Games live only in process memory — after a container restart `GET /api/games/{id}` returns 404, even though the game is sitting in Postgres. On top of that, `PlayerName` is in the DTO, the entity, the migration and the admin filters, but `ChessApiClient.CreateGameAsync` never sends it.
next: Settle which implementation is the real one: if it is .NET, move `src/` and `tests/` to `legacy/` and rewrite the README around `chess-dotnet` — with `docker-compose up`, the `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` variables and the `/admin` and `/swagger` addresses.
Delete `Home.razor`, `Weather.razor` and `Counter.razor` (template leftovers) so the duplicate `@page "/"` goes away, and check whether the application comes up in docker-compose at all.
Add an xUnit project and cover `ChessBoard` with perft tests from several known positions. Without that, the claim that the hand-written engine is correct has nothing behind it.
Protect `/api/admin` with at least a header carrying a token from configuration, and narrow CORS to the frontend's single origin.
Distinguish, in `MoveResult`, a move chosen by the model from the fallback first legal move and record that flag — otherwise the prompt logs are no use for any analysis of how well the model does.
risks: A name collision: the README tells you to clone `chess-agent-system-with-llm`, the directory is called `llm-multi-agent-chess`, and in the portfolio it stands next to `chess-mas`. From the outside this looks like three different projects.

A panel with no authentication plus a frontend container on port 80 means the full text of the prompts is public from the first `docker-compose up`. The {{term:blast|blast radius}} is small, because nobody has deployed this, but the configuration is ready to be copied.
`docker-compose.yml` has a default `POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-changeme`, and `ChessApi/appsettings.json` carries `Password=changeme` outright in a versioned file.
Stale Python pins from the first commit: `openai==1.0.0`, `streamlit==1.24.0`, `python-dotenv==0.19.0` — code dead since August 2025 that nobody has touched since.
repos.headline: 692-line chess engine done, README describes the abandoned Python branch

repos.name: ChessMas
repos.oneLiner: Two LLM agents play chess, and move legality is decided solely by a deterministic rules engine.
repos.summary: A port of the `llm-multi-agent-chess` prototype from Python and Streamlit to .NET 10, assembled by {{term:aspire|Aspire}} 13.4.6 out of six source projects and two test projects. Each side of the board is an independent `AIAgent` from {{term:maf|Microsoft Agent Framework}} 1.15.0, and the choice of backend (Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Foundry, local Ollama or a human) is an entry in `appsettings`, not a branch in the code. The most important decision fits in one sentence: `ChessMas.Engine` is the only authority on legality. The agent calls `get_board_state`, gets a FEN together with the full list of legal moves in UCI and SAN, proposes a move through `propose_move`, and `TryApplyMove` matches the proposal against a `Move` object generated by the engine instead of parsing a string. That is a direct answer to the failure mode of the original prototype, in which the model reconstructed the position from prose and lost track of the board. Cost accounting against real `AgentRunResponse.Usage` and four {{term:otel|OTel}} metrics are bolted on, but the whole thing has **four commits, no persistence and no recorded evidence that a game was ever played here with a real model**.
repos.tests: 26 `[Fact]` methods and zero `[Theory]` across two projects: 15 for the engine, 5 for the cost arithmetic, 6 for the human move gate. None of them needs an API key; the number that pass has not been verified, because what was counted is attributes, not runs.
repos.ci: `ci.yml` does a restore, a Release build and `dotnet test` with the trx logger and an upload of the results artefact; no Docker and no secrets. `pages.yml` publishes the `docs/` directory to GitHub Pages, and `dependabot.yml` watches NuGet weekly in three groups. The CHANGELOG records that the workflow initially triggered on `main` while the default branch was `master`, so for a while it never ran at all.

metrics.label: Model backends selectable in the UI

docs.label: Changelog listing the guessed APIs that did not exist

components.name: HumanMoveGate
components.description: The bridge between a loop running in the background and a synchronous HTTP request: one `TaskCompletionSource` per turn, re-armed after every rejection, with a registry keyed by `gameId` and side. The orchestrator suspends on an `await` instead of polling, and the 91 lines know nothing about chess.

components.name: ChessMas.ServiceDefaults
components.description: {{term:servicedefaults|The shared Aspire project}}: export of traces and metrics over OTLP, health checks, service discovery and `HttpClient` resilience. No domain entities, copyable into any .NET solution.

components.name: GameCostTracker + ModelPricingCatalog
components.description: Multiplies real `AgentRunResponse.Usage` by the price list in the `ModelPricing` configuration section. A model with no entry reports `null`, never USD 0, and every price entry carries a dated `Note` field with its source. It is not portable without rework: `GameCostTracker.cs` has `using ChessMas.Engine;`, and the domain type `ChessMas.Engine.Side` sits in the public surface — `RecordPly(int plyNumber, Side side, long inputTokens, long outputTokens)`, the record `PlyCost(int PlyNumber, Side Side, long InputTokens, long OutputTokens, decimal? EstimatedCostUsd)` and, through the `ByPly` list, `GameCostSummary` as well. `ModelPricingCatalog` on its own is free of it.

components.name: ChessMas.Engine
components.description: The {{term:determinizm|deterministic}} authority on the rules. `GetSnapshot` returns a FEN, the list of legal moves in UCI and SAN, a check flag and the history; `TryApplyMove` is the only place where the board state changes. SAN is computed on a helper board reconstructed from the FEN, so as not to touch the live position.

components.name: ChessMas.Agents
components.description: The tool boundary. `ChessTools` exposes `GetBoardState` and `ProposeMove` as `AIFunction`, each instance bound to one side, so the white agent has no physical way to propose a move for black. The factory has two construction paths: through {{term:ichatclient|IChatClient}} and through `AIProjectClient.AsAIAgent` for Foundry.

components.name: GameOrchestrator + minimal API
components.description: An explicit `while` loop rather than a MAF Workflow graph, because the end condition is judged by the engine, not the model. Five endpoints (`POST /games`, `GET .../state`, `/outcome`, `/cost`, `POST .../move`) and 276 lines without a single test.

components.name: ChessMetrics
components.description: Three counters and a histogram: `chess.moves.proposed`, `chess.moves.rejected`, `chess.ply.duration_ms`, `chess.games.completed`, tagged by side and status. The rejected-proposal rate is intended here as raw material for ranking backends.

components.name: ChessMas.Web
components.description: Blazor Server with a board drawn from scratch out of the FEN field, without any external JS library, and clickable chips of the legal moves for the human. It polls the orchestrator every 400 ms during its own turn and every 1 s otherwise.

overlaps.reason: A direct port of that Python/Streamlit prototype; the README names it as the source and describes which failure mode of that version this architecture fixes.
The README and a comment in `ChessMetrics` point to CopilotScope as the source of the pattern: Aspire composition, OTel from day one, and the approach to scoring.
Both measure model behaviour in an agent loop and count token cost, except that ChessMas does it on a single task and says itself that it is not a benchmark.
The same subject, Microsoft Agent Framework in .NET, from the side of working code rather than book text: `AsAIAgent` and `AIFunctionFactory` are used here and described there.

repos.product: No buyer, and the README closes that route itself, saying that this is not a benchmark of playing strength, that one game proves nothing, and that the cost is an estimate against a price list, not an invoice. This is a credibility project: it shows that the author assembles an agent system in .NET with a hard deterministic boundary, telemetry and cost accounting. If anything here has market value it is `HumanMoveGate` as a human-in-the-loop pattern that knows nothing about chess, and `GameCostTracker` with its configurable price list — but the second only once the `Side` enum has been cut out of its signatures.
highlights: `TryApplyMove` matches the proposal against `Move` objects generated by the engine rather than parsing a string. A human move and an agent move go down **exactly the same path**, with no separate 'trust the human' branch.

The CHANGELOG documents that the project originally did not compile at all, because it was written without the SDK and NuGet, and it names the guessed `ChessDotNetCore` APIs that did not exist: the namespace, `CurrentPlayer`, `MoveType`, `Promotion` as `char?`. Rare honesty in a public repo.
A library trap, written down: castling is emitted twice, as `e1g1` and as the chess960 `e1h1`. Only the standard form reaches the list shown to the model; both are accepted on input.
Underpromotion is modelled as four separate moves (`a7a8q/r/b/n`) rather than a flag, which is a direct consequence of discovering that `Move.Promotion` is a `char?`.

A model with no entry in the price list reports `null` rather than USD 0.00, the UI shows that difference, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` enforces it as invariant no. 4. The whole `ChessDotNetCore` surface is confined to one file, and that is a written-down invariant too.
gaps: **No evidence that a game was ever played here with a real model.** There is no transcript, no screenshot and no saved result, so the entire agent layer is empirically unchecked.
`GameOrchestrator` runs to 276 lines and is the most complex file in the repo, and there is not one test on it. The 26 tests cover the engine, the costs and the human gate.
No persistence and no eviction: games, results and cost trackers live in a `ConcurrentDictionary` that is never cleared. `SECURITY.md` calls this unbounded growth itself.
No authentication on the orchestrator API and no limit on concurrent games. The limits of 200 plies and 5 rejections protect one game; nothing protects the bill.
`POST /games` starts the loop through `Task.Run` without observing exceptions, so a failure of the game loop has nowhere to surface.

The GitHub Pages site cannot be confirmed from the repository, so it has been taken off the links: `pages.yml` says in its own comment that without a one-off Settings -> Pages -> Source: "GitHub Actions" setting the workflow runs and only then fails to deploy. There is no `gh-pages` branch in the repo and no record of a successful deployment, and the existence of the workflow alone is evidence of intent, not of a published site. The site's source sits in `docs/index.html` and can be viewed there.
next: Write `GameOrchestrator` tests with a fake `AIAgent` substituted in. The loop, the rejection limit, the forfeit and the human path are deterministic and need no model; this is the largest hole in coverage.
Play one full agent-versus-agent game and record it in the repo, with a transcript, a rejection count and a cost. Without that the whole thing is an unrun sketch.
Add a TTL or a cap on the number of games in memory, and minimal authentication on the orchestrator, even a shared token, before anything stands outside localhost.
Replace `Task.Run` with a `BackgroundService` or a queue that logs the exception and sets the game status to `failed`.

Cut `GameCostTracker` and `ModelPricingCatalog` out into a separate project with no provider dependencies; a comment in the test csproj suggests this itself, and it is the only candidate for a package in this repo.
risks: `Microsoft.Agents.AI.Foundry 1.15.0-preview.260722.1` and `Azure.AI.Projects 2.1.0-beta.4` are pins on prerelease. The README describes NuGet's downgrade block as the reason it is not possible to drop back to the stable 2.0.1, and announces breaking changes itself.
No authentication plus no spending limit means an exposed instance is an open card on the owner's API account. `SECURITY.md` says so outright, but that is still the default state of the code.

`ChessDotNetCore 1.6.0` is a small single-maintainer library whose surface changed between versions. Confining it to one file limits the cost of migration, not the risk of the upstream being abandoned.

Four commits and the last one from 31 July 2026: without further activity the repository will read as a one-off burst, and the prices in `appsettings.json` age on their own, with one entry marked outright as unverified.
repos.headline: The hard-boundary architecture is done, but nobody has played a single game here

repos.name: claude-scope
repos.oneLiner: Session forensics for a coding agent: the script counts and the model only names the phases — with an adapter boundary so the session source can be swapped.
repos.summary: The `/session-report` skill turns a session's own history into token, timing and conversation-shape analytics, with a visual timeline. The most important decision is a single line of rule: **the model never does arithmetic**. A deterministic, stdlib-only Python script parses the transcript and counts; the model receives only finished numbers, names the phases of work from its own narration, and writes the summary. That ruling carries further: under an agent whose history lives in a database or a cloud store, the model **fetches** raw events and writes normalized JSON, and the script still does all the counting. The second decision of the same class is the source's declared capability tier, which reaches the page — a source that only knows per-turn totals renders one flat block and says so, instead of faking a timeline nobody observed. The whole thing is packaged in the Agent Plugins format, so it installs identically under Claude Code, Copilot CLI and VS Code.
repos.tests: 25 tests in `tests/test_analyze.py`, run by hand: `python3 tests/test_analyze.py`. Each pins one of the format traps and the rendered shape of the JSONL path. The suite is good; nothing runs it automatically.
repos.ci: **None.** There is no `.github/workflows/` directory. No lint, no test and no plugin-manifest validation runs — a repository distributed as an installable plugin has not a single gate in front of publication.

components.name: The analyzer
components.description: Stdlib only, and deliberately so: the script cannot open a database or make a tool call, so the boundary between 'counts' and 'fetches' is enforced by what the script physically cannot do.

components.name: The transcript-format reference
components.description: A catalogue of traps hit on real sessions: duplicate records per API response, subagent sidechains, pseudo-turns fabricated by local slash commands, image payloads masquerading as huge text reads, reasoning blocks whose text arrives redacted to an empty string.

components.name: The session-sources reference
components.description: Describes every source together with its capability tier — and, more unusually, the sources that looked promising but could not be confirmed against a live session. Recorded as unconfirmed rather than guessed at.

components.name: The timeline template
components.description: Self-contained HTML, light and dark, with tooltips and a full event table. One card per turn on a shared clock: phase bands, tool-call ticks scaled by how much text each read back, and the reply block that ends the turn.

components.name: The marketplace manifests
components.description: Two copies of the manifest, in `.claude-plugin/` and in `.github/plugin/`, because different clients read different paths. Exactly the compatibility problem `architecture-standards` solves with a generator — here maintained by hand.

overlaps.reason: The same domain — coding-assistant session observability — approached from the opposite side. That one is an OTLP collector with a store and a dashboard; this is a retro of one session from a snapshot. The definitions of session quality ought to be shared and today are not.

The same Agent Plugins format and the same two-manifest-path problem. That repository generates its plugin tree and validates it independently; here the manifests are written by hand, which is exactly the drift that standard warns about.
Both take an agent's execution trace apart into facts. There the trace is graded against a contract; here it is described and measured — the same event normalization would serve both.

repos.product: A channel, not a transaction, and right now the cheapest one in the whole portfolio: seven commits, fifteen files, installed with one command in three clients. The value sits in the two format references — they are the closest thing to a specification anyone has written for these transcripts, and they, not the script, are why a stranger will find this repository.
highlights: The 'the model never counts' rule is enforced architecturally rather than promised in a prompt: the script is stdlib-only and cannot reach for data, so the split between 'the model fetches, the script counts' cannot be violated by accident.

The source's capability tier reaches the rendered page — the lede, the legend, the stat tiles and a card of its own. Under-claiming costs a little detail; over-claiming invents a session nobody observed. That choice is rare and is made here deliberately.
The stream-json partials trap: summing per-record token counts undercounts output by more than an order of magnitude. Hit on a real session, documented, and pinned by a test.
The privacy policy is part of the design rather than an afterthought: tool outputs never reach the report, and reasoning text is counted but never quoted. The same rule binds any new source.
gaps: **Zero CI.** A repository distributed as an installable plugin runs neither its tests nor any manifest validation. Twenty-five good tests that nothing triggers protect only whoever remembers to run them.
Two marketplace manifests maintained by hand — exactly the copy-paste drift `architecture-standards` solves with a generator. That solution sits next door and is not used here.
Installation is served from the default branch with no release tagging: a consumer has no way to detect that the skill's contents changed.
Adapters exist only for sources verified against a live session, which is honest, but it means the agent-neutrality promise is today demonstrated on one agent.
next: Add a `ci.yml` that runs `python3 tests/test_analyze.py` and validates both manifests. It is one file and it closes the largest gap in this repository.
Generate the second manifest from the first instead of maintaining both, or at minimum add a test that compares them.
Introduce release tagging so that whoever installs can see which version of the skill they are getting.
Reconcile the session-quality definitions with `copilot-scope` — today two repositories measure the same thing with two vocabularies.
risks: The transcript formats are undocumented and unstable between releases. The parser is defensive (skip, never crash), but with no CI a format change will surface only when somebody sees an empty page.

Session data contains the full conversation and every tool output, possibly secrets. The redaction rules are stated and observed, but they are enforced by convention and by tests that nothing runs automatically.
repos.headline: Twenty-five tests pinning the format traps — and not one workflow to run them

repos.name: CogniSim
repos.oneLiner: A dress rehearsal for PI Planning: six LLM agents act out the {{term:safe|SAFe}} ceremony and return four artefacts instead of a transcript.
repos.summary: The input is an increment that is still to be planned — features, teams, business context. The output is the four things that decide whether the real event goes well: PI objectives per team with business value, a cross-team dependency map, a ROAM risk register and a list of open questions. **The transcript is the evidence, the artefacts are the product.** The commercial headline — a dependency your input never declared — is computed deterministically from the data rather than reported by the model. The whole thing runs without an API key: the {{term:playhead|cassette}} replays recorded runs in replay-only mode, and a request with no recording ends in a 503 that says why, never in a plausible-looking empty plan. Six orchestration topologies are wired in and each passes end-to-end in the tests; an unknown topology throws rather than quietly using another one — because a fallback would attribute one topology's results to another.
repos.tests: 120 test methods (110 Fact + 10 Theory) across 6 projects, including 6 architecture tests enforcing the kernel's purity
repos.ci: Six workflows. `ci.yml` has five jobs: build+test, kernel test **in isolation** (proof that it stands on its own), a mechanical line limit on ServiceDefaults, a secret scan and a dependency audit. `deploy.yml` is {{term:tagdeploy|tag-driven}} with change detection. Since 25 August, CI and CodeQL are switched to manual runs only.

The offer is narrow and checkable. What is missing before it can be sold, and the repository lists it itself: input paths (buyers have Jira and spreadsheets, not hand-written JSON), tenancy on runs, and — most of all — **not one live model call**, so nobody has seen what a real artefact looks like.

Architectural boundaries are enforced **mechanically, not by review**: two purity tests plus a line limit in CI, with the reasoning in a test comment that the same rule written as prose has already failed twice in this estate.

The {{term:comparison|comparison type}} has no field into which a best run could be written — the discipline of 'medians and spreads, never averages' is enforced by the shape of the type, not by convention.
The system runs on zero credentials: with no key it serves recorded runs, and an unrecorded request ends in a 503 that says outright why.

No deployment has ever been made. Six Fly config files, four Dockerfiles, a Bicep track and a tag-driven pipeline are written and never run; the addresses in the documentation are a promise.

The experiment comparing the six topologies has not been run, and the results tables are **deliberately empty**. Two decisions only the author can make block it, along with the most serious threat to validity: prompts written for one topology may favour it.
Since 25 August CI and CodeQL are manual only, and the badge in the README shows a workflow that runs on neither push nor PR.

The default model is written into two places as a fallback and has an expiry date — a comment in the code refers to an announced wave of retirements.

Four thousand lines of documentation against nine thousand lines of code. The risk that the documentation starts describing a state the code no longer has is real — for now it is held in check by citing source files next to every number.

repos.name: CogniSim — master's thesis and 2026 analysis
repos.oneLiner: LaTeX sources of a master's thesis on CogniSim, plus a 2026 audit of what underneath it has ceased to exist.
repos.summary: `thesis/` holds the sources of a master's thesis (Warsaw University of Technology, EiTI) describing CogniSim — a multi-agent system on LLMs in which agents play the roles of a software organisation and act out {{term:safe}} and Scrum ceremonies. `docs/` holds six numbered studies from 2026 that check what of that thesis still stands up: a defect audit of the sources, an ecosystem deprecation audit, a migration mapping onto {{term:maf}}, the publication record, related work, and a stack audit of the successor platform. repos.name: combustion-reports
repos.oneLiner: A car's fuel consumption as a curve rather than two numbers from a brochure — with a README section on how **not** to read that curve.
repos.summary: The manufacturer quotes two numbers, city and highway; the car has a curve. The application takes recorded trips and fits a polynomial model of consumption against average speed and against route length, so you can see where a car is genuinely efficient rather than where the brochure says it is. It runs entirely in the browser: no account, no server, no telemetry, state in `localStorage`. What sets this repository apart from everything else in the portfolio is its **'How not to read it'** section — a curve fitted to four points is a drawing, not a model; the fit is anchored at the origin by default, which is not physically true and is a stability trade-off; extrapolation is deliberately short, to 1.2× the furthest sample; and the largest confound is the driver's own right foot. R² is displayed next to every fit precisely so that it can be disbelieved. That is rare: a product that actively makes it harder to over-read its own output.
repos.tests: Five Vitest test files, focused on the polynomial fit and the persistence layer. The storage tests cover the cases applications like this usually break on: an incompatible schema version, a corrupt entry, no access to `localStorage` at all.
repos.ci: Two workflows: `ci.yml` (lint and tests) and `pages.yml`, which publishes the application. A Docker image with nginx is built but published nowhere.

metrics.label: Interface languages
metrics.value: 2 — English and Polish, detected from the browser

components.name: The polynomial fit
components.description: A degree-2 fit, anchored at the origin by default. The anchor is not physically true — an idling car still burns fuel — but without it a handful of samples produces a curve that swings wildly outside the data. The trade-off is documented and can be switched off with a parameter.

components.name: The persistence layer
components.description: Writes are debounced, the snapshot carries a schema version, and a snapshot from an incompatible version is discarded rather than half-loaded. When `localStorage` is unavailable or full, the application keeps working in memory instead of throwing.

components.name: The 'How not to read it' section
components.description: Four warnings against over-reading, written by the author against his own product: too few points, the origin anchor, the short extrapolation, and the driver's own habits as a confound.

components.name: The bilingual interface
components.description: English and Polish, switchable from the navigation bar and detected from the browser on the first visit — exactly the arrangement the portfolio map uses, solved independently.

A browser application holding all its state locally on the user's machine, with the same set of problems: schema versioning, no export, data migration between releases.

repos.product: The closest thing to a product among the things built for their own sake: it solves a real problem, has an audience beyond the author, and needs no infrastructure, so the marginal cost per user is zero. What it lacks to be a product is not features but data export — without it a user who has entered a hundred trips is tied to one browser on one machine.
highlights: A section on how **not** to read its own output. In a portfolio full of repositories honestly listing their own gaps, this is the cleanest case of that same virtue aimed at the user rather than at a reviewer.
R² shown next to every fit — shown, not hidden. The application hands the reader the number that lets them disbelieve it.
The origin anchor is a documented trade-off with a rationale and an escape hatch rather than a hidden implementation decision. Most tools in this class make that decision and never mention it.
The persistence layer degrades correctly: private browsing, blocked cookies and an exceeded quota do not take the application down, they switch it to memory.
gaps: **No export.** All state sits in one browser's `localStorage`: clearing site data destroys everything, and moving to another device is impossible. It is the single thing standing between this application and being useful to a stranger.
The last substantive commit is from 1 August 2026; since then the only things open have been Dependabot pull requests.
The Docker image is built and published nowhere — configuration that does nothing except require maintenance.

Merge the two Dependabot pull requests and decide whether the repository is maintained or frozen — today the badge says one thing and the commit history another.
Publish the image to GHCR or delete the Dockerfile and `nginx.conf`. An unused deployment path is a cost with no benefit.
risks: User data lives in one browser only and cannot be exported. A user who has been entering trips for a year will lose them on a site-data clear — with no warning at all.

repos.name: CopilotScope
repos.oneLiner: An OTLP collector and dashboard that turn AI assistant telemetry into a **session quality score**, not token usage.
repos.summary: Takes {{term:otel|OpenTelemetry}} telemetry from five surfaces — VS Code Copilot, Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, Cursor — on a single endpoint, aggregates it into sessions and computes a composite quality score of 0–100 together with a confidence indicator. The component weights are **published** and renormalised only across the components that have data; a coverage coefficient is exported alongside every score, because the first version pinned every session to somewhere around eighty and that was plainly wrong. Beyond the score itself it computes turn analysis (which turn broke and why), survival of accepted edits, latency usefulness, token economics and a frustration heuristic — the last of these deliberately outside the score component set. The protobuf decoder is written in the repository, so the collector has **exactly one dependency** and the dashboard has none.
repos.tests: 160 test methods (155 [Fact] + 5 [Theory]) across 19 files with assertions, out of 22 files in the test directory. The number passing was not verified in this run — what is counted is the attributes in the code.
repos.ci: Five workflows: build and test of the whole solution, a matrix of four images on GHCR with a smoke test **before** publication, compilation of two LaTeX papers attached to the release, GitHub Pages, gitleaks. Plus dependabot for three ecosystems.

components.name: Dekoder OTLP
components.description: A hand-written protobuf reader (718 lines in total) with field numbers verified against the official `.proto` files. It reads the generic OTLP format and has no notion of a session — it can be cut out as a small library for any OTLP receiver without an SDK.

components.name: The insight pipeline
components.description: A pluggable analyser contract: one class plus one registration gives you a new algorithm, and the dashboard renders the result generically. An analyser exception is caught and reported as missing data rather than bringing down ingest.

components.name: Judge calibration (Cohen's kappa)
components.description: 670 lines: unweighted, linearly weighted and quadratically weighted {{term:kappa|kappa}}, each with a seeded bootstrap of 2000 samples. It measures the **agreement ceiling of the human panel itself** first and has a separate 'ceiling too low' verdict. The arithmetic itself is neutral, but the file imports `CopilotScope.Collector.Domain` and calls `CopilotSession.Percentile` in two places — that is the whole dependency to remove before extraction.

components.name: CopilotScope.ServiceDefaults
components.description: A hundred lines of pure infrastructure: self-instrumentation, health, service discovery, HTTP resilience. Deliberately without a single domain entity.

components.name: QualityEngine v2
components.description: Six components with published weights, renormalised only across those with data, plus confidence = coverage times a sample ramp.

components.name: Dialect normalisation

overlaps.reason: A sister repository: the same shape (OTLP collector, correlation, dashboard), a different domain. A large part of the infrastructure is shared by definition.

Claude Code and Cowork emit no spans by default — 292 lines treat log events as the source of truth for calls, tokens, tools and edit decisions. That is work nobody else has done publicly.

repos.name: CSharp FlashCards 2026
repos.oneLiner: A deck of 269 Q&A flashcards on C# and .NET built as a Beamer deck on a 1080x1920 pt page, compiled to PDF by GitHub Actions on a `v*` tag.
repos.summary: Every question gets its own slide, the answer is the next slide, and the whole lot sits in 24 `areas/*.tex` files pulled in by 24 `\input` directives from `main.tex`. The presentation layer is carried by a bespoke class `mybeamer.cls` (24 section colours, shared `minted` and `listings` configuration, an automatic Outline frame at the start of a section) plus `mybeamer.sty` with the macros `\QuestionSlide`, `\CategoryBadge` and `\TOCButtonTall`. The most interesting decision is in the geometry and it is unfinished: `main.tex` passes `paperwidth=1080pt` and `paperheight=1920pt` to the `geometry` package — phone-screen proportions — and the line below passes the `landscape` option to that same package, which swaps those dimensions round to 1920x1080. The repository holds neither a built PDF nor a LaTeX toolchain, so the final orientation cannot be confirmed from here — the source declares both at once. The second decision is already a failure, and you can see it in the code: `\AnswerSlide` is defined and **never used once**, because 197 `minted` blocks force `frame[fragile]`, so all 269 answers were written by hand instead of through the macro. Delivery is {{term:tagdeploy|release on a tag}} — `xelatex` with `-shell-escape` in the `xu-cheng/latex-action@v4` action, publishing `CSharp_FlashCards.pdf` as a GitHub Release. The content and the pipeline are finished; the wrapping — landing page, title slide, footer links — comes from the previous edition and nobody has updated it.
repos.license: MIT-0 w pliku LICENSE, MIT na odznakach — rozjazd
repos.tests: No tests. There is no test framework and no verification script; the only check is the fact that the LaTeX compile in CI has to succeed, and that fires only on a tag.
repos.ci: Two workflows. `ci.yml` starts **only on a push of a `v*` tag**: it builds `main.tex` through `xu-cheng/latex-action@v4` with XeLaTeX and `shell_escape`, uploads the artefact and publishes a release through `softprops/action-gh-release@v2`. `pages.yml` deploys the `docs` directory to GitHub Pages on a change under `docs/**` or manually; neither workflow builds on an ordinary push or on a PR.

overlaps.reason: The same workshop: a long LaTeX document with its own preamble and class, built with `latexmk` and watched by CI. The conventions from one repo carry over to the other without translation.

repos.product: No buyer. This is study material and interview preparation, given away free as a PDF under the {{term:mit|MIT-0 licence}}, so its function is channel and reputation: it builds recognition for the dev_insight brand and pulls traffic to GitHub. The real audience is a .NET developer ahead of an interview, or someone running a training course. Nobody will pay for the present form, because there is no spaced repetition here, no progress tracking and no interactive version — there is one static PDF, and that is the whole product.
highlights: 269 `\QuestionSlide` calls across `areas/*.tex` and 270 answer `frame`s — the mapping is one to one apart from a single question in `8-design-patterns.tex`, which has two answer frames. Nothing checks this automatically.
197 C# code blocks typeset by `minted` with one configuration (`linenos`, `CodeBg` background, `breakanywhere`) defined once in the class rather than per slide.

`MASTER_PROMPT.md` pulls a **LaTeX repository generator** out of this repo: a manifest of files in order, a branch into four document types and a self-check list. A repo that described itself as a template.

262 of 269 questions carry a `*`, `**` or `***` prefix (55 / 173 / 34); 7 have none, and 6 of those are consecutive steps of a single OAuth flow. The asterisks render literally in the slide title and there is no legend anywhere, so the reader sees noise instead of a difficulty scale.

`main.tex` declares the orientation twice and contradicts itself: lines 1–3 pass `paperwidth=1080pt`/`paperheight=1920pt` to `geometry`, and line 4 passes `landscape`, which swaps the dimensions to 1920x1080. Without a built PDF there is no settling which declaration wins.

`presentations/` is wired into no build and into no `main.tex`, and the theme drags in macros from another field. At the next edition this will be the first thing to mislead.

Replace every reference to `CSharp-FlashCards-2025` in `main.tex` and `mybeamer.cls` with `konradcinkusz/csharp-flashcards` and settle the year at 2026 on the title slide and in the landing page title.
