repos.name: cv-maker
repos.oneLiner: Tailored CV generator in which the model never writes LaTeX: the agent returns JSON, .NET binds it to a template and typesets it in a sandbox.
repos.summary: The user pastes in a job advert, enters their own facts and picks one of two templates; they get a typeset PDF and never see any LaTeX. The key decision is a negative one: **the model does not generate typesetting code**. Agents return JSON conforming to a schema, `TemplateBinder` builds a fully escaped view model out of it, and only that reaches the Scriban template owned by the repository, so by construction the model's output cannot create a control sequence. The second rule is {{term:provenance}} enforced mechanically rather than by prompt: every bullet and heading must cite a `factId` from the candidate profile, and `FactReferenceValidator` rejects content with unresolvable references, so generation fails rather than releasing a PDF with an invented employer. Typesetting itself sits in a separate service with a TeX Live image: no shell escape, `openin_any`/`openout_any=p`, a working directory per compilation and a hard 30 s timeout. The agent layer reads `cv-generation-flow.json` (five agent definitions, one capped revision run) and has a {{term:determinizm|deterministic}} `MockAgentRuntime`, thanks to which the whole pipeline runs offline, with no Azure account and no keys. Identity is lifted out into an external `authservice` — the API validates the token through JWKS and holds no key material at all.
repos.license: MIT, z wendorowanym `templates/altacv-modern/assets/altacv.cls` na LPPL 1.3c odnotowanym w LICENSE
repos.tests: One test project, `tests/CvMaker.Tests`: 51 test methods (43 [Fact] + 8 [Theory] with 44 [InlineData] rows) across 5 files, 1,077 lines; the number of passing cases has not been verified, because `dotnet test` was never run. Covered are `LatexEscaper` (the injection corpus), `FactReferenceValidator`, `TemplateBinder`, `ProfileContentBuilder` and the agent output parser — `CvMaker.Api` and `CvMaker.Web` have no unit tests at all.
repos.ci: Three workflows. `ci.yml` has three jobs: a .NET build and test with a check that the migrations match the model; a sandbox job that starts the renderer image with production hardening and, in separate steps, proves that reading files outside the working directory is refused, that `\write18` is absent and that a compilation is killed on timeout; and an end-to-end job that brings up the full stack from compose and generates a PDF from both templates. `flyio.yml` deploys only on a `v*` tag, and `secret-scan.yml` runs gitleaks as a container over the full history.

docs.label: ADR 0003 — free tier on the user's own model key

components.name: LatexEscaper
components.description: A single-pass escaper for every TeX metacharacter, plus removal of zero-width characters and bidi overrides. A pure `string -> string` function with no I/O and no CV domain model, so it suits any code putting untrusted text into LaTeX.

components.name: LatexCompiler (the rendering service)
components.description: Runs `latexmk` over the bound source: `shell_escape=f`, `openin_any`/`openout_any=p`, a separate working directory per compilation, a 30 s timeout, a 20 MB PDF limit and a 2 MB `.tex` limit. The service has no database, no authorisation and no model credentials — it takes a `.tex` and assets and hands back a PDF, so it is a {{term:hermetyczny|hermetic}} typesetting service for any document.

components.name: IAgentRuntime: Foundry i Mock
components.description: Two implementations of one interface: Azure AI Foundry and a mock that emits only content grounded in facts, so a green test does not pretend the fact gate was checked. `GET /api/runtime` reports the active backend, so a misconfigured deployment does not quietly serve mock CVs.

components.name: Walidacja JWT wobec JWKS authservice
components.description: The API verifies the bearer token against the published JWKS of an external instance and holds no key material — it can check a token, it cannot issue one. Issuer and audience are pinned to CvMaker, so a token from another product of the same {{term:oidc|provider}} will not authenticate.

components.name: FactReferenceValidator
components.description: The provenance gate: it checks that every bullet, entry heading and summary cites a `factId` that exists in the candidate profile. Content with unresolvable references is rejected, and generation fails closed rather than releasing an invented fact.

components.name: TemplateBinder
components.description: Renders `CvContent` into LaTeX source through Scriban, first building a fully escaped view model — the template engine only ever receives safe strings. `StrictVariables` and `LoopLimit 5000` mean a typo in the template is a build error rather than an empty CV.

components.name: FlowEngine + the agent catalogue
components.description: The engine executes a sequence of steps from `cv-generation-flow.json` with `input.*` and `steps.*` placeholder substitution and one condition for the capped revision run. The five agents are versioned data files, not code: `posting-analyst` has an explicit `injectionSuspected` field, `profile-extractor` runs at temperature 0.0.

components.name: QuotaService
components.description: Metering held locally rather than borrowed from the identity service. Consumption is a single conditional UPDATE with `used < limit` in the WHERE, so two concurrent requests will not produce a free generation. The default is 3 generations per 30 days on free, 100 on pro.

overlaps.reason: cv-maker has no identity of its own: it logs in against this service, validates its JWKS and deploys its image from {{term:ghcr}} as `cvmaker-authservice-dev`.
The Channel queue with a BackgroundService, recovery of stuck jobs, the cancellation registry and status polling are ported from there along with the Api/Core/Shared/Web/Tests split.
The repository conventions — minimal API, Blazor client, container images, a single compose file — come from there; PROPOSAL lists this in its reference map.
`docs/architecture/DEVIATIONS.md` is kept directly against section 3 of that repository and lists seven open deviations.
The same area and almost the same name — two repositories about generating CVs, easy to confuse in the portfolio.

repos.product: A buyer exists in theory — a candidate submitting many applications — but there is no revenue model: `QuotaService` knows a free and a pro tier, and there is no payment integration anywhere, while ADR 0003 settles that free is meant to run on the user's own key, and that was never built. The CV generator market is crowded, so as a standalone business this does not hold up. The real value is twofold: the author's own use, because this is the productisation of his manual LaTeX pipeline, and technical credibility — a working example of confining the model's output to a JSON schema, enforcing fact provenance and running untrusted LaTeX in a sandbox with evidence in CI. The second of those is sellable as a reference, not as a SaaS.
gaps: **The repository has no tag at all, and `flyio.yml` only fires on a `v*` tag** — so six Fly configurations are as of today a declaration, not a deployment, and there is no address to show.

`docs/PROPOSAL.md` in paragraph 3 describes a directory tree with `CvMaker.AppHost`, `CvMaker.ServiceDefaults` and `CvMaker.Auth`, none of which are in the repository. The README itself also admits that the earlier claim of three green CI jobs was untrue as of commit `ef5b4fc`.
Cover letters are promised in the README and have a ready `cover-letter-writer` agent definition, but are not built; the same goes for document version history and the bring-your-own-key of ADR 0003.

No {{term:otel|OTLP}} telemetry at all, even though one generation passes through four services — the repository's own deviation register calls this the biggest gap. There is also no resilience handler on `RenderClient` and `AgenticClient`, so a transient error means a lost job.

Multilingual support is blocked by the templates: both use `T1 fontenc`, which breaks Polish characters outside ASCII and handles neither Cyrillic nor CJK. PDF download goes through the API, because there are no signed URLs to the `generated-cvs` container.
next: Run the build and tests locally, and record the actual state of CI — the README has already lied about this once and admits as much itself.
Cut the first `v*` tag. Until there is one, the whole of `flyio.yml` is dead and none of the six `.fly.dev` addresses exists.
Fix paragraph 3 in `docs/PROPOSAL.md`: remove `AppHost`, `ServiceDefaults` and `CvMaker.Auth` from the tree, or mark them as unbuilt.
Close the two cheapest deviations: `AddStandardResilienceHandler` on both HTTP clients (carefully, given the renderer's long timeout) and moving migrations out of `Program.cs` into a hosted service.
Decide about `cover-letter-writer`: either finish the cover letter path, or delete the agent definition and the promise from the README.
highlights: The model never writes LaTeX. Agents return JSON, and the binder builds a fully escaped view model before Scriban sees anything — by construction the model's output cannot create a control sequence.

CI **actually proves the sandbox**: it starts the renderer image with the same hardening as the deployment and checks, in separate steps, that reading files outside the working directory is refused, that `\write18` is absent and that a compilation is killed on timeout. Proof of a security property, not happy-path tests.

The fact gate is mechanical, not prompt-based — `sourceFactIds` that do not resolve to profile facts bring the generation down. That is a distinction most 'agent writes a CV' demonstrations do not make at all.

The whole pipeline (profile, tailoring, binding, typesetting, PDF) runs offline with no Azure account thanks to `MockAgentRuntime`, and `GET /api/runtime` reports the active backend, so a misconfigured deployment does not quietly serve mock CVs.

The repository keeps a dated register of deviations from someone else's reference architecture (review of 2026-08-14: seven items open, six closed) plus three ADRs, one of them accepted and openly unimplemented.
risks: `flyio/authservice.fly.toml` pins `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice:v0.1.0` — a foreign image on a foreign release cycle, whose disappearance or breaking change takes down login here. It is the only use of GHCR in the repository and nothing from here is pushed there.

ADR 0002 deliberately puts the product database and the identity database on one Postgres, so restoring a snapshot is all-or-nothing: rolling back accounts along with CVs. On top of that `AUTHSERVICE_DB_PASSWORD` falls back to the server password, which the ADR itself calls a demo convenience.
Every Fly application name ends in `-dev`, and deployment is triggered by a `v*` tag — there is no separate set of names or configurations for anything production.

A portfolio name clash with `konrad-cinkusz-cv-maker`; on top of that `NuGetAudit` is set as a build error against pins from August 2026, so a new CVE will stop not only a release but the build, without intervention.
repos.headline: CI proves the renderer sandbox, but zero tags means zero deployments

repos.name: DevInsight
repos.oneLiner: Three C# console demos on `net8.0` as companion code for the DevInsight channel, which does not yet have a single episode.
repos.summary: Each directory is a standalone `Exe` project illustrating exactly one language topic. `DevInsight.SOLID.LSP` models `Rectangle` and `Square` as equal implementations of `IShape` rather than by inheritance, so it sidesteps the classic LSP violation instead of describing it. `DevInsight.BitShiftDemos` shows a `[Flags]` enum on `uint`, masking of the shift count by `0x1F`, and packing a firmware version into bits 31..16. `DevInsight.CSharpSamples` touches `TimeZoneInfo` for Europe/London and works out the trading session date from a 23:00 cut-off. The most interesting decision sits in the first of those demos: the `Features` enum **explicitly declares** `Bit32`, `Bit33` and `Bit63` alongside the legal bits, so that the compiler works out the collision itself (1, 2 and `0x80000000`) instead of leaving it in a comment. The whole thing is 224 lines across three `Program.cs` files, zero {{term:nuget|NuGet}} dependencies and zero tests. Two demos are genuinely finished; the third is a sketch that, after all the time zone arithmetic, prints `Hello, World!`.
repos.tests: Zero tests: there is no test project and no file with `test` in its name, even though all three topics (LSP, bit packing, DST boundaries) are purely unit-level and deterministic.
repos.ci: No CI. The `.github` directory does not exist, so not even `dotnet build` runs on push.

metrics.label: Lines of code across the three `Program.cs` files

docs.label: README with a table of the three projects

components.name: BitPacking
components.description: Six static functions on `uint`: `SetFirmware` first clears both bytes with the mask `~((0xFF << 24) | (0xFF << 16))` and only then writes the values, so a second write leaves no rubbish behind from the previous version. `GetFirmware` returns a `(Major, Minor)` tuple, and `Enable`/`Disable`/`Toggle`/`HasFeature` work on the flag mask. No domain type, no dependency.

components.name: Enum `Features : uint`
components.description: Fourteen `[Flags]` values, from `Bluetooth = 1u << 0` to `DeepSleep = 1u << 31`, and after them, deliberately, `Bit32`, `Bit33` and `Bit63`. The collision that comes from masking by `0x1F` is worked out here by the compiler, not described in prose.

components.name: IShape + AreaCalculator
components.description: An interface with a single `Area` property, two equal implementations and `TotalArea(IEnumerable<IShape>)` summing over the abstraction. A comment in the code names the reason `Square` does not inherit from `Rectangle` outright: independent `Width` and `Height` setters would break substitutability.

components.name: ResolveLondon
components.description: Eight lines closing the gap between IANA and Windows identifiers: `TryFindSystemTimeZoneById("Europe/London")` with a hard fallback to `GMT Standard Time`. The only part of this project that does what it promises.

components.name: DetermineTradingDate
components.description: A local function that moves the date on by a day when the London hour is 23 or later. The rule is tied to a specific trading session cut-off, and its result never reaches the program's output.

components.name: DevInsight.sln
components.description: Ties three projects together, two of which sit in `src/` while the LSP demo sits in the root directory. That inconsistency is visible in the README, because the project table mixes `./DevInsight.SOLID.LSP` and `./src/...` paths.

overlaps.reason: The same material: C# language details served in small, self-contained portions. There as flashcards, here as a runnable demo behind a video.

The LSP demo touches the SOLID principles, which function there as a binding standard rather than as a teaching example. If both entries are to live, it is worth deciding which one is the source of the definitions.

repos.product: No buyer, and there is no point looking for one here. This is a pure channel play: the code is there to back up the videos and the author's credibility, not to generate value on its own. The problem is that the channel has not started yet, so today the repository is backing up something that does not exist, and all of its value is deferred to the first published episode.
highlights: The `Features` enum declares `Bit32 = 1u << 32`, `Bit33` and `Bit63` alongside the legal flags, so the collision that follows from masking the shift count by `0x1F` is **worked out by the compiler** rather than described in a comment.

`BitPacking.SetFirmware` clears both bytes with the mask `~((0xFF << 24) | (0xFF << 16))` before writing, rather than only `OR`-ing. This is the correct pattern, and it is missing from most similar examples online.
The LSP demo does not repeat the canonical `Square : Rectangle` mistake; both shapes are equal implementations of `IShape`, and `AreaCalculator` sees nothing but the abstraction.

`ResolveLondon` handles the divergence between IANA and Windows identifiers with a fallback to `GMT Standard Time`, which is precisely the detail on which a time zone demo usually falls over on someone else's machine.

repos.name: Family Budget Calculator — Spain 2026
repos.oneLiner: Single-file family budget calculator with real Spanish IRPF and autónomo contribution maths, in three languages.
repos.summary: Works out a family's monthly balance in Spain: payroll and self-employment income, benefits in kind and expenses, each one an editable entry with its own slider. The tax engine is not a stub: a six-band state scale plus seven autonomous scales, a personal minimum of 5,550 EUR, per-child minimums with a bonus below the age of three, and a 6.35% employee contribution on a base capped at 59,060 EUR. The most interesting engineering decision sits in `calcAutonomoNet`: the contribution depends on net income and net income depends on the contribution, so the function resolves it by **fixed point** — it starts at 300 EUR a month and runs five times through the 15-band table from RD 504/2022 until the result stops moving. The whole thing is one `index.html` file, 2,392 lines and 91,486 bytes, zero dependencies and zero third-party requests, fonts included. State lives in parallel in `localStorage` and in a base64-encoded URL hash, so an entire budget scenario is shared by the link alone, with no server and no account. The thing is {{term:hermetyczny|self-contained}} and finished, and at the same time there is not one test for the four functions that are pure arithmetic and would take an hour to test.

components.name: The autónomo calculator (calcAutonomoNet)

components.description: Annual gross plus a percentage bonus, a 6.35% contribution on a base capped at 59,060 EUR, IRPF reduced by the tax on the minimum, and a monthly figure at 12, 14 or 16 payslips. It reads the global `state.incomes.length` to decide how to split the minimum, and that is the only side effect in an otherwise pure function.

A natural demo for the profile: it works with no login, no install and in three languages, so it is the cheapest evidence you can send anyone by link.

repos.product: No buyer, and there is no point pretending otherwise. The audience is a family weighing up a move to Spain or a switch to autónomo status, who will use the tool once or twice and never come back. Monetisation would need two things that are not here: annually updated tax tables and someone taking responsibility for the result, and the README deliberately disclaims both. The real value is channel value, and in that role it works, because it is checkable evidence that opens in a second.
highlights: A complete app in one file of 91,486 bytes, with zero dependencies and zero third-party requests, fonts included.
The autónomo quota is worked out **iteratively**, because the contribution and net income depend on each other. Five passes over the 15-band table from RD 504/2022 instead of one multiplication.
Eight IRPF scale variants, including Navarre with 11 bands and the Basque Country with 8, alongside the state scale ending at a 300,000 EUR band at 24.5%.
State sits in parallel in `localStorage` and in the URL hash, so a full budget scenario moves between people in one link, with no server and no account.

Three full translations of 109 keys each, in perfect step: parsing the `I18N` object as JavaScript gives the same key set in es, pl and en, zero missing and zero surplus in either direction. On top of that, attribute substitution through `data-i18n-attr` and `navigator.language` autodetection on the first visit.
gaps: **Zero tests for the tax engine.** The four fiscal functions are arithmetic over band tables, that is the easiest thing to test for regressions in the whole portfolio, and not one of them has a single reference case.

The 2026 constants are written into the JS with no year field, no legal source in a comment and no expiry date. When the rules change nothing will signal the {{term:drift|drift}}, and the UI does not show which year the calculator is working to.

The README tells you to pick branch `main` in the Pages settings, while the badge in the same README shows `master`. One of the two is wrong and on a fork it will break the deployment for anyone who follows the instruction.

The URL hash holds the family's whole budget in base64, so it goes into browser history and everywhere the link is pasted. The data genuinely does not leave the browser, but the link carries it out.
The Basque Country and Navarre are computed on the autonomous scale alone, with the state scale skipped. That is a deliberate approximation, described as foral, and it diverges from the real system.

Add `.github/workflows` with one job: HTML validation plus a script comparing the key sets of the three i18n dictionaries.

repos.name: judge-worker
repos.oneLiner: A TypeScript worker that pulls agent traces off a BullMQ queue and scores them with an LLM judge — a judge checked by mutants, not assumed.
repos.summary: The producer pushes one job per trace through `addBulk`, the worker consumes them from Redis, **revalidates the trace with a Zod schema at the consumption boundary** — the queue is treated here as a trust boundary, not as its own memory — and scores it against a pinned rubric. The default judge is `MockJudgeProvider`: a deterministic heuristic reasoning only over the structure of the trace (tool call order, presence of events, results), never over content, which makes it injection-proof by definition and lets the whole demo run without an API key. The `--live` flag switches to the Anthropic Messages API with the response shape enforced by `zodOutputFormat`. The most interesting decision is not in the queue layer but in `cohenKappa`: when every pair of scores falls into one category, the function returns `null`, not `1.0`, because two raters who always say the same thing have proved nothing. That case actually occurred for the `tone` rubric and the repository reports it as a number that weakens its own claim. It was built as evidence for one quoted line of a job advert and says so plainly in the first section of the README.
repos.tests: 103 `it()`/`test()` calls in 32 `describe` blocks, spread over 15 files in `test/` — counted with grep, because `node_modules` does not exist in the container and the suite has not been run. `FINDINGS.md` still says 7 files and 30 tests, which are the figures from an earlier commit.
repos.ci: Four workflows: `ci.yml` runs lint, format:check, typecheck, build and `test:coverage` on Node 22 with a `redis:7-alpine` service; gitleaks runs over the **full history**, on PR/push and every Monday; `docs.yml` builds Jekyll and pushes to GitHub Pages when markdown changes. CodeQL is declared, and the condition that made it skip itself — the repository being private — no longer holds; no first run has been recorded in this entry yet.

components.name: Producer with a queue-depth limit
components.description: `enqueueBatch()` refuses to insert a batch that would exceed `QUEUE_DEPTH_LIMIT`, throwing `QueueDepthExceededError` rather than growing quietly. It accepts an explicit limit override and its own `Queue` instance, because `loadEnv()` is memoised before the CLI has parsed its flags — a trap that previously falsified the backpressure test in silence.

components.name: CircuitBreakerJudgeProvider
components.description: A decorator over any `JudgeProvider` with a closed → open → half-open state machine, so that a run of failing jobs does not burn the SDK's retry budget against an unreachable endpoint. The only thing tying it to the domain is a two-method interface, which generalises trivially.

components.name: Kalibracja — kappa Cohena
components.description: Unweighted {{term:kappa|kappa}} over a pair of score sequences, returning `null` on zero variance instead of apparent perfect agreement. A pure statistical function with not one domain dependency — it suits any LLM judge calibration.

components.name: Kolejka dead-letter z CLI do requeue
components.description: A separate `<name>-dead-letter` queue carrying a truncated failure reason; `pnpm run dlq -- requeue` restores an entry through the normal `enqueueBatch()` path, so it gets the same depth limit and the same job options. The entry disappears only after a successful requeue, not before.

components.name: Log-redaction policy
components.description: `safeResultFields()` is an allow-list of `JudgeResult` fields used everywhere a result is logged, so a new field does not become loggable through object spread at the call site. `truncateForLog()` trims the error text from an external dependency before it reaches the dead-letter queue.

components.name: Consuming worker with a cost ceiling
components.description: Revalidates the payload with Zod, scores it, counts the cost through `RunCostTracker` and **pauses itself** once `MAX_RUN_COST_USD` is breached. A job that has exhausted its attempts lands in the dead-letter queue rather than vanishing.

components.name: MockJudgeProvider
components.description: A heuristic judge reading only the structure of the trace, never the semantics. {{term:determinizm|Determinism}} is not a testing convenience here but a security property: a judge that does not read the content cannot be talked round by an instruction inside it.

components.name: Judge mutants and the harness
components.description: Five subclasses each breaking exactly one property of the output: inverted verdict, missing justification, compliance with an injected instruction, ungrounded optimism, no check for an absent confirmation. Each test has two stages — a sanity check against the real judge, then an assertion against the mutant.

overlaps.reason: The README and FINDINGS say plainly that the scoring contract, the {{term:kappa|kappa}} calibration protocol and the {{term:mutation|mutation testing}} discipline were carried over from there — as a pattern, not as code, because that one is in .NET.
The same judge calibration arithmetic, only there it runs over production telemetry and without a single human label. Here there are 30 labels and the number came out.
Built against the constraints in `AI-EVALS.md` and `00-REFERENCE-ARCHITECTURE.md`, with two deliberate departures written down as ADR-1 and ADR-2.
The same family of problem — measuring the quality of an LLM judge — although judge-worker does not refer to it directly.

repos.product: **No buyer**, and that is not a flaw of this repository but its definition. It was built for one quoted line of a Senior Backend Engineer (Data Infrastructure) advert at Langfuse, in the language and the queue technology that team actually uses, and it says so in the first section of the README. As {{term:evidence|evidence}} it works very well: a complete reliability layer, real numbers from real runs and honestly marked limits of measurement. As a product it has no audience — nobody will buy a worker that scores traces in the shape of one repository's fixtures, and the market for that is already held by the company the application was addressed to.
highlights: Five hand-written judge mutants, all caught, each breaking a different property — and a separate `mutation pass diversity` test checks that diversity **mechanically**, instead of relying on the author's inspection.

`cohenKappa` returns `null` rather than `1.0` when there is no variance in the scores. That case actually happened for the `tone` rubric and the repository reports it in `FINDINGS.md` as a number that weakens its own headline.

Backpressure proved by load, not by declaration: 600 traces, a depth limit of 100, a scoring delay of 150 ms — 100 scored, 500 rejected. `FINDINGS.md` also describes two bugs that had previously falsified this test in silence: a shared Redis connection and the memoisation of `loadEnv()`.
`pricing.test.ts` breaks CI when `PRICING_LAST_VERIFIED` is older than six months. An out-of-date price table becomes a loud failure instead of a quietly false cost figure.

The reliability layer is complete and every part of it has its own test: the depth limit, retry with backoff, dead-letter with requeue, the circuit breaker, the cost ceiling that pauses the worker, and a graceful shutdown timeout that reports which jobs it interrupted.
gaps: **`FINDINGS.md` reports 7 test files and 30 tests, while the repository has 15 and 103.** The figures are from an earlier commit and were not refreshed after the CLI, circuit breaker, cost, metrics and redaction tests were added. It is the only place where the repo states a number that has drifted from the code — and it happens to be the file whose entire value rests on its numbers being true.

Calibration has been run **against the mock only**, and the human labels and the mock's heuristics were written by the same person in the same sitting. The repo says so plainly, but a kappa of 1.0 still does not measure the quality of the judge, only the author's agreement with himself.
The `--live` path has no {{term:mutation|mutation}} coverage at all and has never been run against the real API — it is tested with an injected `fetch`, so end to end remains unchecked.

No real {{term:otel|OTel}} telemetry: there are pino logs and Prometheus metrics, and the log field vocabulary is borrowed from the GenAI OTel conventions, which can be misread. `SPEC.md` corrects this itself.

Deploying the documentation needs a one-off manual switch of Settings → Pages → Source to GitHub Actions, which the workflow cannot do for itself. The README links to that site as the full documentation; whether it responds has not been verified.

The documentation site is still not confirmed as published. The permissions block that followed from the repository being private went away when it was made public, but the header of the Pages workflow says itself that deployment needs a one-off manual switch of the source in the settings — which the workflow cannot do on its own behalf.
risks: LICENSE assigns copyright to `dev_insight`, which clashes with another portfolio entry (slug `dev-insight`) and looks like an artefact of copying between repositories.

The repository is built for one company's advert and names it. Once the recruitment closes, the README will start reading like an out-of-date application, and the value of the channel will drop to zero without a single commit.
The price table in `src/observability/pricing.ts` is hard-coded and was verified on 2026-08-17. The staleness test gives it six months, after which CI goes red for a reason unconnected to the code.
No secret is in the repository, but `--live` reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment, and the only brake on spending — `MAX_RUN_COST_USD` — is off by default.
next: Refresh the numbers in `FINDINGS.md` against the current commit. A file whose claim is 'real numbers from real runs' cannot report stale ones.
Fix the copyright line in LICENSE to the right owner — today it carries the name of another repository.

Run `pnpm run calibrate -- --live` with a real key over the 15 fixtures (a dozen seconds, pennies) and record that {{term:kappa|kappa}} next to the mock one. It is the cheapest thing that turns the repository's weakest claim into a measurement.
Add a mutation counterpart to `SilentInjectionComplianceJudge` for `LiveJudgeProvider` — check whether the real judge resists the attack in `adv-003`.

The repository's visibility is settled — it is public, so CodeQL no longer skips itself. Check the first run and record the result; until then the 'code scanning in CI' layer remains a declaration rather than a control.

repos.name: Konrad Cinkusz — CV (Switzerland)
repos.oneLiner: A LaTeX repository of CVs and cover letters in which the git tag is the switch that decides what CI compiles.
repos.summary: Job-application documents in two typesetting styles: AltaCV (two-column, vendored class `altacv.cls` 1.7.4) and academic (the `curve` class, rubrics in `academic/`, publication list through biblatex). The whole thing is held together by `build-matrix.json` — one source of truth that maps the tag scheme `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` onto a list of source→PDF pairs: MAJOR picks the style, MINOR the specialisation for a particular vacancy, PATCH does not change the build plan. `build.sh` reproduces the same switch locally through `jq`, and CI adds a third path: on a pull request `changed-docs.sh` parses `\input`, `\makerubric`, `\addbibresource` and local `\usepackage` so that it compiles only those documents the diff actually touches. The most interesting decision is exactly here: instead of a full regression run, the repository computes the LaTeX dependency graph from the contents of the files, which is cheap and knowingly incomplete. The result is a {{term:determinizm|reproducible}} artefact per tag rather than a file in the cloud, but the non-technical side has been left behind: no tests, no pushed tags, and a README that links to the repository's previous name.
repos.license: Inconsistent: `LICENSE.md` is LPPL 1.3 with LianTze Lim as maintainer (inherited from AltaCV), while the README declares MIT
repos.tests: No tests — `find` over the pattern `*test*` returns no file at all. The only verification is that LuaLaTeX compiles the document in CI.
repos.ci: One workflow, `ci.yml` (252 lines), two jobs. Pushing a `v*` tag builds the plan from the matrix and publishes a release through `softprops/action-gh-release@v2`; a pull request compiles only the documents named by `changed-docs.sh` and updates a single comment carrying a link to the artefact; `workflow_dispatch` with style/specialization inputs lets you build any combination from any branch.

components.name: changed-docs.sh
components.description: Computes the LaTeX dependency graph from the diff: it reads `\input`, `\include`, `\makerubric`, `\addbibresource` and local `\usepackage`, adds the shared assets (`photo.jpg`, `latexmkrc`) and prints only the documents the change touches. Editing `academic/skills.tex` flags 7 of the 11 academic CVs, editing `academic/education.tex` 10 of 11, and `academic/settings.sty` all 11; editing the README flags nothing.

components.name: build.sh
components.description: 52 lines of a generic `latexmk -lualatex` runner driven by a JSON file: it takes a style and a specialisation, computes the plan through `jq`, copies the PDFs into `dist/`, and for style 0 packs the lot into a ZIP. The only things hard-coded are the matrix filename and the output directory.

components.name: build-matrix.json
components.description: A declarative map from tag to a list of `source|output` pairs, read identically by `build.sh`, `changed-docs.sh` and CI. The structure is neutral, the contents are not: these are named CVs and letters for named companies.

components.name: Workflow CI

highlights: The git tag is the build switch: MAJOR picks the style, MINOR the specialisation, PATCH does not change the plan. The scheme is described consistently in the README, in `build-matrix.json` and in the header of `ci.yml` — a {{term:tagdeploy|tag-driven release}} applied to documents rather than to images.

Counted by running `changed-docs.sh -` for every file in `academic/`: a rubric for a single vacancy (e.g. `skills_anthropic.tex`) gives 1, `summary.tex` 2, `work_authorization.tex` 6, `skills.tex` and `hobbies.tex` 7 each, `employment.tex` and `projects.tex` 8 each, `education.tex` 10. The academic style is assembled from interchangeable rubrics, so a variant for a vacancy is a swap of two files rather than a copy of the whole CV — hence 17 specialisations across 32 unique source files.

repos.name: konradcinkusz (GitHub profile + portfolio map)
repos.oneLiner: GitHub profile and hub repository: one manifest describing forty-three repositories, plus a site that renders it.
repos.summary: The repository does two things at once and both are committed today. The first is the profile README — the first thing anyone arriving at the rest of the estate sees. The second is the portfolio map: a site in plain HTML, CSS and JS with no build step and no runtime dependencies, which renders five tabs from a single manifest — portfolio, consolidation, operating model, a sortable index and a glossary of forty-three terms. The data sits split across `data/`, one file per repository, and **a second time** under `data/en/` — Polish is the source, English a translation with an enforced shape. `scripts/build-manifest.mjs` glues both trees into the one `site/data/portfolio.json`, and `--check` mode detects {{term:drift|drift}} of the committed copy against the sources. The most interesting decision is in the validator: the schema of repository keys is **closed**, and referential integrity is checked across files, so an unknown slug, a {{term:kernel|kernel}} with one consumer, a repository assigned to two {{term:poziom|tiers}} or a dead glossary reference stop the build. This is the only place in the portfolio from which forty-three repositories are visible at once — and that is why it sits at tier P0 despite not containing a single line of business logic.
stack: Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, zero dependencies
repos.tests: No unit tests; nine control scripts instead: manifest drift, the validator (closed schema, referential integrity **and parity between the two language trees**), the i18n audit (no reader-visible string outside `ui.json`, no unknown enum value), the served-manifest assertion, existence and visibility of the repositories through the GitHub API, a structural smoke test of the site, a theme-token audit, a rendering test in Chromium across five combinations of language, theme and width, and **a test of the health collector's thresholds against a fake API** — every threshold has a fixture it must fire on, and a clean repository it must stay silent on.
repos.ci: `validate-portfolio.yml` on push, PR and manually, with a filter covering `data/**`, `site/**` and `scripts/**`: ten steps, nine of them checks, from manifest drift through browser rendering to the single-file build. A second job builds the image and probes the container: unprivileged user, `/healthz` outside the SPA fallback, headers on every path, and compression for a **proxied** request too. `flyio.yml` on a `v*` tag: `--check` for drift first, creates the app if it does not exist, deploys, and **after** the deployment demands both language bundles from the served manifest — because a health check proves nginx came up, not that the data arrived.

components.name: Builder manifestu
components.description: 104 lines building **both** language bundles: `data/` produces `pl`, `data/en/` produces `en`, and the `ui.json` from each tree goes into the shared `ui` block. It forces the filename to equal the slug. `--check` compares the result against the committed copy and fails CI on any drift; one comment points at `architecture-standards` as the source of the pattern, and another explains why the builder does **not** count its own commits.

components.name: Repository-existence checker
components.description: Asks `api.github.com` about every repository in the manifest and compares the real visibility and `archived` flag against what is claimed. First, though, it establishes **what this token can actually see**: the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` is scoped to this one repository, so a 404 on any other means nothing — those entries are skipped and counted, not reported as deleted.

components.name: Smoke test strony
components.description: A structural HTML test with no browser: it pairs tabs with panels, checks that every local asset exists and balances the sectioning tags. It knows not one concept from the portfolio domain, so it will work on any static site with tabs.

components.name: Obraz i konfiguracja serwera
components.description: nginx 1.27-alpine serving `site/` as static files, with `/healthz` taken out from under the SPA fallback, no-cache on the manifest, a seven-day cache on assets and security headers. The container runs as an unprivileged user and has its own HEALTHCHECK.

components.name: Tag-driven Fly.io deployment
components.description: The `konrad-portfolio` app in the waw region, shared-cpu-1x 256 MB, `min_machines_running = 0`. The workflow explicitly checks for the presence of `FLY_API_TOKEN`, creates the app on demand and verifies the deployment by fetching the manifest, not by a health check.

components.name: Walidator manifestu
components.description: A closed `REPO_KEYS` set, slug uniqueness, referential integrity, every repository in exactly one {{term:poziom|tier}}, and every glossary reference resolving — **all of it once per language**. Then it compares the two trees element for element: the same list lengths, the same identifiers, the same file paths, and no English string identical to its Polish twin while carrying a Polish diacritic.

components.name: Renderer manifestu
components.description: 769 lines with no dependencies: fetching the manifest, language selection and a switch with no reload, five tabs, filters by cluster and visibility, index sorting, the repository side panel, kernel-consumer highlighting, and the micro-syntax that links prose to the glossary.

components.name: Data sources
components.description: The Polish source and its English twin under `data/en/`: `meta.json`, `clusters.json`, `consolidation.json`, `ops.json` with the operating model, `glossary.json` with 43 terms, `repos/<slug>.json` one per repository, and `ui.json` — 235 strings the page says on its own behalf. This is content about this particular portfolio, not a schema to reuse.

overlaps.reason: `build-manifest.mjs` quotes the drift-validator pattern directly from that plugin directory, and `data/ops.json` points at the `FLY-IO-DEPLOYMENT.md` there as the source of the deployment schema.
Two static sites about the author in the same cluster, competing for the same calling-card role.
The same recruitment material in a different format, both in cluster F.
An overlapping function: generating material about the author from structured data.
The README and `meta.json` link to the channel as the main axis of distribution, so both describe the same channel of reach.

repos.product: No buyer, and none should be looked for here. This is channel and credibility: the GitHub profile is the first thing a recruiter or a prospective user of the other forty-two repositories sees. The map is a decision tool for one person, the owner, and in that role it has real indirect value, because it is the only place from which 34 repositories, their duplications and the {{term:wip|WIP}} limits are visible at once. The site itself is not a product and there is no sense in positioning it as one.
highlights: The validator has a **closed** set of repository keys and checks integrity across files: an unknown slug in `overlaps`, a repository assigned to two {{term:poziom|tiers}} or a dead glossary reference stop the build. A {{term:kernel|kernel}} with one consumer is a warning, not an error — that is a judgement, not a schema violation.

`data/ops.json` is a complete operating model, not a declaration of intent: 9 principles, 5 attention tiers covering **exactly 34 slugs with no repeats**, 7 rituals with a timebox and an artefact on the way out, 12 health checks with a signal, a threshold and an action, 7 WIP limits, 12 automations and 6 plan horizons with a completion test.

The site has no build step and zero dependencies at run time. The only development dependency is a browser for the rendering test — which caught a boot-ordering bug that left the page blank, three layout overflows and a `[hidden]` rule losing to `display: flex`.

The manifest is a **generated and committed file**, and that rules one thing out: it cannot carry its own commit count. An attempt to fill that in from git at build time ended in a chase — every commit invalidated the file it had itself written a moment earlier, and `--check` failed on the next run. Those numbers are gathered by the nightly collector, for this repository on the same terms as for the other forty-two.
gaps: **The repository is public, so the profile README renders — and the whole manifest was published along with it.** That was one decision, not two: the profile works, and dossiers for thirteen private repositories are legible from that moment to anyone who opens `site/data/portfolio.json`. The consequence is described in `risks` below, and flipping visibility back does not undo it.

The manifest is a **snapshot from a single day** for the forty-two other repositories. The nightly collector meant to take that away is written and tested against a fake API, but has **never run live** — it needs an account-wide token that does not exist yet. Until then the numbers on the cards come from a one-off read.

The project table in the README is still written by hand, even though the same manifest could generate it. This is exactly the problem the {{term:drift|drift validator}} has already solved for the manifest itself.
The site has not been deployed even once — the Fly configuration and the workflow are written and never run.
Entries about private repositories point at documents the reader will not open. The renderer greys such links out and gives the reason, but there is no way to fix it without opening the repositories.
next: Review the thirteen entries about private repositories and strip anything from them that should not be public — the descriptions of confirmed security holes above all. This is the first item on the whole portfolio's list, ahead of anything else.
Cut the first tag and check whether the deployment actually passes — including the step that verifies the served manifest.
Build `scripts/build-readme.mjs` and generate the README's project table from the manifest, to remove the divergence at source.
Add the nightly health collector, writing `data/health.json` and opening **one** issue with the breached thresholds.
Move the reusable CI workflow for .NET here; sixteen copies of `ci.yml` across the estate come to one `workflow_call` and three lines at the consumer.
risks: **This risk has materialized.** The repository is public and the manifest went with it. The entries about private repositories name file paths, class names and **confirmed security holes** in a live, paid product — and they are legible to anyone today. Flipping visibility back does not undo it: a public commit is public forever and does not reach the clones, forks and scrapers that were already there. The only action that changes anything is to review the thirteen private entries and strip from them what should not be public.

repos.name: landing-page (Franke label)
repos.oneLiner: A static one-page sales site for an external client, built on an off-the-shelf template and abandoned after five days.
repos.summary: One `index.html` file (621 lines) plus three CSS sheets, five scripts and nine images. The page is entirely in Polish and sells one person's services: a TikTok account audit, video-recording training and packages from 400 to 3000 PLN, with banner, about me, counters, offer, pricing and contact sections. The visual base comes from the LayoutFlow template, which is honestly recorded in the first line of `style-global.css` and in the footer. Authorship can be settled from the history, and it comes out more modestly than the code alone would suggest: the whole `js/` directory — all five files, `scripts.js` and `bliss.js` among them — arrived in a single commit `13493ae` together with the template package (`read-license-and-terms.txt`, `owl-slider`, `contactform`), and not one of them has a single later commit, so there is no basis for attributing any line of JavaScript to the author. What is his own is what shows in the diff since the import: the content and section layout of `index.html` and the cuts in `style.css`, 704 insertions and 576 deletions in total. In the style layer, 63 dimensions in `style.css` are counted in `vw` units, and a separate `style-responsive.css` with three breakpoints is responsible for the breaks alone; that separation of scaling from breaks also came with the template — the import had 91 `vw` dimensions and the same three breakpoints — the author only trimmed them. The rest of the repository is libraries vendored locally: jQuery 2.2.0, counterUp, Waypoints, Font Awesome Free 6.1.1 and Linearicons, which makes the page almost {{term:hermetyczny|self-contained}} and leaves Google Fonts as its only dependency on the network.
stack: CSS3 (3 stylesheets from the template, 1,083 lines, style.css trimmed by the author)
repos.tests: No tests: the repository contains not a single test file, nor configuration for any test runner.
repos.ci: No CI. There is no `.github` directory at all, so {{term:dependabot}} does not run here either, even though every library is vendored locally and nobody will refresh them.

An identical end product, a one-page presentation of a person in HTML, except that there it is generated from data and here it is written by hand. Comparing the two shows how much of this page could be expressed as a template plus data.

repos.product: No buyer. This is a finished piece of freelance work for one specific client, the Franke label brand, not a product or a library. Its portfolio value is the lowest in the whole set, because the visual layer comes from an external template and the author's own contribution amounts to the content and section layout in `index.html` and the cuts in `style.css` — the `js/` directory stands exactly as it arrived with the template. The one thing it proves is that a project for an external client was delivered in full in five days.
highlights: A complete sales page with an offer, counters and **three package tables** (three `div.pricing-table` blocks in `index.html`, lines 250, 351 and 472: STANDARD 1100, PREMIUM 1900, VIP 3000 PLN) delivered in **13 commits between 11 and 15 June 2024**, with a readable history: `remove contact form`, `add pricing`, `deleted reviews slider`.

No build process at all. There is no `package.json`, no bundler and no compilation step, so the page works once the directory is copied onto any static server, and will work exactly the same way in five years.

**63 dimensions counted in `vw`** in `style.css`, with every layout break moved out into a separate `style-responsive.css` with three breakpoints. Continuous scaling is separated from the jumps here, but the credit is not the author's: the template import in `13493ae` had 91 `vw` dimensions and the same three breakpoints.

Scrollspy that highlights the active menu item, with smooth scrolling, fits into **679 bytes** of `js/bliss.js` and is configured solely through global variables from the HTML. The file came with the template in commit `13493ae`, is minified, carries no authorship marker and has no later changes, so it is not the author's code.
The template's provenance is declared in two places: in the first line of `style-global.css` and in the page footer. Nobody pretends the visual layer is the author's own.
gaps: **The README is a 34-byte stub written in UTF-16 with a BOM**, reading `# landing-page`. It does not say what the project is, who it was built for, where the template comes from or how to run it.
`index.html` links the sheet `bxslider/jquery.bxslider.css` on line 19, and there is no `bxslider` directory in the repo. Every page load ends in a 404 visible in the console.

The menu item **Cennik points at `#testimonials`** (line 74), because the pricing section on line 245 inherited the identifier from the deleted reviews slider. The navigation works by accident, not by design.

The template owner's e-mail address (redacted here — this entry is public and the address belongs to somebody else) sits in two places inside an `` tag with no `href` attribute, and `` in the footer is filled in by nothing, so it renders as `Copyright © | Template By`. Those are the two most visible elements of the contact page.

The dead `owlCarousel` and `datepicker` calls in `js/scripts.js` are {{term:drift}} left by two template features the author cut out: the markup and the `owl-slider` and `contactform` directories vanished from the repo in the commits `remove contact form` and `remove unnecessary files`, while `scripts.js` was left untouched since the import.
risks: The repository publishes a third party's personal and business data: a first name, photographs, an e-mail address, TikTok and Instagram accounts and a full price list. Consent to this cannot be confirmed from the repository, and the June 2024 prices may already be out of date.

There is no LICENSE file, while libraries under four different licences are vendored in, `jquery.counterup` under GPL v2 among them, alongside a commercial template. The legal status of redistributing this repo is unsettled, and adding {{term:mit|MIT}} will not settle it.
jQuery 2.2.0 dates from 2016 and no longer gets fixes; Waypoints 2.0.3 and counterUp 1.0 are older still. Vendoring them locally means nobody will notice.
The name `landing-page` carries no information. In a list of repositories it is noise, not an entry.

Remove the `bxslider` link from line 19 and the `owlCarousel` and `datepicker` calls from `scripts.js`, and move the pricing section's identifier from `#testimonials` to `#pricing` along with the menu link.
Add `href="mailto:..."` at both occurrences of the address and hard-code the year in the footer. That is three lines, and they repair the only conversion path on this page.

repos.name: LangChain, LangGraph and Async Python
repos.oneLiner: Sources of a book on LangChain 1.x, LangGraph and async Python for an engineer arriving from .NET: 17 chapters, 6 appendices.
repos.summary: The repository is 8,698 lines of LaTeX across chapters, appendices and front matter (17 chapters, 6 appendices), plus a preamble and a pipeline that builds the PDF. There is one thesis and it is defended consistently: after the 1.0 release of 17 October 2025, `langchain` became a thin layer over the `langgraph` runtime, so most material on the web describes an architecture that no longer exists. The most interesting engineering decision is not about the content but about **discipline**: the whole editorial debt is countable and counted by CI. The `make debt` target tallies stub chapters, missing screenshots, `verifybox` blocks and diagrams, and the `build.yml` workflow publishes the same counters to the GitHub Step Summary on every build. A `verifybox` block marks a listing that was not run against the pinned versions, and across 8,450 lines of chapters and appendices there are **zero** of them. The only occurrence in the repository is a specimen in the box legend at `frontmatter/introduction.tex:157`, which the Makefile deliberately excludes from the counter and documents with a comment. The author enforced his own rule instead of declaring it. Diagrams are text: 45 Mermaid sources are committed, the rendered PDFs are gitignored, and when a render is missing the macro prints the diagram source, so a build without `mermaid-cli` still shows the reader the structure.
repos.license: dual: MIT for the code, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the prose
repos.tests: No automated tests: there is no pytest, no `pyproject.toml` and no dependency file. The LaTeX build plays the role of the test, plus a CI step that fails on an unresolved cross-reference; the four measurement scripts in `code/` (702 lines) are not run in CI.
repos.ci: Three workflows. `build.yml` has three jobs: rendering every `.mmd` through mermaid-cli with a failure on error, a `latexmk` compilation with a grep for `Reference.*undefined` in `main.log` and publication of the debt counters to the Step Summary, and an advisory job comparing the nine pins against PyPI. `release.yml` attaches the PDF to a GitHub Release on a `v*` tag, `pages.yml` publishes `docs/`.

components.name: Missing-artefact macros
components.description: `\mermaidfig`, `\needscreenshot` and `\chapterstub` turn a missing artefact into a visible placeholder and at the same time add an entry to the `.dgm` / `.shots` manifest. When the rendered PDF is absent, `\mermaidfig` prints the Mermaid source outright, so an incomplete build still carries the content.

components.name: Editorial-debt counters
components.description: The `debt`, `shots` and `stubs` targets grep the sources and return four numbers, which CI copies into GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY. The debt is therefore visible on every push instead of living in the author's head; it moves to any text repository once you swap the names of the macros being grepped.

components.name: The Mermaid diagram pipeline
components.description: The rule `figures/diagrams/%.pdf: figures/mermaid/%.mmd` renders each of the 45 sources through `npx @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli@11` with `--pdfFit`, auto-detects the browser and generates `figures/mermaid/.puppeteer.json` itself. The input is any source directory, and a shared `figures/mermaid/config.json` keeps the palette out of the individual diagrams.

components.name: MeteredFakeModel
components.description: A subclass of `FakeMessagesListChatModel` that counts model calls and context size before answering from a script. It measures the structural cost of any LangGraph graph with no provider and no second of waiting; here it handles five {{term:topologie|topologies}} hand-built from `StateGraph` and `Command`.

components.name: The preamble and eight environments
components.description: 447 lines: 17x24 cm geometry, a custom `listings` language named `pythonx` and eight tcolorbox frames (note, warning, versionbox, verifybox, exercisebox, projectbox, dotnetbox, chapterstub). A defensive `\IfFileExists` for babel, newtx and inconsolata degrades the build instead of wrecking it, and a comment flatly forbids mapping U+00A0, because that kills `listings`.

components.name: Dependency-free landing page
components.description: 7,602 bytes of a single HTML file with its own CSS variables and `prefers-color-scheme` support, without a single external resource. It duplicates the status and the measurement tables from the README, so it drifts away from it by hand.

components.name: Pin check against PyPI
components.description: Pulls nine `\newcommand` macros out of `preamble.tex`, queries `pypi.org/pypi/<dist>/json` and prints a Markdown table with a `behind` marker. The distribution dictionary is hard-coded and it never fails the build, because the CI job carries `continue-on-error`.

components.name: Benchmark serwisu agentowego
components.description: 182 lines: uvicorn in a separate process, driven over real HTTP through httpx, the provider mocked at 100 ms, 400 requests per cell, three scenarios (clean, blocking, `to_thread`). The docstring records two earlier methodological errors, and that is why the script now calibrates against a no-op endpoint and flags cells close to the client's ceiling.

overlaps.reason: The sister volume, linked directly from the README and the landing page: the same preamble, the same debt counters and the same rule of 'measurement rather than assertion', only for the .NET stack. Both also share the same hole: the most expensive experiment in the book has not been run.
The same subject area, LLM agents. The contents of that repository were not checked in this run, so the overlap is declarative.

Experiment 5 measures the structural cost of multi-agent topologies with a fake model; that benchmark scores the quality of the same arrangements on tasks. The half of the experiment that has not been run is exactly what that repo can already count.

repos.product: No buyer in the transactional sense, and the licence settles it: the prose is under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so commercial redistribution of the text is ruled out, and there is no sales path anywhere in the repository. The real value is {{term:evidence|evidence}} for recruitment and consulting in the LLM agent space, resting on verified API surface and original measurements rather than rewritten documentation. A training course or a print edition could be the earning channel, but nothing in the repository prepares for either: there is no print version, no mailing list and no offer page.
highlights: **Zero `verifybox` blocks across 8,450 lines of chapters and appendices.** The environment exists in the preamble and is counted by CI (`grep -rc 'begin{verifybox}' chapters appendices`), and yet not one of the 82 listings carries the mark — every one was put through the pinned versions. The only `\begin{verifybox}` in the repository is a specimen in the box legend at `frontmatter/introduction.tex:157`, that is, text explaining to the reader what the box means, not a listing that was never run; the Makefile excludes it from the counter and says why. The convention was enforced, not announced.

The consistency run caught **the book's own error**: the default `recursion_limit` in `langgraph` is 10007, not 25. The old value survived the entire draft inside a `console` block that nobody ever ran, and was corrected in the chapter and in the appendix (commit 9435b1f).

The four measurement scripts (702 lines) are {{term:hermetyczny|hermetic}}: none of them needs a model provider. Experiment 1 hits a hand-written HTTP server on localhost instead of `asyncio.sleep`, because sleeping only proves that the scheduler can schedule.

Experiment 5 was split into a structural part and a quality part, and only the second needs a budget. The number of model calls is a property of the {{term:topologie|topology}}, so a counter on a fake gives the same answer as a real provider: a supervisor makes five calls against a single agent's two, and three of them are routing, not work.
45 Mermaid sources committed as text with the PDFs gitignored, so a diagram change reviews as an ordinary diff.
gaps: **The `\pyfile` and `\pyregion` macros are defined, the scripts carry `--8<--` markers, but there is not a single call in `chapters/` or `appendices/`.** All 82 listings are retyped by hand, so the book and the code can drift apart silently in exactly the way the project's own conventions forbid.

Three measurements that need a paid provider have not been run: answer quality across multi-agent topologies (ch. 11, the book's headline experiment), tool-selection accuracy against tool count (ch. 6) and cache hit rate (ch. 12). The tables in Appendix B stand empty and are meant to stay empty.
The claimed 244 pages and 'zero overfull vboxes' come only from the README and CLAUDE.md; the repository holds neither `main.log` nor the PDF, so without a build there is no way to confirm it.

The scripts in `code/` have no linter, no test and no dependency file, and they do not run in CI, even though all of them execute in seconds without a provider. Nobody will notice when they stop running.

The Ops Copilot mini-project is a separate repository, which 17 `projectbox` frames treat as a contract, and which according to the notes has only stage 00 implemented. The README describes both repositories as one whole.

The book refers to the companion project `llm-book-mini-project` — a public repository in which seventeen chapters have stages defined and one is implemented. That repository is not on this map, so its state has not been verified here at first hand.
risks: The nine pins in `preamble.tex` age fast: `langchain-core` alone had 49 stable releases between January and July 2026, and the job comparing them against PyPI carries `continue-on-error`, so {{term:drift|drift}} will never stop the build.
The dual licence is misleading in the README: the {{term:mit|MIT}} badge stands next to the CC BY-NC-SA badge, and only `LICENSE-CONTENT` says that the prose cannot be used commercially.
`release.yml` fires only on `v*` tags, and `git push --tags` returns 403 through the sandbox proxy. In practice no release will exist without tagging from a local clone.
The measurement scripts declare neither dependencies nor versions, so reproducing the same numbers a year from now will be guesswork about which release of `langchain-core` was installed at the time.
next: Wire the listings in through `\pyregion` wherever the `--8<--` regions already exist. That closes the only route to the book and the code drifting apart silently, and the macro is ready.
Add a light Python job to `build.yml`: ruff plus a run of `bench_concurrency.py`, `structural_cost.py` and `context_cost.py`. None needs a provider and all of them run in seconds.

Build the PDF and put the verified page count and the current overfull hbox counter into the README instead of numbers from memory; while you are there, fix the two stale lines in CLAUDE.md (the number of experiments run and the number of diagrams).
Add a dependency file with exact versions to `code/`, so the measurements can be repeated after the next LangChain release.
State plainly in the README that Ops Copilot is a contract today rather than a working system, or implement the next stages. The reader has no way to settle it.
repos.headline: Full draft with zero verification debt, but 82 listings still retyped by hand

repos.name: listing-search-bench
repos.oneLiner: The same evaluation method as agent-eval-bench, applied to a hybrid ranker: the specimen changed, the instrument's shape did not.
repos.summary: A behaviour contract written before the pipeline existed, 28 scenarios stored as data across five classes, and a Layer 1 harness that grades the **execution trace** of a real hybrid retrieval pipeline: which candidates the lexical path returned, which the vector path did, how they were filtered and ranked, and what was **never a candidate at all**. The point is singular: a ranking-weight tune, a filter refactor, or a listing trying to talk its way out of a hard constraint should fail a build rather than a customer. This is the second instance of the same method as `agent-eval-bench` — and that is exactly what makes it interesting in the portfolio: it demonstrates that the instrument is portable across domains. Twenty-two per cent of the assertions check **absence** — that something was never a candidate, never in a response, never re-applied — which is the half of evaluation almost everyone skips. A mutation pass breaks the pipeline four ways and requires every variant to be caught; the findings document adds that catching them on the first run is weaker evidence than it looks.
repos.tests: Two layers plus a mutation pass. Layer 1 is deterministic — no model, no network, no credential — and covers 28 scenarios with 128 assertions, 28 of which check absence. Layer 2 is a rubric judge with pinned rubrics and a hashed prompt. Alongside them, 46 xUnit attributes, including `NoHttpRouteReachesTheIndexTests`, which checks the single write path rather than declaring it.
repos.ci: Four workflows: `ci.yml` (the gates — hard constraints must pass 100%, behaviours are compared against a baseline), `codeql.yml`, `nightly.yml`, and `build-overview-pdf.yml`, which assembles the overview document in English and Polish.

metrics.label: Mutation pass
metrics.value: 4/4 caught, with a caveat recorded in FINDINGS

docs.label: The contract, written before the pipeline

components.name: The behaviour contract
components.description: Twelve behaviours, seven hard constraints, four rubrics — written before `src/ListingSearch.Service` existed. Every behaviour cites its proof, so the contract cannot quietly drift from the scenarios.

components.name: Scenarios as data
components.description: 28 YAML scenarios across five classes: happy, ambiguity, exclusion, adversarial, degradation. The adversarial class matters most — it tests a listing trying to talk its way out of a hard constraint using its own text.

components.name: The scenario runner
components.description: Runs the **real** pipeline in-process and injects faults at the index seam, so the degradation class measures genuine failure behaviour rather than a mock of it.

components.name: The ingestion consumer — the only write path
components.description: Reads `listing.published`, `listing.price_changed` and `listing.delisted`, idempotent by `event_id`. That no HTTP route reaches the index is **checked by a test**, not stated in the README.

components.name: The hybrid ranker
components.description: A second, genuine vector retrieval path merged with the lexical one by `HybridRankerStage` — never the other way round. Layer 1 checks the structure of the ranking; Layer 2 grades whether the best match actually lands on top.

components.name: The findings document
components.description: The one place the counts are recomputed, and the one that weakens its own result: the mutation pass caught 4/4 on the first run, and the document says outright that this is weaker evidence than it looks.

overlaps.reason: The same method, a different specimen — and that is this repository's entire thesis. There the measurement is 'did the agent ask before it wrote'; here it is 'does the ranker respect hard constraints when a listing's text tries to talk it out of them'. The harness, the scenario classes, the layer split and the mutation pass are common and ought to be one kernel.
Implements the AI evaluation standard from `docs/guides/AI-EVALS.md`. Deviations from it are accounted for and fixes flow back into the standard — the loop is closed in both directions.

repos.product: Public proof of methodology, built on a synthetic corpus, and the repository says so outright: it is not a deployed service and not a contribution to any production codebase. Commercially it is a work sample — precisely the one you show a team that has a search ranker with no contract and no way to detect that a weight tune has just broken a hard constraint.
highlights: The contract was written **before** the pipeline, and every behaviour cites its proof. That is the difference between an evaluation and tests written after the fact against whatever the code already does.

Twenty-two per cent of the assertions check absence. It is easy to check that a good result is in the response; it is harder and far more important to check that an excluded one was never even a candidate.
Layer 1 needs no model, no network and no credential, so the gate runs on every pull request and on every fork. The rubric judge sits separately and does not block a build without keys.

The mutation pass proves the suite **can** fail — and the findings document itself flags that catching all four variants on the first run is weaker evidence than it sounds. Weakening one's own result like that is rare in this portfolio.
gaps: Six open Dependabot pull requests against a single open issue — the repository about gates has the most neglected update queue of everything added in this pass.
The corpus is synthetic. The repository says so outright and that is honest, but it means the relevance rubric was validated against data the same side invented.
The mutation pass has four variants. Four is too few to say anything about the suite's sensitivity beyond those four failure modes.

The harness shared with `agent-eval-bench` is not extracted — two repositories carry two copies of the same method today, and that is exactly the duplication the consolidation analysis exists to catch.
next: Merge the Dependabot queue — six pull requests on a repository whose thesis is that gates should work.
Extract the Layer 1 harness and the scenario classes shared with `agent-eval-bench` into one kernel. Two specimens is the minimum at which that is even discussable, and it has just been reached.
Extend the mutation pass beyond four variants, and record which of them the suite lets through, if any does.
Run the bench against a non-synthetic corpus, even a public one — today the weakest link in the evidence is the data, not the instrument.
risks: The repository is proof of methodology on synthetic data. Presented as proof that a **production** ranker is safe, it would claim more than was measured — and only the findings document stands between the two.
repos.headline: A second specimen of the same method — and the first moment the shared harness may fairly be called a kernel

repos.name: llm-book-mini-project
repos.oneLiner: The companion project to the LangChain book: fourteen stages, each with a contract, and not one of them implemented.
repos.summary: Ops Copilot is meant to be an internal operations assistant: it answers questions about orders and incidents by querying real systems, and it can take exactly one irreversible action — sending an email — only from behind a human approval gate. It is built a stage at a time across the seventeen chapters of `llm-book`, and each stage directory carries a `README.md` stating what that stage must demonstrate and what its tests must prove. **It is a skeleton today: the stage structure and tooling are in place, no stage is implemented**, and the repository says so outright at the top of its README. One rule is worth more than all the rest: **every stage's tests pass without a single real model call.** Not 'mostly', not 'except the integration ones'. A stage that needs a live provider to demonstrate anything has been designed wrong — and the book devotes a chapter to saying so. The second deliverable is the final stage's `DECISIONS.md`, which the repository states plainly matters more than its code.
repos.tests: The tooling is in place — pytest, ruff, mypy in strict mode, a CI gate — and there are exactly zero substantive tests, because there is nothing to test. What each stage directory does carry is a contract stating what its tests will have to prove; a test specification written before the tests.
repos.ci: A single `ci.yml` running the toolchain gate. Stage `00-skeleton` exists precisely to prove that gate is real, and it is the only claim in this repository that can be verified today.

metrics.label: Real model calls in the tests
metrics.value: 0 — that is the rule, not the outcome

components.name: The stage contracts
components.description: Fourteen directories, each with a `README.md` stating what the stage adds and what its tests must prove. The contract is written before the implementation — the same pattern as `docs/SPEC.md` in `listing-search-bench`, applied to teaching material.

components.name: The toolchain gate
components.description: uv, ruff, mypy in strict mode and pytest, wired into one workflow. The zeroth stage exists to prove the gate is real before anything starts passing through it.

components.name: The zero-model-call rule
components.description: Stated as a project rule rather than a performance goal: the suite should be fast enough to run on every save, deterministic enough to bisect, and honest enough that a green build means something.

components.name: The decision log as the deliverable
components.description: The final stage is to produce a `DECISIONS.md`: the choice, the rejected alternative, the reason and the cost. The repository says outright that a reviewer reads that document and nobody reads the code.

overlaps.reason: This is that book's companion project and its only executable artefact. The chapters reference the stages, so an unfinished skeleton is a hole in the book rather than a separate repository of no consequence.
The same pairing: a book plus a project meant to prove it. Worth deciding once whether every book in the portfolio carries an executable companion, because today the answer differs from book to book.
Stage 11 is to add a twenty-case evaluation set with a regression threshold in CI. That is exactly the method the other repository has already implemented — no reason to write it a second time here.

repos.product: A channel, and one carrying debt: the book is public and points at a project that is empty. This repository's value will not be its code but its `DECISIONS.md` — the document explaining why a single agent rather than a supervisor, why an idempotency key rather than a distributed transaction, why SSE rather than WebSockets. Documents like that are scarce online, and they are the ones that get cited.
highlights: The 'zero real model calls in the tests' rule, stated without exceptions. Most projects of this kind start with that rule and lose it at the first hard stage; here it is written down as a design condition before anything exists.

Every stage has a contract written before the implementation, saying what it must demonstrate and what its tests must prove. A skeleton with fourteen contracts is worth considerably more than a skeleton with fourteen empty directories.
The status is stated honestly in the README's first paragraph. The repository does not pretend to be further along than it is — and for the companion to a public book that is the only right call.
gaps: **No stage is implemented.** Fourteen contracts and no code, against a book that is already public and already points at them.
The last commit is from 5 August 2026. The repository stands exactly where the skeleton was put down.
The `DECISIONS.md` the repository calls its most important deliverable does not exist — and it is the one thing that could be written now, without implementing anything.
Stage 11 plans an evaluation set with a regression threshold — the method from `agent-eval-bench`, repeated for a third time in this portfolio.
next: Implement stages 00–02. The three simplest stages turn the repository from a skeleton into something a reader of the book can run, and that is the whole difference.
Write `DECISIONS.md` now, from the decisions already made while designing the stages. It needs no implementation at all and it is the stated principal deliverable.
Add a visible note about the companion project's status to the book's README, so a reader does not land in an empty directory without warning.

Rather than writing the evaluation from scratch in stage 11, import the method from `agent-eval-bench` and describe the differences — better teaching material than a third implementation of the same thing.
risks: A public book pointing at an empty repository works against the credibility of both. It is the only entry in this pass where delay costs something already published.
repos.headline: Fourteen stage contracts, zero implementation — against a book that is already public

The history runs to one commit (`b4320e0`, 2026-08-26 09:33), and all four git references — two local and two remote — point at the same tree with the same single file. The stated intent is mathematics for AI engineers, but nothing beyond the title supports that: no list of topics, no choice of format, not one paragraph of content. The most interesting engineering decision in this repository has not been taken yet, and it is the decision about format, because it determines whether this becomes notebooks, a LaTeX book or an MkDocs site. In its current state, any maturity rating above `stub` would be invented.
repos.tests: No tests, and nothing that could be tested: `git ls-files` returns one entry, `README.md`.
repos.ci: no CI — the `.github` directory does not exist, so no run has ever happened.
