repos.name: Microsoft Agent Framework for .NET Engineers
repos.oneLiner: A full draft of a book on {{term:maf|Microsoft Agent Framework}} 1.0 for .NET engineers, written against the framework's source, not its documentation.
repos.summary: Twelve chapters and four appendices in LaTeX, addressed to an engineer who has shipped ASP.NET Core services and has just been handed the job of putting an agent into production: agents and tools, {{term:mcp}}, memory and state, workflows as a graph of executors and edges, five orchestration patterns, middleware, {{term:otel|OpenTelemetry}}, evaluation, hosting and the harness. The most interesting decision is editorial, not typographic: every listing copied out of the documentation instead of compiled against the SDK carries a `verifybox` block visible in the PDF, and `build.yml` writes the count of such blocks and the list of missing screenshots to the step summary. Debt therefore cannot accumulate quietly, because both the reader and CI can see it. The material came from reading the upstream code, which overturned the brief's assumptions repeatedly: `AgentThread` does not exist in the shipped package (127 occurrences of `AgentSession`, zero of `AgentThread` in the generated XML), a type mismatch on a workflow edge is a silently dropped message with no exception and no event, and declarative workflows are not the builder graph written out in YAML but a list of actions with Power Fx expressions. The build fails on an unresolved `\ref`, so a book with a broken reference will not be released. What is missing: the `code/` directory contains nothing but a `.gitkeep`, and two fully designed measurement experiments have not been run, so the tables in Appendix B stand empty on purpose.
repos.license: Dual: MIT for the code, macros and tools; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the text (LICENSE-CONTENT)
repos.tests: There are no tests and there cannot be any with the repository in this shape. The only automatic verification is compiling `main.tex` with `-halt-on-error`, plus a grep for `Reference.*undefined` in `main.log`, which stops both the PR build and the release.
repos.ci: Three workflows: `build.yml` compiles the PDF on every push and PR through `xu-cheng/latex-action`, gates on unresolved references, uploads the artefact for 14 days and publishes two debt ledgers to `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`; `release.yml` builds from a `v*` tag and attaches the PDF to the release with `contents:write` scoped to a single job; `pages.yml` publishes `docs/`. {{term:dependabot}} updates the actions once a month.

The page count disagrees with itself: the README and the site say 236, CLAUDE.md says 246. The PDF is in `.gitignore`, so settling it means building.
next: Run the cheaper cold-start experiment (10.5.3) and fill in its table in Appendix B. It needs a smaller budget than the orchestration benchmark and it unblocks the first hard numbers in the book.
Run the orchestration benchmark (7.7) and **keep the raw event streams**, not only the summary rows: chapters 9 and 12 are to re-score them, and recovering the traces costs a second run.
Do one dedicated version-bump pass: `\mafcore` to 1.15.0, `\mafdate`, the train table in Appendix A and the timeline in chapter 1 all at once, never as a side effect of a chapter.
Assemble minimal projects in `code/` for the listings covered by a `verifybox`, and delete the block only after it actually compiles.
Push a tag from a local clone ({{term:tagdeploy|pushing a tag is the only trigger for a release}}), so that the PDF link advertised in the README starts returning anything.
highlights: The debt is counted and published automatically: `build.yml` writes the list of missing screenshots and the count of `verifybox` blocks to the step summary. A debt ledger that updates itself on every push is rarer than it should be.

The build fails on an unresolved `\ref` — a grep for `Reference.*undefined` in `main.log` gates both the PR and the release. A book with a broken reference will not be released, even though LaTeX confines itself to a warning.

The findings come from reading the upstream code, not the docs: `AgentThread` does not exist in the shipped package (127 occurrences of `AgentSession` and zero of `AgentThread` in the generated XML), and a type mismatch on a workflow edge is a silently dropped message whose only trace is the `edge_group.delivery_status` tag on a span.

Appendix A describes the {{term:nuget}} packages as four parallel release trains with different dates and states outright that no single MSBuild property will pin them all. That observation is absent from Microsoft's documentation.

Version numbers live only as `\mafcore` and `\mafext` in `preamble.tex`, and CONTRIBUTING forbids writing a version into a chapter — which makes a version bump one change rather than a sweep across 9,055 lines.
risks: The dual licence is a trap for the reader: the prose is under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 with its NonCommercial clause, the code and macros under MIT. Anyone copying a passage of a chapter into commercial material breaks the licence with no warning.
The README and the site advertise a permanent link to the latest PDF, and the repository has **not a single tag**, so `release.yml` has never fired and the release probably does not exist.
23 uncompiled listings are a promise to the reader that ages faster than the text: with two release trains of slippage, some of the API may already have moved under them.

The working directory is checked out on the `claude/portfolio-html-app-w6306n` branch, not on `main`, and the last commits are nothing but {{term:dependabot|Dependabot}} merges. The last substantive work was the index and consistency pass, so the project is closer to dormant than active.
repos.headline: A full draft and countable debt: 23 uncompiled listings, zero of two measurements

repos.name: parcel-number-generator
repos.oneLiner: Three warehousing services built directly against the architectural constitution — and not one of them is deployed anywhere.
repos.summary: The PNG system issues parcel tracking numbers from a finite pool: never the same number twice, honouring sub-ranges withheld from allocation, without leaking daily volume. Alongside it, a service records events raised against parcels and the warehouse, and an operator console sits over both. It is the most interesting case in the portfolio from a methodological point of view: the repository grew out of a 2018 .NET Framework 4.5.2 solution modernised directly against `architecture-standards`, then absorbed the notification service from a separate `komunikaty` repository (itself modernised from a 2019 WinForms application). The consolidation is documented in ADR-0004 — one of the very few places in the whole portfolio where the 'merge two repositories' pattern was actually carried out rather than merely proposed. The gates are real: CI fails a pull request whose model has drifted from its committed migrations, for both services and both database providers, builds three images and runs them under `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production` to check that the startup guards still refuse to boot without a connection string and without a token issuer.
repos.tests: Two test projects, 112 `[Fact]`/`[Theory]` attributes (the README cites 139 cases — theories expand to more than one apiece). They cover pool arithmetic and the allocation strategies, the API surface of both services, mapping, and the purity of the shared kernel. A separate class enforces that no HTTP route reaches where it should not.
repos.ci: Six workflows: `ci.yml` (tests, `dotnet format`, migration-drift checks for both services and both providers, the architecture guards, three image builds with startup-guard smoke tests, gitleaks over full history, a transitive vulnerability audit), `codeql.yml`, `secret-scan.yml`, and three Fly.io workflows. Warnings are errors, NuGet advisories included.

components.description: Plumbing only, with an 800-line ceiling enforced by a script in CI rather than by prose. Exactly the same pattern as in `architecture-standards-init-example`.

components.description: A separate migration set per provider, for both services. The drift gate in CI compares the model against the committed set — a schema change without a migration does not pass.

components.description: The repository's own register of what it does not yet satisfy: what, against which principle, since when, and what closes it. The roadmap is finished when the *Open* table is empty.

overlaps.reason: Built directly against that constitution and measured by it in `02-GAP-ANALYSIS.md`. The deviations register exists here because §3a of that document requires it.
DEV-2 is waiting on a decision about which identity issuer is trusted. `authservice` is the obvious candidate — both services already validate tokens against a JWKS and hold no key material.

The same shape: a shared kernel with a line ceiling, an in-memory database fallback, migrations from a hosted service that starts after Kestrel. Greenfield there, modernization here — the same rules produce the same skeleton from two different starting points.

repos.product: A proof of method, not a transaction. The commercial value is not in issuing parcel numbers — it is in the documented path from a 2018 .NET Framework 4.5.2 solution to three .NET 10 services with migration gates, startup guards and a full-history secret audit. That is precisely the work a modernization consultant is paid for, and here it is shown end to end, including the parts that did not land.
highlights: A consolidation actually carried out: the notification service moved in from a separate repository, with an ADR recording what was harmonized. In a portfolio full of merge proposals, this is one of the few that happened.

The status code carries what the caller should do next: 201 with `complete: false` for a partial batch, 409 when the pool is exhausted and retrying will never help, 503 under contention with `Retry-After`. The difference between 'impossible' and 'try shortly' lives in the protocol, not in the documentation.

A fresh clone runs with no credential at all — an in-memory database fallback — but in Production the startup guard refuses to boot without a connection string and an issuer. CI runs the built images under `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production` for the express purpose of checking that the guards still fire.

The secret audit covers full history, not just HEAD, and is written up as a four-step release procedure of which two steps cannot be performed by a commit. This is the lesson that was missing in `quorum`.
gaps: **Nothing is deployed.** DEV-1: the workflow can stand up the whole estate from a single tag, but no Fly app exists, there is no `FLY_API_TOKEN`, and no migration has touched a real database. Every deployment claim is argued, not measured.
DEV-2: no identity provider is configured. A deployment would be open were it not for the guards — which means the JWKS validation path has never been exercised against a real issuer.
DEV-7: the open-source release is unfinished. The repository has been public since 2026-09-01, but the description and topics (#20) and the GHCR packages (#29) remain outstanding.
Six open Dependabot pull requests out of thirteen open items. Phase 2 of the roadmap exists precisely to clear them, and it has not started.

The 'never the same number twice' guarantee is today proven against an in-memory database. Phase 3 of the roadmap turns it into a measurement against a real engine — until that runs, the system's strongest claim is tested in the weakest place.
next: Close phase 1 of the roadmap: the repository description and topics, a badge row that matches reality, a rendered documentation page. These are minutes of work and they unblock legibility for anyone from outside.
Merge the six Dependabot pull requests in one pass — CI is strong enough to make that safe, and every week of delay raises the cost.
Point `Jwt__Authority` at `authservice` (DEV-2). It needs no code change — the wiring is conditional and already in place — and it unblocks the first deployment.
Push the first `v*` tag and replace the text of DEV-1 with what the first deployment actually measured.
Move the uniqueness proof onto a real database engine under concurrency — it is the one claim in this repository that must not be left resting on an in-memory database.
risks: The entire deployment path is untested in practice: the health-check grace period, the `.flycast` wake path and JWKS validation have never once run. The image builds and smoke tests in CI bound the 'works on my machine' class but not the platform class.
The repository has been public since 2026-09-01 with the release unfinished. A public commit is public forever, and re-privating does not reach the clones and forks that already exist.

repos.name: Primates
repos.oneLiner: A dead classifieds monolith rewritten as seven .NET 9 services with Aspire and tag-driven deployment to Fly.io.
repos.summary: The old classifieds monolith (FSE) was rewritten from scratch as seven ASP.NET Core services: identity with RS256 and JWKS, adverts with a taxonomy and publication broken into five steps, an append-only points ledger, stateless media, chat over Claude, and an ephemeral promotion-expiry job. Aspire composes it locally; production is Fly.io. The most interesting decision is not the split but the way the domain was recovered from the legacy code: entities in three services were not rewritten by hand but generated by a parser over the EF snapshot, and `tools/verify-model-usage.py` checks that every property used in fluent configuration, in LINQ and in initialisers actually exists on the entity. The script caught four real defects, among them an index on the non-existent column `AdvertTraffic` and an `IsActive` flag that is not in the schema. The shared {{term:servicedefaults|ServiceDefaults}} kernel has a mechanical ceiling of 800 lines enforced in CI (542 today) plus architecture tests that block entities and `DbContext` from entering it. The documentation is stronger here than the code: 14 ADRs, a register of deviations, and an audit that gives itself a score of 22 items out of 103.
repos.license: brak pliku LICENSE w repozytorium; `src/Primates.Web/package.json` deklaruje MIT, ale to metadana odziedziczona po legacy aplikacji Angulara
repos.tests: One test project: `tests/Primates.ArchitectureTests` with 2 [Fact] attributes and 1 [Theory] over 4 rows of InlineData, so 6 cases, all about the ADR-002 rules for {{term:kernel|the shared kernel}}; the 23 `.spec.ts` files in the Angular app are CLI-generated 'should create' stubs that CI does not run, and the points ledger, the publication pipeline and both frontends have not a single test.
repos.ci: Five workflows. `flyio.yml` (35 KB) is the backbone: {{term:tagdeploy|triggered by a `v*` tag}}, a test gate (kernel-size-check, Release build, dotnet test), change detection against the previous tag, a build matrix pushing to `registry.fly.io`, and deployment in dependency order with verification of the JWKS endpoint. The rest are manual scale/destroy, publishing `docs/index.html` to Pages, and a manual PDF build of the business analysis from LaTeX; there is no secret scanner in any of them.

overlaps.reason: The AppHost runs the image `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice:v0.3.1` as a second token issuer (ADR-013), and its own IdentityService stays as a compatibility path. It is the only consumer that stood that service next to an existing identity rather than in its place.
The whole repository is measured against the P1-P15 checklist from there, and `docs/architecture/07-STANDARDS-FEEDBACK.md` returns corrections to the standard itself. The coupling runs both ways.
AgentService is another agent over Claude with tools and a confirmation gate, so the same class of problem as tooling for running agents.

repos.product: No buyer. This is not a sellable product but a reference implementation of the estate standards on a real, ugly domain inherited from a dead monolith. The value is twofold: evidence of migration competence (seven services, JWKS, tag-driven deployment, its own compliance audit) and a testing ground from which rules later travel to architecture-standards and authservice. The business analysis and ADR-011 describe a revenue model for the portal in the form of points and a Pro subscription, but no paying user exists and nothing in the repository suggests otherwise.
gaps: **CI deploys neither BlazorWeb nor authservice.** The files `flyio/blazorweb.fly.toml` and `flyio/authservice.fly.toml` exist, but the words 'blazor' and 'authservice' do not appear in `.github/workflows/flyio.yml` even once, and the SERVICES array in detect-changes does not contain them. The second frontend and the new token issuer have no path to production.
There are no tests outside the kernel. The six cases are about the ADR-002 rules; item 16 of the standards checklist is red for all seven deployables and the documentation records this itself.

**Zero git tags in this clone, with deployment triggered only by a `v*` tag.** From the repository there is no way to confirm that any release actually went out, and the `primates-*.fly.dev` addresses come from the `app=` lines in fly.toml and from `docs/deployment.md`, not from a query. The history contains fixes for deployment errors, so something was being run, but that is circumstantial.

{{term:otel|OTLP}} export is wired into the kernel, and no fly.toml sets `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`. The deployed environment exports telemetry nowhere, and item 4 of the standards audit says so outright.

Seven of the eight Dockerfiles have `org.opencontainers.image.source` pointing at `konradcinkusz/FSE`, a source that no longer exists; only `src/Primates.AgentService/Dockerfile` points at `konradcinkusz/primates`. The images in registry.fly.io sign themselves with a repository that is not there.
next: Add BlazorWeb and authservice deployment to `flyio.yml`, or delete their fly.toml files. The current state promises a deployment that does not exist.
Move the Google Maps key out of four Angular modules into the existing `assets/config.json` and add gitleaks to the workflow. The key is in the history, so rotation is necessary anyway.
Add a LICENSE file and correct `org.opencontainers.image.source` in seven Dockerfiles to point at this repository.
Push a `v*` tag and confirm that the cold-environment rule really does bring the whole estate up from nothing. Today that is a promise untested from the repository.
Write characterisation tests for the points ledger and the publication pipeline before anything in them changes.
highlights: The shared {{term:kernel|kernel}} has a **mechanical ceiling**: `kernel-size-check.sh` fails CI above 800 lines (542 today), and `SharedKernelTests.cs` blocks entities, `DbContext` and types with domain names from entering. The same rule has already failed twice in this estate when it was only written down in a document.

The entities were not rewritten by hand but generated by a parser over the EF snapshot, and `verify-model-usage.py` caught **four real defects**, among them an index on the non-existent column `AdvertTraffic` and an `IsActive` flag that the schema does not contain.

The cold-environment rule in the deployment: a service whose application on Fly does not yet exist is always selected for the build, so the whole environment comes up from the first tag without a manual `fly launch`. The deployment order verifies the JWKS endpoint before the rest starts.

`docs/BUSINESS-ANALYSIS-COVERAGE.md` is an audit of its own code against 103 business analysis requirements, citing files and lines, ending in a verdict of **22 done / 52 partial / 29 missing**. A document that gives itself a bad mark.

The agent over Claude has no capability beyond the logged-in user: the five tools are wrappers over authorised endpoints called with his token, and every tool that spends points pauses the turn and waits for explicit confirmation.
risks: **A committed Google Maps API key** in four Angular modules and no secret scanner in any workflow, even though phase 0 of its own migration plan requires one. The key is in the git history, so rotation is the only real remedy. The key prefix has been removed from this entry, because this entry is public.

No LICENSE file, in a repository cited from other repositories in the estate; the Angular `package.json` declares MIT, which is metadata inherited from the legacy code and can be read as the licence for the whole thing.

Two token issuers run in parallel deliberately (`Jwt:AdditionalAuthority`), but an account created in authservice is a different principal from the same account in IdentityService. ADR-013 admits that there is no continuity of the user identifier.

Angular 10 with ngcc, rxjs-compat and core-js 2.5.1 is an abandoned dependency chain with no security support. 169 TS files stay in the repository with no decision about what to do with them, and some admin screens call four `/Admin/*` endpoints that the backend does not have.

repos.name: rsna-knee-abnormalities-efficiency-lb
repos.oneLiner: A multimodal 2.5D pipeline for a Kaggle knee-MRI challenge — the one repository in the portfolio with no licence file.
repos.summary: A deep-learning pipeline for the RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection challenge: detecting twelve findings from knee MRI combined with radiology-report text, over a DINOv2 imaging branch and a multilingual text branch, with an explicit weak-supervision strategy and diagnostics tooling. Four Python files, fifteen hundred lines, three commits — the smallest and rawest entry in this pass, and it joins the map mainly because it is the portfolio's only attempt at medical imaging and its only Kaggle competition entry. It is also the only public repository on the account **with no licence file**, which for a repository touching medical data and described as carrying full documentation is a real omission: with no licence nobody has the right to use the code, and default copyright reserves all rights. The repository carries no CI, no tests and no recorded run results — it has been frozen since 15 August 2026.

repos.name: SupercompensationApp
repos.oneLiner: The supercompensation model carried over from sport to Agile sprints — the one thing in this portfolio that is deployed and simply works.
repos.summary: A Blazor WebAssembly application that computes the fatigue → recovery → supercompensation curve for a team across successive sprints, with configurable fatigue depth, supercompensation peak and baseline increment. Three tabs: configuration with spreadsheet-style team editing, an interactive chart with coloured phases, and a day-by-day table with filtering. The mathematical model is written out in the README as formulas with their ranges — unusual, and it lets the arithmetic be checked without reading the code. This repository's value in the portfolio is different from its subject: **it is the only entry added in this pass that is genuinely deployed and reachable at a public address.** Against seven other repositories whose deployment workflows have never once run, this one, with its automatic GitHub Pages deploy, is the proof that the loop from commit to working page is closed at least once in this portfolio.
repos.tests: 68 `[Fact]`/`[Theory]` attributes — the densest test coverage relative to size of anything added in this pass, against 18 C# files. A mathematical model is exactly the kind of code that tests well, and that has been taken advantage of.
repos.ci: Four workflows: `ci.yml`, `codeql.yml`, `secret-scan.yml`, and `pages.yml`, which publishes from `master` automatically. That last one is the only deployment workflow in this pass that actually runs.

repos.name: TinyTransformer
repos.oneLiner: A transformer encoder block written from scratch in C# on bare `float[,]` arrays, with no numerical library at all.
repos.summary: One transformer encoder block built on `net9.0` from the BCL alone: the static `MathOps` class supplies `MatMul`, `Transpose`, `AddBias`, `SoftmaxRows`, `ReLU`, variance and the initialisers, and on top of it stand six network layers, from `Embedding` to `TransformerEncoderBlock`. The data path is complete and internally consistent: the embedding returns a `[T x dModel]` matrix, attention scales the `Q·Kᵀ` product by `1/sqrt(dK)`, and the block closes two residual connections and two normalisations in a post-norm arrangement. The most interesting engineering decision sits in the tests rather than in the production code: attention is verified by **equivariance under a permutation of the tokens**, that is, reversing the order of the input rows must reverse the output rows, and `LayerNorm` by a statistical property (mean 0, variance 1 in every row) instead of by comparison against a hard-coded table of numbers. `Linear` was given a second constructor taking ready-made `W` and `b` so that the tests do not depend on the random number generator, which gives {{term:determinizm}} in the one place where initialisation is random by definition. Only the forward pass is finished, however: there are no gradients, no training and no weight saving, so the model computes on parameters nobody has trained. Work stopped at the seventh commit on 30 September 2025 and the repository has stood still since.
repos.tests: 24 `[Fact]` methods across 10 files plus a shared `TestsBase`, zero `[Theory]` and zero `[InlineData]`; 486 lines of tests against 487 lines of Core code. The count comes from counting the attributes in the code, because the review environment had no dotnet SDK and a run could not be confirmed.
repos.ci: No CI. The `.github` directory does not exist, there is no `yml` or `yaml` file anywhere in the repository, so those 24 tests are not run on any push.

components.name: MathOps
components.description: The project's only numerical layer: `MatMul` in an i-k-j loop, `Transpose`, `Add`, `AddBias`, scalar multiplication, `Mean`, `Variance`, `ReverseRow` and overloaded initialisers. `SoftmaxRows` subtracts the row maximum before exponentiating, that is, it applies the standard numerical stabilisation instead of computing straight from the formula.

components.name: SelfAttention
components.description: Single-head self-attention: four `Linear` projections onto Q, K, V and the output, the product of Q with the transpose of K, scaling by `1/sqrt(dK)`, softmax across rows and the context back to `dModel`. There is no causal masking and no multiple heads, so it suits an encoder and does not suit a decoder.

components.name: TransformerEncoderBlock
components.description: The repository's substantive destination: attention, adding the input, `LayerNorm`, feed-forward, adding again, a second `LayerNorm`. Four layers hidden behind a single `ILayer`, and at the same time the only class in the project without a test file of its own.

components.name: Linear
components.description: An affine layer `Y = X W + b` with weights initialised at a scale of `sqrt(2/(din+dout))`. The second constructor takes ready-made `W` and `b`, solely so that the assertions do not depend on the generator's seed.

components.name: ILayer i IEmbedding
components.description: Two contracts over primitives: `Forward(float[,])` and `Lookup(int[])`. They are what let the block be assembled from interchangeable parts, but inside `ILayer` sits a `TODO: add Tensor class` comment, which is an admission that an interface this narrow will not carry back-propagation.

components.name: TestsBase and the test set
components.description: A shared base with tolerance-based matrix comparison and data generators, and above it 24 tests of MathOps and the layers. The `float[,]` assertions built on FluentAssertions are {{term:hermetyczny|hermetic}} and domain-neutral, so they carry over to any other numerical code in C#.

components.name: ConsoleApp
components.description: A dozen or so lines of demo: five tokens, `dModel` 16, `dK` 16, hidden layer 32, seed 0. It computes `Forward`, then prints the string `Encoded sequence` and nothing else; the `posEncoding` and `seqLen` variables are dead.

components.name: Diagramy PlantUML
components.description: A conceptual diagram of the language model and a class diagram of the solution. Both describe the intended state, not the code: the solution diagram declares a `TinyTransformer.Autograd` package with `Tensor` and `TensorOps` classes, which are not among the repository's 35 files.

overlaps.reason: The same material: the linear algebra and activation functions behind neural networks, here as working code instead of a lecture.
The same way of working: the mathematical apparatus implemented from scratch instead of calling a ready-made library.
A shared LLM domain, but from the opposite end of the stack: the mechanics of the model here, the application layer over ready-made models there.
A natural source of material for a chapter on what exactly an attention block computes, before the book starts talking about the framework layer.

repos.product: No buyer, and there is no point looking for one. For anything of working use there are ONNX Runtime and TorchSharp, so this code will never reach production and that was never the intent. The value is in credibility and teaching: it is evidence that the author can take the attention mechanism apart into matrix multiplications and write it without a framework, which counts for something in an interview about LLM work and as material for an article or a book chapter.
highlights: A test of attention's equivariance under a permutation of the tokens: it reverses the order of the input rows and checks that the output reverses the same way. That is the right way to test attention and most tutorials do not do it.
`SoftmaxRows` subtracts the row maximum before exponentiating. Deliberate numerical stabilisation, not a naive transcription of the formula.
`LayerNorm` is tested by a statistical property, mean 0 and variance 1 in every row, instead of by comparison against a pasted-in table of numbers.
486 lines of tests against 487 lines of production code, with 24 `[Fact]` methods and zero NuGet dependencies in the Core project.
`Linear` has a second constructor taking ready-made `W` and `b`, added solely so that the tests do not depend on the random number generator.
gaps: **The README is one line**, `# TinyTransformer`, 17 bytes. No description, no way to run it, no reason for the repository to exist.
No back-propagation, no gradients and no training loop. The model computes on random weights, so the output has no semantic meaning, and `ILayer` in its present shape will not carry it.

Positional encoding does not exist, although the conceptual diagram shows it, and `Program.cs` carries a dead `posEncoding` variable and a comment about building it. This is one of several divergences between the code and its own diagrams, and not the only one; the rest are collected in the point below.

`diagram_solution.puml` describes a non-existent `TinyTransformer.Autograd` package with `Tensor` and `TensorOps` classes, the layers `EmbeddingAuto`, `SelfAttentionAuto` and `TransformerEncoderBlockAuto` (in the code they are `Embedding`, `SelfAttention` and `TransformerEncoderBlock`, and only `FeedForwardAuto` carries the `Auto` suffix), plus the tests `FeedForwardTests` and `TransformerBlockTests` (the repository has `FeedForwardAutoTests`, and block tests do not exist at all). Seven class names and a whole package with no counterpart among the 35 files in git. A design intention presented as a description of the state.

The console demo prints the heading alone and does not print the output matrix, and `TransformerEncoderBlock` is the only layer without a test file. Anyone who clones the repo and runs the project will see nothing.
next: Write the README: what this is, why it is done without a library, what shape the data has on input and output, and how to run `dotnet test` and `dotnet run`.
Fix the demo so that it prints the block's output matrix, and remove the dead `posEncoding` and `seqLen`.
Add a GitHub Actions workflow with `dotnet build` and `dotnet test` on `net9.0`, and while you are there raise the xunit 2.4.2 and Test.Sdk 17.7.1 pins.
Add tests for `TransformerEncoderBlock`: shape preservation and a mean close to zero across the rows after the second `LayerNorm`.

Settle the project's status: either positional encoding and autograd, or close it as a finished forward-pass exercise with the diagram reconciled. The present suspension is the worst of the three options.
risks: The name `tiny-transformer` is exceptionally common in the ML teaching ecosystem and does nothing to distinguish the repository in a search.
`LICENSE.txt` is an unfilled {{term:mit|MIT}} template with literal `[year]` and `[fullname]`, so formally it names no copyright holder.

The name `FeedForwardAuto` is a leftover from the autograd plan and misleads, because nothing there is automatically differentiated; likewise the `BasicTestsBase` class in `BasicMathOpsTests.cs` pretends to be a base class while being an ordinary set of eight tests.

The code has stood still since 30 September 2025 at seven commits, and without CI there is no telling whether the 24 tests still pass. With no README to close the argument, the whole thing reads as an abandoned sketch rather than a finished exercise.
repos.headline: Forward pass closed, no back-propagation, README is one line

repos.name: WSB — Bayesian Network Inference
repos.oneLiner: An exact inference engine for Bayesian networks written from scratch, plus a Blazor app that does not use it and computes its own wrong numbers.
repos.summary: The repository has two halves that share a name and share no code. The first is `WSB.BayesianNetwork.Logic`: the Enumeration-Ask algorithm from Russell and Norvig written without any probabilistic library, with a console harness that sweeps all 6561 evidence combinations. The second is a full-stack application — Blazor WebAssembly (37 `.razor` components) talking over REST to an ASP.NET Core host (9 controllers), CQRS on MediatR, EF Core 7 with Npgsql, RS256 tokens validated against the {{term:oidc|JWKS}} of a separate `authservice` instance. The web application **does not reference the tested engine**, it duplicates the probability calculation in its own service layer instead. The most interesting decision is not in the code but in `docs/research`: the author could not run .NET in the environment where the study was done, so he wrote a 229-line replica of the engine in Python, validated it against the existing unit tests, and only then used it as an instrument — and with that instrument he showed that the demo network has underspecified CPTs and that the web calculation path does not return posteriors at all. This is a repository whose best product is the evidence of its own errors.
repos.tests: Exactly 4 `[Fact]` tests in a single project, all of them against the engine; the expected values (0.461538 for the WetRain network, 0.336689 for the Alarm variant) were derived by hand from the CPTs in the comments, not copied from the algorithm's output. The web calculation path has no test at all, which the README and the gap analysis both state outright. The run was not verified — there was no .NET SDK in the review environment.
repos.ci: Four workflows. `build.yml` does a restore, a Release build and `dotnet test` over the whole solution, and then **applies a hand-written EF Core migration against a `postgres:16` service** — the migration was written without local access to a database and this is its only verification. Only two of the other three disable themselves: `deploy.yml` (flyctl) checks `if [ -z "$FLY_API_TOKEN" ]` in the script and finishes with `exit 0`, and `reset-demo.yml` (cron every 6 hours) puts `if: ${{ vars.DEMO_APP_URL != '' }}` on its steps with a 'not configured yet' branch; without the secret and without the variable both end in a no-op. `pages.yml` has no such guard — the file contains not one `if:`, nor any reference to `vars.` or `secrets.` — so it fires on every push that touches `html/` and, as its own header says, the `actions/deploy-pages@v4` step **fails** with 'Pages site not found' until the repository owner switches Settings → Pages → Source to 'GitHub Actions'. That is a red run, not a quiet skip.

metrics.label: Queries in the console sweep
metrics.value: 6561 (3^8), of which 648 give a meaningful posterior

docs.label: Study 01 — underspecified CPTs in the StockBN network
LaTeX paper tying both studies together
Analysis of 18 conformance points against the standard

components.name: docs/research — the studies, artefacts and the article
components.description: Two formal studies using the validated-replica method: 229 lines of Python reproducing the engine, 56 lines of sweep analysis, 295 lines of a transcript of the web calculator and a 601-line LaTeX paper. Every artefact is committed, so the result can be reproduced without a .NET SDK.

components.name: Weryfikacja migracji EF Core w CI
components.description: A step that brings up `postgres:16` as a service and runs `dotnet ef database update` with a pinned `dotnet-ef` 7.0.5 and a dummy auth metadata address. A domain-neutral pattern for any repository where migrations are written by hand.

components.name: WSB.BayesianNetwork.Logic
components.description: `BaseInference` with normalisation and a domain, a working `Enumeration` and an `Elimination` that is a stub throwing `NotImplementedException`. The CPT sits in a fixed `double[10,10,10,10]` array, so cells that were never written return 0.0 silently — that is the source of the defect described in study 01.

components.name: WSB.Console
components.description: The demo harness and benchmark: it builds the StockBN, Alarm and WetRain networks, times a full sweep of 3^8 evidence combinations with a `Stopwatch` and dumps the result to `output_<timestamp>.txt`. This is what produced the 4374 / 1539 / 648 split.

components.name: WSB.Service — warstwa CQRS
components.description: 28 command and query files on MediatR, and inside them both parallel calculation paths: the live `EnumerationCalculator` and the `CalculateCommand` that no controller can reach. Neither of them calls the engine in `WSB.BayesianNetwork.Logic`.

components.name: Server (WSB.Server)
components.description: A host with a versioned API, `/health` and `/alive`, a `MigrationHostedService` applying migrations in the background and a `WriteAccessAuthorizationFilter`. Without `Auth:MetadataAddress` set the process does not start at all — it throws `InvalidOperationException` while building the container.

components.name: Client (WSB.Client)
components.description: An editor for networks and probability tables, a query box and a live Mermaid diagram of the network being built. The sign-in page talks directly to `authservice`, with refresh token rotation and 2FA; `DataServiceBase`, however, has no retry policy and no timeout.

components.name: docs/architecture — ADR-y i audyty
components.description: Six documents, including 11 ADRs that also record decisions **not** to do something (ADR-004 deferring variable elimination, ADR-005 deliberately leaving the duplicated logic in place) and an open-source readiness {{term:audit|audit}} with an inventory of what had been sitting in the scrubbed git history.

overlaps.reason: The application has no signing key of its own: it validates RS256 against the JWKS of that service's instance (ADR-010/ADR-011), and the deployment runbook stands both applications side by side on Fly.io. With HS256 on that side the JWKS is empty and every token is thrown out while both services look healthy.

The whole of `docs/architecture` and `docs/research` is written directly against that repository's conformance checklist and research standard. This is a real use of that repository, not a declaration.

repos.product: No buyer, and the README admits it in the *What this project is not* section — the project does not compete with pgmpy or with any PGM library. It started as a coursework assignment, then grew into a reference full-stack application and into a test case for the author's own documentation standard. The value is credibility and teaching: it shows an exact inference algorithm written by hand, and an author who publishes a formal study of the errors in his own code instead of quietly fixing them.
gaps: **The web calculation path does not work.** Study 02 showed that the parser falls over on the hints the server generates, the result never reaches the UI, there is no normalisation, and the numbers returned (1.7 and 4.0) are not probabilities. This is the application's main function and its most important unpatched defect.

The StockBN demo network has underspecified two-parent CPTs: of the 6561 sweep queries 4374 are degenerate, 1539 return NaN through a division by zero in `Normalization`, and 648 give a meaningful posterior. `P(b)` comes out as 0 despite a prior of 0.99.

The two halves of the repository are not joined up — the application duplicates the logic instead of referencing the tested engine, and `Elimination.cs` is an empty stub. ADR-004 and ADR-005 record this as a deliberate deferral, which does not change the state of the tree.

A latent bug in the `BaseInference` constructor: given a non-empty variable list `_vars` is left `null` and inference throws `NullReferenceException`. It works only because `Enumeration` always passes `null`. On top of that the comments about evidence encoding are systematically inverted against the code (they say 0 = true, the code uses 1 = true).
No screenshots, no {{term:otel|OTLP}} telemetry, no retry and timeout policies on HttpClient, no secret scanner in CI. None of the three declared addresses was confirmed to be live.
next: Write characterisation tests for `EnumerationCalculator`, then replace both web calculation paths with a call into `WSB.BayesianNetwork.Logic`. That closes point 16 of the gap analysis and study 02 at the same time.

Fill in the two-parent CPTs in StockBN (eight `SetProbabilities` calls, following the Alarm network) and guard `BaseInference.Normalization` against division by zero. Without this 23.5 per cent of queries still return NaN.

Close out `06-OPEN-SOURCE-READINESS.md`: delete or repoint the `v1.0.0` and `v1.0.1` tags, which still point at history from before `git filter-repo`. The audit itself calls this the only blocker to going public.

Settle the name collision: `fly.toml` says `wsb-bayesian-inference`, the `LABEL` in the Dockerfile and the Pages link in the README say `BayesianInference`, and the repo slug is `bayesian-inference`. Turn Pages on and check what address the one-pager actually lands at.
Plan the move off .NET 7 onto an LTS version together with EF Core and the base images — today the whole stack sits on an unsupported release.
highlights: Enumeration-Ask written from scratch, without any probabilistic library, and the expected values in the tests (0.461538 and 0.336689) are **derived by hand from the CPTs in the comments**, not copied from the algorithm's output. That is the difference between a correctness test and pinning current behaviour.

A method for studying code you cannot run: a replica in Python, validated first against the existing unit tests and only then used as an instrument. 580 lines of artefacts, all committed — and this is the one thing in this repository that could be carried anywhere else.
Two formal research studies find serious errors in the author's own code, with numbers: `P(b)` = 0 against a prior of 0.99, and the 4374 / 1539 / 648 split across 6561 sweep queries.

CI does not only build and test, it applies a hand-written EF Core migration against a real `postgres:16` container. The migration was written without local access to a database and this step is its only verification.
The README has its own *What this project is not* section and states outright that the two halves of the repository are not joined up and that the web calculation path is unverified.
risks: The `v1.0.0` and `v1.0.1` tags still point at history from before the rewrite (`git filter-repo`, 2026-08-15), so once the repository is public they lead to deleted PDFs carrying a student number. The author's own audit calls this the only blocker.

The public demo is designed with no sign-in for either reading or writing, protected only by a data reset every 6 hours (ADR-008). With a live deployment that means write access to the database is open to anyone.

The whole stack sits on .NET 7 — a release out of support — including the `sdk:7.0` and `aspnet:7.0` images, so security holes will not be patched. `appsettings.Development.json` carries a committed `postgres/postgres`, and there is no secret scanner in CI.
Dead code stays in the tree: `CalculateCommand` cannot be reached from a controller and, according to study 02, returns infinity, and `Elimination.cs` throws `NotImplementedException`.
repos.headline: Two halves that never meet — and the author proved it himself in two studies

repos.name: Zoo Companion
repos.oneLiner: Single-tenant B2B app for a zoo: a staff panel, public exhibit pages behind a QR code and a Claude chat with two tools.
repos.summary: An admin panel for the staff of one zoo (exhibits, animals, species, keeper notes, feeding times, photos), public `/exhibit/{slug}` pages reachable from the sign at the exhibit through a QR code, and a Claude-based chat restricted to that zoo's data. The stack is .NET 10, {{term:aspire|Aspire}} 13.4.6 as the composition root, Blazor Server, EF Core on Postgres and the Anthropic package 12.40.0. Staff authentication is pushed out entirely to an own instance of the sibling `authservice`, so the repository holds neither a user store nor a signing key; login goes through a plain `POST /admin/login` endpoint outside the Blazor circuit, because a SignalR circuit cannot write a cookie. The most interesting decision is in the agent layer: the tool surface is **two read-only tools**, `list_exhibits` and `get_exhibit_details`, so there is no approval gate and no suspended-turn state, and `ZooDataQueries` is the single data reader shared by the chat and the public page, so the two cannot drift apart on the facts. The whole thing came out of one implementation pass: five commits, the last on 18 August 2026.
repos.tests: None. The repository has no test project and no test file, and `ci.yml` carries an explicit comment `No test project yet - Phase 0 has no automated tests` against 1,044 lines of C#.
repos.ci: One workflow, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: checkout, setup-dotnet 10.0.x, `dotnet restore` and `dotnet build ZooCompanion.slnx -warnaserror`. No test step, no image build, no deployment.

docs.label: Architecture and the reasoning behind the choices

components.name: Warstwa konsumenta authservice
components.description: `AuthEndpoints` maps login and logout outside the Blazor circuit, `AuthserviceLoginClient` calls `POST /api/v1/auth/login` on the external instance, and `JwtClaimsPrincipalFactory` turns the returned token into the cookie's ClaimsPrincipal. A JwtBearer scheme configured alongside it validates tokens through JWKS, so one application serves a cookie for the UI and a bearer for the API.

components.name: ZooCompanion.ServiceDefaults
components.description: The shared {{term:servicedefaults|infrastructure kernel}}: {{term:otel|OpenTelemetry}} for logs, metrics and traces, health checks, service discovery and the standard HttpClient resilience handler. A comment in the code cites principle P2 from `architecture-standards` as the reason there is not a single domain entity in here.

components.name: QrCodeService
components.description: Sixteen lines wrapping QRCoder: in comes a string and a pixel-per-module count, out comes a PNG at error correction level Q. The `/admin/exhibits/{id}/qr` page renders the result as a data URI so staff can print the sign without downloading a file.

components.name: LocalMediaStorage
components.description: Writes uploaded photos to disk under `wwwroot/uploads` with a Guid name, plus `GetPublicUrl` and `Delete`. Its only assumption is that WebRootPath exists; having no blob storage dependency is a deliberate limitation for the single-instance pilot.

components.name: ZooChatAgent + ZooChatTools
components.description: A tool-calling loop on the Anthropic SDK: at most 6 iterations, 1,024 output tokens, conversion of TextBlock and ToolUseBlock blocks, an error returned as a bilingual message rather than an exception. The system prompt confines the agent to this zoo's animals and exhibits, forces an answer in the language of the question, and forbids inventing names, species or feeding times.

components.name: ZooDataQueries
components.description: The only place that reads exhibit data, shared by the public pages and the agent's tool implementations. It returns the projection records `ExhibitSummary`, `ExhibitDetail` and `AnimalDetail`, so a drift in facts between the chat and the page would require writing a second reader.

components.name: ZooCompanion.AppHost
components.description: The {{term:aspire|Aspire}} composition root: two Postgres databases (its own and a separate one for authservice), the authservice container with a bind mount for the RS256 key, and the Web project with the identity provider's address injected. The key path is read straight from configuration, because the mount has to be declared synchronously.

components.name: Model danych i MigrationBackgroundService
components.description: Six entities, a unique index on `Exhibit.Slug` and explicitly declared cascade behaviours rather than the defaults. `MigrationBackgroundService` runs `MigrateAsync` only once Kestrel has started, so the health probe does not read a long migration as a failed deployment.

overlaps.reason: A real runtime dependency: zoo-companion runs its own instance of the `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice` image and has no local user store at all. Another data point for the 'one codebase, N instances' pattern.
The idea was carved out of the same 'Primates: from A to ZOO' analysis, and BUSINESS-CASE.md documents that primates never built institutional features for zoos beyond a placeholder category.
The code and `.github/copilot-instructions.md` cite that repo's P1-P15 principles directly: AppHost as the composition root, migrations rather than EnsureCreated, secrets only from the environment.
The same Blazor Server plus Aspire plus Postgres shape, named in the README as a pattern already validated there and in AgentHelm.
The README names it as the source of the pattern of a narrow, explicitly enumerated agent tool surface rather than open access to the database.

repos.product: The buyer is defined more sharply than in most of the portfolio: an institution - a zoo, a wildlife park or an aquarium - buying a licence for a visitor-facing product, sold directly by the founder as an autónomo in Spain. Two specific pilot targets are named, Río Safari Elche and Bioparc Valencia, but no contact is confirmed, there is no price, and phase 0 is openly a free installation in exchange for a case study. The real commercial status is therefore a hypothesis with a working demo, not a pipeline. BUSINESS-CASE.md itself admits that a market of some 26 zoos in Poland is not a business without international expansion, and that is the most honest sentence in the whole repository.
highlights: The full path from business analysis to running code in **five commits**: BUSINESS-CASE.md, ARCHITECTURE.md and ROADMAP.md come before the implementation and agree with it.

The case for the product existing rests on an audit of someone else's code, not on a declaration: BUSINESS-CASE.md gives evidence (the `Zoos` bazaar id 104, one category `DisplayToThePublic`, one transaction type `Visit`, a subscription price table) that zoo features were never built, in FSE or in primates.
The repository holds no user store, no password and no signing key: RS256 in `authservice` means the application needs nothing but the identity provider's URL.

The agent's tool surface is deliberately two read-only tools, so an approval gate and a suspended-turn state simply do not exist. A comment in the code compares this directly with the far heavier `AgentService` from primates.
CI builds with `-warnaserror`, and migrations start only once Kestrel is listening, so the health probe does not read a long migration as a failed deploy.
gaps: **Zero automated tests** against 1,044 lines of C#. There is no test for `ZooChatTools.ExecuteAsync` and none for the `ZooDataQueries` projections, though both have obvious edge cases (a missing argument, an unknown tool, a slug that does not exist).

**No deployment and no public URL.** ARCHITECTURE.md names Fly.io as the target, but the repo has no `fly.toml` and no `infra` directory; the image from the Dockerfile is published nowhere, and {{term:ghcr}} appears only as the source of someone else's authservice image.

The roadmap ticks off the public pages as 'ES primary / EN fallback', while `Home.razor` and `ExhibitDetail.razor` render only the `*En` fields. The Spanish fields are collected in the admin panel and **never shown to a visitor**; the bilingual behaviour works only in the chat, through the prompt.
No role control of any kind: ARCHITECTURE.md admits itself that any account existing in the attached authservice instance can log in as zoo staff.
The public chat endpoint calls Claude with no rate limit, no cap on history length and no session limit. That is one exposure to the world away from an unbounded bill.
risks: `LICENSE` states the copyright as `dev_insight`, not the author and not the project name. It is a file copied from a sibling repo and the same mistake appears in at least two others.

The authservice image is pinned to the `latest` tag in both `docker-compose.yml` and AppHost. A change to the `POST /api/v1/auth/login` contract or to the response shape breaks login with no warning at all in this repository.

`JwtClaimsPrincipalFactory` reads claims through `ReadJwtToken`, that is **without verifying the signature**. A comment justifies this by trusting the server-to-server connection, which holds exactly as long as `Authority` does not point at an untrusted host.

The model in `appsettings.json` is the alias `claude-sonnet-5` with no pinned version, and the startup password `ChangeMe123!` sits in plain sight in `docker-compose.yml` and in `AppHost/Program.cs`. Both are acceptable on a laptop and both would travel further unchanged.
next: Add `tests/ZooCompanion.Tests` and a `dotnet test` step in `ci.yml`; the comment in the workflow asks for it itself. The first four tests are `ZooChatTools.ExecuteAsync` on a missing argument, an unknown tool and a slug that does not exist, plus `GetExhibitDetailBySlugAsync`.
Settle the bilingual question: either render the `*Es` fields on the public pages, or untick the checkbox in the roadmap. Today the roadmap tells an untruth about its own code.
Add rate limiting and a cap on history length to the chat endpoint before anything is exposed publicly.
Write `fly.toml` for web and `flyio/authservice.fly.toml` following the pattern in ARCHITECTURE.md, and while you are there pin a specific authservice image tag instead of `latest`.
Arrange the first conversation with Elche or Valencia. It is the only task blocking phase 0 that cannot be closed with code.
repos.headline: Phase 0 complete in five commits: no tests, no deployment, no customer

kernels.name: authservice — identity as an image
kernels.description: A login service lifted out of a private monorepo and published as a versioned {{term:ghcr}} image. The consumer pins a tag in configuration and has **no** source dependency at all.
readiness: One codebase, N independent instances, no shared root of trust
The job that publishes the image needs none of the secrets required for deployment
The pattern is written up as a proposed standard, with an explicit note that it rests on one data point
kernels.blocker: There is no tag at all. Six repositories pin a version of an image whose existence cannot be confirmed — so the pattern is documented and the artefact is not.

kernels.name: {{term:playhead|Record/replay cassette}}
kernels.description: Recording and replaying model calls at the {{term:ichatclient}} seam. 250 lines, one package dependency, {{term:hermetyczny|hermeticity}} enforced by an architecture test and a separate CI job that builds the kernel in isolation.
readiness: Already physically extracted into `kernel/replay/` with its own project file and its own tests
No domain vocabulary; neutrality is tested, not declared
The first consumer is named and justified: an evaluation harness without replay cannot tell a regression from randomness
kernels.blocker: The name is provisional and has not been checked against the package registry. Check it **before** publishing — changing the identifier after the first install is a breaking change.

kernels.name: {{term:servicedefaults|ServiceDefaults}} — the shared host core
kernels.description: Authentication against JWKS, database provider selection, rate limiting with a uniform 429 response shape, background migration after the server starts. Ten projects in the portfolio do the same thing; **four wrote it independently from scratch**.
readiness: The CogniSim version has its cleanliness enforced by an architecture test and a mechanical line limit in CI
The authservice version has the best worked-out background migration, with a readiness signal
The primates version has the richest web layer
kernels.blocker: **There is no single version you can lift out.** Four implementations have 188, 177, 169 and 101 lines of database provider selection alone, and every one of them is different. First decide which is the reference and write that decision down — then extract.

kernels.name: Judge calibration ({{term:kappa|Cohen's kappa}})
kernels.description: Agreement between an LLM judge and human labels: unweighted, linearly weighted and quadratically weighted kappa, with a bootstrap and a confidence interval, plus a **ceiling taken from the mutual agreement of a human panel**, computed before the judge is scored.
readiness: The arithmetic itself is neutral: it computes agreement over ordinal labels and nothing else
The only dependency to remove is an import of the collector's domain namespace for a percentile helper — **two calls**
The CopilotScope version is the richest: 340 lines with three weighting variants and a separate 'ceiling too low' verdict
The other two consumers already have their own, thinner implementations — consolidation here removes code rather than adding it
kernels.blocker: None of the three implementations has been run against real human labels. Extracting a library will not fix the fact that nobody has labelled a sample yet.

kernels.name: An OTLP decoder without the SDK
kernels.description: A hand-written protobuf reader plus decoders for traces, metrics and logs, with the field numbers verified against the official `.proto` files. It receives {{term:otel|OTLP}} without pulling in the whole SDK.
readiness: It reads the generic OTLP format and knows nothing of sessions or sensors — the neutrality here is structural
Two versions exist: 718 lines in copilot-scope and 1063 lines in hydro-scope; the newer one is a superset
Both have their own decoder tests, so the extraction starts with coverage
kernels.blocker: Two consumers is the minimum, not comfort. If one of these repositories is archived after the extraction, the library drops to one user and goes back inside.

kernels.name: {{term:runstore|Run store}} and comparison
kernels.description: It stores a **run**, not a single span, with idempotent ingest and scoring off the request path. The {{term:comparison|comparison layer}} reports medians and spreads and has no field for a best run.
readiness: The distribution arithmetic itself is a hundred per cent generic
The run record needs parameterising — today it carries the ceremony's domain fields
The same data shape arose independently as the permission gate's {{term:audit|audit trail}}
kernels.blocker: Do this only once K1 has **two actual** consumers on main. That is the {{term:wip|work-in-progress limit}} rule, not a preference.

kernelsRejected.name: ArtefactExtractor — pulling artefacts out of a transcript
kernelsRejected.reason: It knows what a PI objective, a cross-team dependency and a ROAM risk are. That is not a dependency you can parameterise — it is **the entire value** of the component. Extracting it would leave an empty shell.

kernelsRejected.name: QualityEngine — the session quality score
kernelsRejected.reason: Six weights are an opinion about what a good session with an assistant means. An opinion is not a library; published as a library, it immediately becomes somebody else's metric that you have to answer for.

kernelsRejected.name: Roslyn analysers
kernelsRejected.reason: They encode the specific P1–P15 principles of this constitution. Outside it, half the rules need reconfiguring and the other half make no sense. What is reusable is the harness that runs them, not the analysers.

kernelsRejected.name: ConfirmationTokenStore — the write gate
kernelsRejected.reason: The pattern is neutral and tempting, but today it has **one** consumer. A library with one user is a project moved into a different directory, paid for with a separate CI run and a separate release.

kernelsRejected.name: Blazor BFF with a token pair in the cookie
kernelsRejected.reason: The layer is good and repeatable, but its surface is one application's routes. What repeats is a pattern to describe in a guide, not code to package.

kernelsRejected.name: Architecture tests
kernelsRejected.reason: The mechanism is portable, but every assertion refers to one repository's assembly names. Distribute it as a template in a guide, not as a package.

duplications.problem: **{{term:kappa|Cohen's kappa}} implemented three times, in two languages.**

sideA.what: `Calibration/Agreement.cs`, 340 lines, three weighting variants and a bootstrap

duplications.resolution: A third copy sits in the evaluation harness (228 lines). Together, 618 lines computing the same statistic. **One library, two consumers who delete code the moment they take it** — this is kernel K3 and the cleanest consolidation in the whole portfolio.

duplications.problem: **The OTLP decoder written twice, in files with identical names.**

sideB.what: `Core/Otlp/` — 1063 lines in files with **the same names**

duplications.resolution: These two repositories share nine identically named `.cs` files. The newer version is a superset of the older one, so the direction is settled: lift it out of hydro-scope and wire it into copilot-scope. This is kernel K4.

duplications.problem: **{{term:servicedefaults|ServiceDefaults}} in eleven projects, four written independently.**

sideA.what: 169 lines of database provider selection, 166 lines of authentication

sideB.what: 145 lines of authentication and a separate migration layer, all of it done differently

duplications.resolution: Aspire generates this project in every new solution and nobody references it — it gets copied. The convenience of the template is the source of the largest duplication in the portfolio. This is kernel K2, and also the hardest one, because you have to **pick the reference version first**.

duplications.problem: **Eight repositories have a licence file carrying somebody else's copyright line.**

sideA.what: MIT with a name copied from another project

sideB.what: the same thing, the same line

duplications.resolution: It affects eight repositories. One of them is public today — but six of the rest are candidates for opening, so the defect will surface at exactly the moment it does the most harm. This is not eight typos, it is one template copied eight times: **one session, eight commits**, and it is the cheapest fix with a real legal effect in the whole map.

duplications.problem: The {{term:audit|audit trail}} and the {{term:runstore|run store}} are the same data structure.

sideA.what: The run record as a compliance function — who, when, with what permission

sideB.what: The run record as a research function — what, how much, with what result

duplications.resolution: The same shape arose twice for two different reasons. Kernel K5 merges both, but only after K1 has two consumers — because merging the store is weeks of work and merging the cassette is hours.

duplications.problem: Fly.io deployment scaffolding written again from scratch in six repositories.

sideA.what: `flyio/` with nine configuration files, an infrastructure analysis and a document about secrets

sideB.what: The same thing, six files, the same directory layout and the same two documents

duplications.resolution: Six infrastructure analyses and eight documents about secrets describe the same pattern. The configuration code has to stay per-repo, but **the documents should be one guide** — and that guide already exists in the constitution. Replace the six copies with a link.

duplications.problem: Sixteen `ci.yml` files and **no two of them are identical**.

sideB.what: The same thing, in a different order, with different action versions

duplications.resolution: The classic pattern: copy, then drift. One `workflow_call` in a hub repository and three lines in each consumer replace sixteen files that are ageing independently.

duplications.problem: The LaTeX book build chain assembled five times.

sideA.what: `main.tex` + a 291-line preamble + a Makefile + three workflows

sideB.what: The same structure, with the preamble grown to 447 lines

duplications.resolution: On top of that, three lighter variants in the decks and the articles. The preamble and the Makefile are one template repository plus `git subtree` — and the traps (the non-breaking space mapping, a missing language in `babel`) are already written up in both and **should not be discovered a third time**.

duplications.problem: {{term:mutation|Mutation testing}} configured three times, differently each time.

sideA.what: Ten analyser variants with a test that the mutant gets through

sideB.what: Four broken agent variants, each with an assigned scenario

duplications.resolution: The third version is in judge-worker. Here the duplication is **apparent and healthy**: this is a method, not code, and every domain needs its own mutants. At most, the description of the method belongs in a guide.

boundaries.title: runtime ⟂ source code
boundaries.reason: {{term:roslyn}} analysis works on source code, the replay harness on agent runs. A different moment in the cycle, a different artefact, **a different buyer**. Gluing them together gives a product you cannot describe in one sentence — and a product without one sentence has no buyer.

boundaries.title: production telemetry ⟂ test scenario
boundaries.reason: Session observability and the evaluation harness use the same words — judge, rubric, score — and measure something entirely different. There the unit is **a session that happened**, here **a scenario that was designed**. What they share is the {{term:kappa|calibration}} arithmetic, and that is all: any further shared code would be a coincidence.

boundaries.title: content ⟂ product
boundaries.reason: The book is a {{term:kernel|channel}}, not a product, and trying to turn it into a product damages it in both directions: it stops being citable and never starts earning. The book sells the library, the library sells the service — in that order and with no shortcuts.

boundaries.title: evidence system ⟂ kernel
boundaries.reason: An evidence system **consumes** a kernel and never defines it. The moment the shape of the library starts following the needs of one proving ground, the library stops being a kernel and the proving ground gains a dependency it did not want.

boundaries.title: tool ⟂ attestation
boundaries.reason: A tool that produces evidence and a service that attests to evidence are two different businesses. {{term:atestacja|Attestation}} means taking on liability, and liability needs a legal entity and insurance. You sell the tool, the client's auditor attests — the same functionality, no transferred risk.

openPaid.rule:
**Open** — what you run locally and what produces a file.
**Paid** — what remembers, compares, integrates with your systems and survives an audit.
This is the {{term:opencore|open core line}}, drawn inside one repository rather than between repositories.
openPaid.openRole: Role: channel, credibility, citability. No revenue — and that is how it is meant to be.
openPaid.paidRole: Role: revenue. A platform fee plus charging per run. Not {{term:perseat|per seat}}, not {{term:outcome|per outcome}}.
open: K1 · {{term:playhead|record/replay cassette}} — on {{term:nuget}}, a README with one claim
K3 · judge calibration — pure arithmetic, no domain
K4 · an OTLP decoder without the SDK
K0 · authservice — an image in {{term:ghcr}}, the pattern already proven
agent-eval-bench — the scenarios and the schema, not a service
CogniSim — the reference engine, without the memory layer
The books and decks — {{term:mit|CC-BY}}, in full

paid.name: Rehearsal
paid.what: Import from Jira and Azure DevOps, artefacts, a report. You pay for the input and for the memory, not for the engine.

paid.name: Evidence Pack
paid.what: Retention, the link between a run and the version of the roles and the model, an {{term:evidence|audit export}}. It answers 'prove it', not 'debug it'.

paid.name: A gate for the team
paid.what: Breach history, trends, per-repository policy, a management report. The analysers stay open.

paid.name: Workshops and rollout
paid.what: The scenario, the facilitation, a licence for the material. The shortest path to a first invoice and the only one that does not need a product.

pricingNotes: **Do not sell {{term:atestacja|compliance attestation}} without a legal entity and insurance.** A tool that produces evidence and a service that attests to evidence are two different businesses, and the move from the first to the second is irreversible and is not something you do by accident in the copy on a sales page.

**Marketing headline yes, invoice by runs.** The metric 'the independence nobody has counted' is persuasive precisely because the client does not count it today — and for exactly that reason you cannot {{term:outcome|invoice}} against it.

**Do not close the engine.** The risk of a one-person project with no customers being cloned is close to zero; the risk of a .NET enterprise bouncing off an AGPL-style licence is a certainty. This is not an ideological choice, it is a reading of the adoption precedent.
