principles.title: The bottleneck is attention, not code
principles.body: An agent will write more than you can get through — that is already true, not a forecast. Every decision in this system optimises one quantity: **how many decisions it takes to stop the portfolio rotting**. Anything that increases the number of things needing a look is a cost, even when it is free in tokens.

principles.title: A repository with no declared level of service does not exist
principles.body: Each of the forty-three repositories has exactly one {{term:poziom|attention tier}} and it is written down, not implied. The tier is not there to tell you what to work on — it is there so that you can **deliberately not work on** twenty repositories in a given week and not feel guilty about it.

principles.title: The tier follows blast radius, not affection
principles.body: A kernel consumed by five systems has a {{term:blast|blast radius}} of five; a playground has zero. That is why a two-hundred-line library can matter more than a twenty-thousand-line application, and why extracting something as a kernel **raises** the demands on it instead of lowering them.

principles.title: A public repository is a promise; a private one is not
principles.body: Opening a repository takes on an obligation: the README has to be true, CI green, the licence present, and an issue has to get an answer. So the default decision is **private**, and opening is a separate act with a checklist — not a reflex after the first successful build.

principles.title: A constitution instead of memory
principles.body: The most expensive failure in this estate is an agent reconstructing architectural rules from whatever code it happens to see, instead of reading the ones already written down. So the rules live in one repository, are installed as {{term:plugins}}, and every new project starts by loading them.

principles.title: Extraction by artefact, never by source
principles.body: When a second system wants the same service, it gets a **versioned image or package**, never a submodule or a project reference. One codebase, N independent instances, no shared runtime and no shared root of trust. This pattern has worked once and is documented — the rest of the consolidation is repetitions of it.

principles.title: Do not fill empty tables with plausible numbers
principles.body: Several repositories in this portfolio have fully designed experiments and empty results tables. **That emptiness is functional.** A number nobody has measured is worse than no number, because it looks like evidence, it survives review, and it comes back a year later as somebody else's citation.

principles.title: Every ritual leaves an artefact
principles.body: A ritual that leaves nothing in the repository is a meeting with yourself. A review ends in a commit, a log entry or a closed issue — and that, not the feeling of having done something, is the evidence that the ritual happened.

principles.title: Closing counts as much as starting
principles.body: Archiving a repository is an outcome, not a failure. A repository that has no buyer, is not a channel and is not a kernel costs attention and returns nothing — and the only way to make it stop costing is to close it openly, with one paragraph of explanation in the README.

tiers.name: Foundation
tiers.definition: The things everything else depends on. A failure here propagates to the rest of the portfolio, so the strictest regime applies, however small the repository itself is.
tiers.slo: Red CI fixed the same day. An issue from an outsider gets an answer within 48 h. A release is always tagged and described in the CHANGELOG.
tiers.budget: Up to 40% of portfolio time. Always takes precedence over everything below.

tiers.name: Product under construction
tiers.definition: Four things that have, or could have, a named buyer. This is the only tier where new functionality is built — everything below is maintained, not developed.
tiers.slo: Red CI within 72 h. An active quarterly goal with a 'done when' test. A public README that matches the facts, including a list of what does not work yet.
tiers.budget: Up to 40% of the time, but never on more than two at once — the rest waits in the queue.

tiers.name: Channel
tiers.definition: Artefacts that accumulate reach without further work: books, decks, knowledge bases, research work, channel material. They do not earn and are not meant to — they are the only route by which anyone finds the rest.
tiers.slo: The build has to pass, because publication is automatic. Content touched on its own rhythm, not a weekly one. No commitment to answering issues.
tiers.budget: Up to 15% of the time, in blocks — a fragmented hour does not move a chapter forward.

tiers.name: Maintenance
tiers.definition: Works, is built, is not being developed. Usually large systems that took the most investment and from which what is drawn today is mainly evidence of skill and code for kernels.
tiers.slo: No time commitment on CI. Dependency updates grouped monthly. New functionality only when it is a test of a kernel's portability.
tiers.budget: Up to 5% of the time, in one monthly block for the whole group at once.

tiers.name: Frozen
tiers.definition: Finished, abandoned or somebody else's. No work beyond security. Candidates for archiving — and archiving here is an outcome, not a failure.
tiers.slo: None. Dependabot switched off, or grouped into one PR per quarter. Issues switched off wherever the repository has no maintainer.
tiers.budget: Zero. One quarterly review of the whole group decides what to archive.

cadence.what: Go through **only** the notifications from P0 and P1. Open nothing else. If anything is red on those seven repositories, you do nothing else today.
cadence.output: Zero or one fixing commit. No task list for tomorrow — this is not planning.
cadence.timebox: A hard 10 minutes. After the tenth minute you close the tab, even halfway through.

cadence.what: Run the health collector and read **only the breached rows**. Against each breach write one of three decisions: fixing it this week, dropping the repository's tier, archiving it.
cadence.output: An updated `data/repos/*.json` and a recomputed manifest — which means this page tells the truth on Monday.
cadence.timebox: 30 minutes. Fixes do not fit in that window and are not meant to.

cadence.what: One block on **one** thing from P1 — the one closest to its 'done when' test. You do not start a second, even if the first gets blocked; you write the blockage down and end the block.
cadence.output: A commit, or a 'blocked by X' entry in the repository's decision log.

cadence.what: A second product block plus one channel session: a chapter, an episode, a post. The product block always comes first — the channel is more enjoyable and would eat the lot.
cadence.output: Progress in P1 **and** one channel artefact. One without the other is a failed Saturday.
cadence.timebox: 2 h product + 1 h channel, in that order.

cadence.when: Last Sunday of the month · 90 minutes
cadence.what: The dependency train: one run across the whole of P3 at once. Grouped Dependabot, one merge per repository, no reading diffs where CI is green and tests exist.
cadence.output: The bot queue in P3 zeroed. A list of the repositories where CI fell over — those come back as individual tasks.
cadence.timebox: 90 minutes for eleven repositories. If it does not fit, the problem is the lack of grouping, not the lack of time.

cadence.what: Consolidation review. One question: **has any kernel gained a second consumer?** A kernel with one consumer goes back to its source repository; it does not wait.
cadence.output: An updated 'consolidation' tab — or a decision to reverse the extraction, written down plainly.
cadence.timebox: 45 minutes. This is a review, not a design session.

cadence.what: Tier and archiving review. Every repository gets three questions: does it have a buyer, is it a channel, is it a kernel. Three 'no's mean P4, and a second consecutive 'no' in P4 means the archive.
cadence.output: Changed tiers in the manifest, archived repositories, one paragraph in the README of each one closed.
cadence.timebox: Half a day once a quarter. This is the only moment at which anything may be moved up.

healthChecks.name: Red CI on P0/P1
healthChecks.signal: The last run of the `ci.yml` workflow on the default branch, through the GitHub API.
healthChecks.threshold: P0: any failure at all. P1: a failure older than 72 h.
healthChecks.action: Stop everything else. Red CI on the foundation is not a task in a queue — it is the only task.

healthChecks.name: CI that does not run itself
healthChecks.signal: A workflow whose only trigger is `workflow_dispatch`, even though its badge hangs in the README.
healthChecks.threshold: Any instance at all on P0, P1 or P2.
healthChecks.action: Either restore the `push`/`pull_request` trigger, or remove the badge. A green badge for a workflow that does not run is false testimony.

healthChecks.name: Dependabot debt
healthChecks.signal: Open PRs authored by `dependabot[bot]`, counted per repository. Today: **83 open PRs across the portfolio, 76 from the bot — 92%**.
healthChecks.threshold: More than 10 in one repository, or more than 60 across the whole portfolio.
healthChecks.action: Turn on grouping in `dependabot.yml` (one PR per ecosystem, not per package) and clear the backlog in one run of the train. {{term:dependabot|Dependabot debt}} is attention debt, not security debt.

healthChecks.name: The bot drowning out the human
healthChecks.signal: The share of bot PRs among all the open PRs in a repository.
healthChecks.threshold: Above 80% on a public repository.
healthChecks.action: Clear the backlog immediately. At that share the first real pull request from a stranger will sink — and that is the one thing a repository is public for.

healthChecks.name: Age of the oldest open PR
healthChecks.signal: `created_at` of the oldest open pull request.
healthChecks.threshold: Above 90 days at any tier above P4.
healthChecks.action: Close it with a comment, or merge it. A PR older than a quarter is a decision that was not taken — and a decision not taken costs more than a bad one.

healthChecks.name: Commits with no release
healthChecks.signal: `git rev-list --count <ostatni-tag>..HEAD`.
healthChecks.threshold: Above 30 on a repository that publishes an image or a package.
healthChecks.action: Tag it. A consumer pins a version, so an unreleased commit is code nobody can use — that is, work that does not exist yet.

healthChecks.name: README drift
healthChecks.signal: The numbers in the README (tests, components, versions) compared with what is actually in the repository.
healthChecks.threshold: Any discrepancy at all on a public repository.
healthChecks.action: Fix the README, not the number. This is the same class of error as a console block nobody ran — it looks like evidence and it survives review.

healthChecks.name: Dead links
healthChecks.signal: A check of every external URL in the README and `docs/`, and of every `*.fly.dev` address promised in the documentation.
healthChecks.threshold: Any 404, and **any deployment address with nothing standing behind it**.
healthChecks.action: Fix the link, or write plainly that the deployment is described and not running. An address that does not answer is worse than no address.

healthChecks.name: Visibility that disagrees with the map
healthChecks.signal: `private` from the GitHub API compared with the `visibility` field in the manifest.
healthChecks.threshold: Any discrepancy at all.
healthChecks.action: Fix the manifest — `scripts/check-repos.mjs` does it automatically in CI. A map showing a private repo as open promises the reader a link that will return 404.

healthChecks.name: No licence file
healthChecks.signal: The presence of `LICENSE` in a public repository.
healthChecks.threshold: Absent = immediate.
healthChecks.action: Add MIT, or take the repository back to private. Public code without a licence is formally all rights reserved — nobody may legally use it, which defeats the whole point of opening it.

healthChecks.name: An experiment that has not been run
healthChecks.signal: A designed experiment with an empty results table, present in the repository for longer than a quarter.
healthChecks.threshold: Two quarters without a run.
healthChecks.action: Either plan a budget and a date, or write in the document that it will not be run and why. **Do not fill the table.** There is no third option.

healthChecks.name: A kernel with one consumer
healthChecks.signal: The number of repositories actually consuming the extracted library or image.
healthChecks.threshold: Fewer than two, for two quarters after the extraction.
healthChecks.action: Reverse the extraction. A library with one user is not a kernel, it is a project moved to a different directory — and you pay for it with a separate CI, a separate release and a separate README.

wipRules: **At most two P1 repositories are active at once.** The third waits in the queue, and that is the whole rule. Four products active at the same time are four products at 25% readiness, which is zero products.

**One kernel extraction at a time.** Extraction is contagious — after the first successful one you see candidates everywhere. The second starts only once the first has **two actual consumers on main**, not in a plan.
**A new repository only after closing another** — archived, or raised to P1 and released. Thirty-five is not a target; it is a ceiling that has already been reached.
**At most one open pull request authored by a human per repository.** Two means the first is blocked, and a blocked PR rots and breeds a merge conflict.
**You do not open a repository until it passes the opening checklist.** Licence, a README that matches the truth, green CI, a secret scan, closed issues. Opening is a commitment, not an event.
**You do not start an experiment you have nothing to pay for.** A designed and unrun experiment is debt that lights up in the health check every quarter until a decision is taken.

**A blocking hour is a lost hour.** If a block gets stuck, you write the blockage down and finish — you do not switch to another repository. Switching turns one blocked thing into two half-finished ones.

automation.name: The portfolio manifest as the source of truth
automation.how: Every repository has two files: `data/repos/<slug>.json` in Polish and its twin `data/en/repos/<slug>.json` in English. `scripts/build-manifest.mjs` merges both trees into the one `site/data/portfolio.json` that is served. Adding a repository is two new files, not an HTML edit — one alone fails, because the validator compares the trees element for element. CI rejects a manifest that fails the schema, referential integrity, or parity between the languages.

automation.name: A drift validator on the generated manifest
automation.how: `build-manifest.mjs --check` regenerates the file and stops the build if the committed version differs. The same {{term:drift|pattern}} that architecture-standards uses to police the plugin catalogue — and the same class of problem.

automation.name: A check on repository visibility and existence
automation.how: `check-repos.mjs` asks the GitHub API about every slug in the manifest and stops the build when a repository has disappeared, been archived or changed visibility. It is the one check a person will not perform reliably across forty-three entries.

automation.name: The nightly health collector
automation.how: One scheduled workflow in the hub repository: for each slug it fetches CI status on the default branch, open PRs split between bot and human, the age of the oldest PR, commits since the last tag, the date of the last push, visibility and archive status. Thresholds are **per tier** — red CI on P0 breaches immediately, on P3 only after sixty days. It writes `data/health.json`, recomputes the manifest and opens **one** issue for the whole estate, which closes itself once the thresholds come back under the line.

automation.name: Grouped Dependabot
automation.how: One PR per ecosystem instead of one per package, through `groups:` in `dependabot.yml`, plus a weekly interval instead of a daily one. Across the twelve repositories that have Dependabot today, that is the difference between ten PRs and one.
automation.where: to roll out: <repo>/.github/dependabot.yml in every P1–P3 repository

automation.name: A reusable CI workflow
automation.how: One `ci-dotnet.yml` with `workflow_call` in the hub repository; every .NET repository calls it in three lines instead of copying sixty. Today `ci.yml` exists in sixteen repositories and each one is a separate copy.

automation.name: A secret scan everywhere there is code
automation.how: `secret-scan.yml` is in eight repositories today. It should be in every one that holds code — this is exactly the kind of check whose absence you notice once, and by then it is too late.

automation.name: Tag-driven deployment
automation.how: Pushing a `v*` tag runs the tests, detects the changes against the **previous tag**, builds the images and deploys in dependency order. A service whose Fly app does not exist is always selected — that is the one thing that lets you stand up a cold estate with a single tag. {{term:tagdeploy|The pattern}} is documented and works in eight repositories.

automation.name: Agent plugins as the way to distribute rules
automation.how: Architectural rules are installed by the agent, not pasted into the prompt — this is the {{term:skille|skills system}} applied to your own standards. Every P0–P2 repository names in `AGENTS.md` the plugin the agent is to load before working, so that a fix to a rule propagates without touching forty-three files.

automation.name: Image publication independent of deployment
automation.how: The job that publishes an image to {{term:ghcr}} must not require any secret that the deployment needs — otherwise someone who never stands up their own instance cannot release a version for consumers. This error happened once in this estate and was fixed the same day.

automation.name: The profile's project table generated from the manifest
automation.how: The profile README maintains the project list by hand today and it has already drifted: it points at a repository that is not on the map, and omits four that are. That table should be generated from the same manifest, by the same drift validator.

automation.name: The agent start-up playbook
automation.how: One saved prompt per type of task — review, modernisation, recovery — plus a rule about where the agent writes the result: always in `docs/architecture/` of the **target repository**, never in the rules repository. Without that, the rules collect content about other people's systems and stop being rules.

steps: Add `LICENSE` to every public repository that lacks one, or take it back to private.
Fix the project table in the profile README — today it points at a repository that is off the map and omits four that are on it.
Restore automatic triggers everywhere a CI badge hangs over a workflow that only runs by hand.
Turn on Dependabot grouping in the twelve repositories that have it, and clear the backlog in one run.
Archive the two dead repositories off this map that are sitting on forty-one bot PRs from 2020–2023.
quarterPlan.doneWhen: The health collector passes with no breaches, and the number of open PRs across the portfolio drops below twenty.

quarterPlan.goal: The first kernel has two consumers on main.
steps: Push the record/replay cassette to NuGet under its final name, checked in the registry beforehand.
Wire it into the evaluation harness — that is the consumer which, without it, cannot tell a regression from model randomness.
Wire it into the cheapest agent playground as a portability test; if it does not go in within an hour, the kernel is not neutral enough and goes back for a fix.
Write a README with one thesis and no commercial intent.
quarterPlan.doneWhen: Two repositories reference the published package and their tests pass without a network.

steps: Pick one reference implementation of `ServiceDefaults` from the four that have drifted apart, and write the decision down.
Extract from it a package containing only what is genuinely shared: authentication, database provider selection, rate limiting and background migration.
Switch two systems over, starting with the one closest to the reference version.
Add an architecture test that keeps the package from referencing anything domain-specific — that rule in prose has already failed twice in this estate.
quarterPlan.doneWhen: Two systems build on the package, and their local `ServiceDefaults` has slimmed down to the genuinely specific parts.

quarterPlan.goal: One experiment gets run and written up.
steps: Pick the cheapest of the designed experiments — the one that needs no provider, because it measures a property of the topology, not of the model.
Run it, keep the **raw event streams**, not just the summary rows; recovering traces by re-running is expensive.
Enter the results in the table that was empty, and mark plainly which numbers are hard and which are indicative.
Publish it as a post or a preprint — that is the only channel that reaches the buyer in risk and compliance.
quarterPlan.doneWhen: One empty table in the portfolio stops being empty, and does so without a single number nobody measured.

quarterPlan.goal: One product has a named buyer and a price.
steps: Pick one of the four P1 projects and drop the other three to P3 for the length of this horizon.
Write the one sentence you sell it with, and test it on five people in the target role — not on engineers.
Build the paid layer: retention, history, export. Not functionality — memory.
Price it per run or per retention slot, never {{term:perseat|per seat}} and never {{term:outcome|by outcome}}.
quarterPlan.doneWhen: There is a page with a price on it, and at least one person outside the circle of friends has asked for access.

quarterPlan.goal: The portfolio shrinks to a size that can be managed.
steps: Archive everything that has answered 'no' to all three questions for two quarters: buyer, channel, kernel.
Consolidate what survives into at most twenty active repositories.
Rewrite the README of every closed repository into one paragraph: what it was, what it proved, why it ended.
Reassign attention tiers to what is left — last quarter's tiers are already out of date.
quarterPlan.doneWhen: There are no more than twenty active repositories, and each has a written tier and a passing health check.

body: What a given set of tools treats as the **unit of work**. In cluster A the unit is an *agent run* — a sequence of model calls ending in a result. In cluster B the unit is a *code file or a policy*. In cluster D — a *document for a reader*.

The substrate decides what can be shared, and it is the only criterion that predicts it. Two projects on the same substrate can share a store, share scoring and share replay. Two on different substrates can share nothing — apart from infrastructure that does not know what they are.

The practical consequence: the question 'can these be joined up' always comes down to the question 'do both record the same thing'. If not, the shared code will carry both vocabularies in its signatures at once and will stop being anything at all.
glossary.where: the basis of the whole split into clusters A–F

body: An extracted library or service used by **at least two** projects at once. It comes about by lifting a component that is already domain-neutral into a separate artefact with its own name, its own versioning and its own CI.

A kernel lowers the cost of maintenance and works as a channel. **It is never a sales offer.** 'A platform that can do six things' has no buyer, because it answers no particular pain — and a buyer pays for pain, not for capabilities.

A sufficient test: if after extraction the library has one user, it is not a kernel but a project moved to a different directory. If a domain type appears in its public signatures, it is not a kernel but the domain under another name.

The layer that records and replays model calls, hooked in at the {{term:ichatclient}} level. The key is a hash of the request — the same messages and the same options return the same recorded response. Three modes: `Record`, `ReplayOnly`, `ReplayOrRecord`.

It closes a gap that checkpoint replay closes in none of the six frameworks examined (Agent Framework, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, Pydantic AI): restoring a checkpoint runs the graph again but **does not serve the earlier model responses**. It replays the orchestration, not the model.

It gives four things at once: a mode that needs no API key, hermetic tests, a free rehearsal of the protocol before any budget is spent, and reproducibility of every recorded run. The key covers `ChatOptions.Instructions` as well — without that one agent would replay the other's response, and that was a real bug found during the build.
glossary.where: cognitive-multi-agent-simulation, `kernel/replay/` — the only component already physically extracted inside the repository

body: The project {{term:aspire}} generates in every new solution: telemetry, health checks, resilience, service discovery. In the template it is about a hundred lines, and it is copied rather than referenced.

There are **ten** such projects in this portfolio. In four of them the same files have grown in parallel: `AuthenticationExtensions.cs`, `DatabaseProviderExtensions.cs`, `RateLimitingExtensions.cs`, `MigrationBackgroundService.cs` — and every copy is different by now. This is not code copied once; it is four independently maintained implementations of one thing.

That makes it the largest unrecognised kernel in the portfolio and at the same time the hardest: there is no single version to lift out — you have to pick a reference one and unwind the divergence in the rest.

A store that holds a **run**, not individual spans. The distinction is deliberate: a span store is a tracing backend, and the Aspire dashboard already is one — whereas every research question ('which topology plans better', 'is this prompt change a regression') is about the run as a whole.

The columns are the things you group by: topology, model, ensemble and its {{term:fingerprint}}, turn count, tokens, time. Artefacts sit there as JSON, because they are read whole and never queried field by field.
The same data shape arose independently twice: once as a research feature, once as the permission gate's {{term:audit|audit trail}}. It is one of the three duplications worth merging.

The layer that compares many runs. It reports **medians and spreads, never means and never the best run** — a best-of-N comparison measures luck, and a mean over a long-tailed latency distribution measures the tail, not the typical case.

The discipline is enforced by the shape of the type, not by convention: the comparison type has no field into which the best run could be put. That is the right way to enforce a methodological rule — a rule stated in prose will not survive a deadline.

A registry of versioned agent role definitions together with the fingerprint ({{term:fingerprint}}) of the exact set that produced a given run. Without it you cannot say whether the difference between two runs comes from a prompt change, a model change or randomness.
A hash that uniquely identifies the set of definitions used in a run. It lets you answer the question 'are these two results comparable at all' before you start comparing them.
Without a fingerprint a results table is a set of numbers with no common basis — and that is worse than no table, because it looks like evidence.
glossary.where: a column in the run store; a precondition for every experiment

body: The same input state gives the same result. Language models are non-deterministic by nature, so without a replay layer two runs of the same test can differ with no change in the code at all.

The practical consequence is sharp: **an evaluation harness without replay cannot tell a regression from the model's randomness.** You run a few hundred assertions, three fail — and you do not know whether it was a change in the code, a change in the prompt, or the model having a worse day. That is exactly the gap {{term:playhead}} closes.
glossary.where: the basis of kernel K1; the gap in agent-eval-bench

body: A test that cannot touch the network. Not 'usually does not touch it' — cannot, because in replay mode the layer it would have to go out through has nowhere to call.

That distinction settles two things at once: the test suite will not quietly start costing money, and CI will not quietly start failing because a provider had an incident. A missing recording ends in an exception, not in improvisation.
glossary.where: a condition every stage of the agent projects has to meet

body: The variants of how agents hand the floor to one another: who speaks next, when the run ends, whether there is an arbiter. Sequential, Concurrent, RoundRobin, Director, Handoff, Magentic.
Running the same scenario on each of them and comparing the results is also a ready-made ablation plan — comparing topologies is the same experiment as comparing architectures.

The key cost observation: the number of model calls is **a property of the topology, not of the model**. You can count it with a fake model in a second and the result will be identical to a real provider's. Quality is not.

Deliberately introducing small faults into the code to see whether the tests catch them. A mutant that survived means a test that guards nothing. 'Zero survivors' means every fault introduced was caught.

It is the only method that measures **the quality of the tests** rather than the quality of the code — and so the only argument that green CI actually means something. In this portfolio it is applied in three places: to the analysers, to the LLM judge and to the CI gate.

The C# compiler exposed as a library: it gives access to the syntax tree and the full semantic model. A Roslyn analyser 'knows' that a given name is a particular type from a particular namespace — unlike text matching.

That is the difference between an architecture gate and competitors built on `glob` and `grep`: precision in exchange for being single-language, which puts a hard ceiling on the size of the market. That ceiling has to be accepted knowingly, not discovered a year in.
A CI gate that checks only what changed in a given pull request, not the whole repository.

Without it every new rule lights up thousands of warnings in existing code, the team switches the tool off in the first week, and that is the end of the deployment. Diff scoping is not a performance optimisation — it is a condition of adoption.
The answer to the question 'which lines in this file were written by AI and which by a human', at the level of a diff or a commit. There is no industry standard for it today.

The first attempt in copilot-scope did not pass its own audit: it was a per-session average computed by the editor, not line-by-line attribution. That result is worth more than a successful deployment — it shows that the signal has to be designed from scratch, and that the author can throw out his own work.
glossary.where: archgate (designed from scratch), copilot-scope (the failed first attempt)

body: A record of what the agent did, when, and under which permission.

Two purposes are worth telling apart, because they have different retention and format requirements. *Debugging* answers an engineer's 'why did this not work' — it needs detail and a short window. *Evidence* answers a lawyer's 'prove the agent acted within its permission' — it needs immutability, a link to the version and long retention.
The observability category closed around the first. The second was left empty, because that is not those teams' buyer.
glossary.where: AgentHelm; the same data structure as the run store

body: A mechanism for supplying an agent with instructions and procedures on demand, instead of pushing everything into the system prompt. The agent loads a skill's description only when it is needed — progressive disclosure.
The format already exists in this portfolio and is ready: {{term:plugins}}. Every further repository that builds its own skill mechanism instead of using it is a duplication.
glossary.where: architecture-standards; a candidate common format for every agent in the portfolio

body: A format for packaging organisational rules and procedures in a shape a coding agent can install — Claude Code, Copilot, VS Code and any other compatible client. Plus a catalogue generator and a drift validator in CI, that is, a mechanical check that the published plugins still agree with the source.

The loop is closed: a policy is at once documentation to read and a rule the agent loads before it works. It is the only artefact in the portfolio that changes how the rest of the portfolio gets built.
glossary.where: architecture-standards — five plugins, a catalogue, a drift validator

body: A CI job that regenerates a derived file from the source and breaks the build if the version in the repository differs. It does not check correctness — it checks that what was generated and what was committed are the same thing.

The pattern is cheap and solves exactly one class of problem: files that have to be committed (because something reads them without a build) but are generated. The plugin catalogue, the portfolio manifest, the repository table in the README — all three are the same case.

The successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, formed out of their convergence. It gives typed workflows, checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, declarative definitions in YAML and native {{term:mcp}} support. Available for .NET and Python.
In a well-built system it is isolated to a single project — every other service treats a run as data. That makes swapping the engine real rather than theoretical.

The abstraction from `Microsoft.Extensions.AI` representing 'something you send messages to and which sends a response back'. Independent of the model provider and shared across the whole .NET AI ecosystem.

The cassette hooks in at exactly this level — which is why it knows nothing about the domain, and why it can be extracted in hours rather than weeks. The choice of seam decides the cost of extraction more than the quality of the code does.
glossary.where: the layer kernel K1 runs on

body: The standard for connecting tools and data sources to models. Handed to the Agentic AI Foundation at the Linux Foundation; over a thousand public servers.

It has two uses for this portfolio: the evaluation harness tests an agent through an MCP adapter, and the hosted product imports a real backlog from Jira or Azure DevOps over MCP. The first is technical, the second is commercial.
glossary.where: agent-eval-bench; the integration channel for the hosted product

body: The standard for communication between an editor and a coding agent — 'LSP for agents'. Co-authored by Zed and JetBrains.

A market note: the ACP agent registry is already official and built into Zed and JetBrains, so the protocol layer has stopped being a free niche. What is left is not the protocol but **permission policy and evidence** — and that is a different product from a cockpit.
Standardised telemetry attribute names for model calls (`gen_ai.*`). All of them still carry draft status — none is stable.

Normalising telemetry from several providers is exactly the same work, done privately. It is a credibility route — a proposal to the conventions, a talk, a post — not a product. The value lies in a name landing in a document that will outlive the project.

The orchestration layer for running several services locally at once, with a telemetry dashboard. It generates a {{term:servicedefaults}} project in every solution, and that convenience is precisely the source of the largest duplication in this portfolio.
A deliberate limit: Aspire describes development, and production is described by separate deployment files. Keeping the two apart costs a little repetition and saves divergence between environments.
OIDC is a sign-in standard built on top of OAuth 2.0; JWKS is a published set of public keys used to verify token signatures. RS256 is the signing algorithm.

It has one non-obvious operational consequence: a service whose JWKS all the others fetch sits on the request path of every one of them — and not only on the first request, because validators refresh their cache. Such a service **cannot scale to zero**.
glossary.where: authservice (K4) and the six systems that consume it

body: GitHub's container image registry. Publishing a versioned image there turns an internal component into an artefact another project uses **without copying code** — an artefact dependency instead of a source one.
It is the only completed extraction in this portfolio and the pattern to repeat: one codebase, N independent instances, no shared runtime and no shared root of trust.
glossary.where: authservice v0.3.1 and five other images

body: The package registry for .NET. For an engineer with no distribution and no recognisable name it is the cheapest way to become findable — the effect compounds with no further work, unlike a post that has to be promoted every week.
The state of things: three package identifiers are declared across the whole portfolio and **none is published**. It is the cheapest unused channel on the entire map.
glossary.where: archgate declares three packages; the distribution axis, row 01

body: A pipeline triggered by pushing a `v*` tag, not by pushing to a branch. Change detection compares against the **previous tag**, not the previous commit; the image is built once and deployed many times; deployment order follows the dependencies, and a service skipped in the middle of the chain does not block what comes after it.

The rationale is one sentence: a deployment should be an act, and the tag is its record. The rule easiest to forget: a service whose Fly app does not exist must always be selected — that is the only thing that lets you stand up a cold estate with one tag.
glossary.where: architecture-standards / FLY-IO-DEPLOYMENT.md; seven repositories have this workflow

body: Open engine, closed commercial layer. The line runs not between repositories but inside one of them: **what is open is what you run locally and what produces a file; what is paid for is what remembers, compares, integrates with your systems and survives an audit.**
In short: the library records, the service remembers and exports. That one line settles every borderline case without discussion.
Permissive licences — they allow use, modification and commercial embedding. MIT for code, CC-BY for specifications and documents.

The choice rests on adoption precedent, not on ideology: AGPL-style licences effectively block adoption in .NET enterprise organisations, which is exactly the target segment. The risk of a solo project with no customers being cloned is close to zero; the risk of an enterprise bouncing off the licence is a certainty.
glossary.where: thirty-seven repositories on an MIT-family licence; six with no licence file

body: The per-seat model broke down once one agent started doing the work of several people. Pure per-seat is now a small fraction of the agent tooling market, and the dominant pattern is a platform fee plus a metered layer.
The conclusion for this portfolio: bill per run or per place in retention, not per user.
glossary.where: the rationale for the pricing model

body: You pay for the result, not for access. It works only when the outcome is countable inside the product, resistant to gaming, controlled mostly by the software **and already measured by the customer**.

The last condition is the blocking one here and is worth understanding precisely: the metric 'undeclared dependencies per run' is convincing exactly because nobody counts it today — and for the same reason you cannot invoice against it. It works as a headline; the invoice goes per run.
glossary.where: the pricing model for the hosted product

body: Handing over recorded runs in a format an auditor accepts: with retention, with the run tied to the version of the roles and of the model, with reproducibility. It answers 'prove it', not 'debug it'.

It is the only place in this portfolio where {{term:determinizm}}, the {{term:audit|audit trail}} and the {{term:fingerprint}} meet in one product — and so the most defensible position this map contains.
glossary.where: a paid product; fed by K1 and K3

body: Certifying that a system meets a requirement — as distinct from supplying a tool that produces the evidence. Attestation means taking on liability, and liability requires a legal entity and professional indemnity insurance.

The right first move: **you sell the tool, the customer's auditor attests.** The same functionality, no transferred risk. That decision can be changed later and is not reversible, so it is not one to make by accident in the copy on a sales page.
glossary.where: a constraint on the audit product

body: The person responsible for how large planning events run and for coordination between teams.

A caveat that has to be said plainly: in an AI-native model teams shrink and cycles shorten — so the budget for this particular role is under pressure. Which makes the dress rehearsal a good way in and a bad foundation.
glossary.where: a buyer on the distribution axis

body: Certified consultants who roll SAFe out in organisations. They have a relationship with the buyer that a solo builder will not build — which makes them a channel, not competition.
The window is now: the whole training portfolio is moving to AI-native releases, so consultants are looking for fresh material and are unusually open to somebody else's tool.
glossary.where: a channel on the distribution axis

body: The declared level of service for a repository: how much attention it gets, how fast red CI is answered, whether its dependabot is looked at at all.

A repository with no declared tier gets attention whenever you happen to think of it — that is, at random, and in practice once it has already broken. The tier is above all a tool for deliberately **not dealing with** twenty repositories in a given week, without guilt.
A hard cap on the number of things started and unfinished. Not a guideline — a limit: a breach is a signal to **close** something, not to work longer.

One person's portfolio does not die from a shortage of ideas. It dies from forty-three things started and none finished — because each of them levies a tax on attention whether or not you are working on it.

Open pull requests from the bot that updates dependencies. A single one is free; a hundred change the nature of the repository — the list of PRs stops being something you read and becomes something you scroll past.

The concrete cost: when the PRs hold nothing but the bot, the first genuine pull request from a person will sink and go unnoticed. Dependabot debt is not security debt — it is attention debt, and it is the debt that ruins the channel, not the dependencies.
How many other things break when this one breaks. A kernel consumed by five repositories has a radius of five; a playground has a radius of zero.

Blast radius, not size and not recency, should decide the {{term:poziom|attention tier}}. That is why a small library is sometimes more important than a large application — and why extracting a kernel **raises** the demands on it rather than lowering them.
glossary.where: the criterion for assigning an attention tier

body: A measure of agreement between two raters, corrected for the agreement that would arise by chance. Used to calibrate an LLM judge against a human: without it 'the judge scored 8/10' is a number with no unit.
It is exactly the kind of rigour that separates an evaluation harness from a dashboard — and at the same time the thing almost nobody does, because it requires labelling a sample by hand.

Scaled Agile Framework — a method for scaling agile work across many teams. Its central event is PI Planning: two days, several dozen to several hundred people, producing objectives, dependencies and risks.

Two things matter for this portfolio: the event is expensive and countable (which gives the dress rehearsal its price), and its product is **artefacts, not a transcript** — which sets what the programme should return in the first place.
